*Readings of the 4h build* (where the specification was silent):

* `sealoop`'s L18 rebuilds the record stream with the prelude calls inlined and then reads it
  again through its existing reader; a file with no prelude function is processed exactly as
  before.
* Capacity: the nodes counted are the copies, the `tmp`s, the `iblk` and the `xblk`, and the
  replaced `call` stops counting; the prelude functions' own nodes and locals are not counted
  (they are dropped). Both limits are checked as each node or local is added and reported at the
  position P of the outermost inlined call. Each inline call copies the whole body, so about 188
  calls of `setdiff` in one program reach `program too large: nodes`, which LANGUAGE.md §3.1's
  capacity bound allows.
* The no-cycle check of the prelude's call graph runs along the inline stack.
* The `.i` loop variables are numbered at their `forr` (post-order), literally as §3.5.4 says: in
  `meshgrid`, `xj` is `.i5`, `i` is `.i6` and `j` is `.i7`.
* Under a `bind`, the release of an owned argument `tmp` comes after `mov D R1`; under an `eval`
  of an owned result, the argument `tmp` is released first, then R1.
* Several `iret`s of one `iblk` share R1 … Rk, numbered at the first `iret`'s `mov`.
* An empty `_` arm under L16 still writes its `else B`.
* Every site in inlined code carries the call's line, the sites of `chkb`, `rcount`, `iaddc` and
  `rcall` included.
* `sealower`: R1 … Rk are new registers that the `iblk` pushes on its value stack; after `enddo`,
  a destination D > 0 gets `mov D R1`, except when the frame is an `asg` whose x1 equals D (rule
  15 (d)'s V, or the `asg set` of a scalar `ref` parameter), where R1 replaces V with no `mov`.
  Under a `tbind`, `mov L Ri` comes before T2's releases; a scalar-local `tasg` component is
  handed to rule 2 (d)'s step. An `iret` releases the scope entries down to the scope height
  recorded at the `iblk`'s entry. The rule-12 pre-pass does not visit `iblk` bodies. R30's parent
  inline `xblk` is found as "last sibling + 1".

**Projected for phase 5** (the phase-5 specification, Decisions 58–73; estimates of own lines
from the sizes measured after 4h, ±30 %). Phase 5 changes `seaopt`, `seagen_a64` and `seagen_x64`
and adds the shared module `passes/lib/ralloc.bas` (§4.9.2), built into both code generators; no
other pass changes, and no `DATA` line is added (no contract change).

* `seaopt` (§5.8): the analyses (loops, definitions, array registers, private bases) 150–250; the
  fact walk with check and overflow elimination (T1) 450–700; division by constants and `f64`
  division by powers of two, with its own 128-by-64-bit limb division for the magic numbers (T2, L-am:
  loading `limb` would cost 801 lines) 150–250; value numbering, redundant loads and copy
  propagation (T3) 150–250; if-conversion (T4) 40–70; promotion (T5) 120–200; copy-on-write
  versioning with the block copier (T6) 200–320; strength reduction (T7) 150–250; hoisting and
  constant commoning (T8) 200–320; unswitching (T9) 100–180; clean-up, renumbering and the table

Three readings. (1) **`seacheck` passes 7 000 built lines at the upper end of its increment, and no
behaviour-neutral compaction closes the gap.** Its earlier increments landed inside their estimates
(4g 594 against 600–950 for 4g and 4h), so the upper end is a real possibility. The patterns that
freed 690 lines in `sealower` at 4h-0 mostly do not apply: `seacheck` is written in the `SUB`/`CALL`
style (124 `SUB`s, 709 `CALL`s, 9 `GOSUB`s, no `DEF`), so C1 (fall-through entries and tail calls of
`GOSUB` code), C4 (multi-line `DEF` text helpers) and C6 (one shared child-evaluation `GOSUB` loop)
have nothing to work on; C2 (merging consecutive `REM` lines up to 250 bytes, every comment's text
kept) is measured on its 4 979 own lines (598 `REM` lines, 319 of them following another) at 219 lines
at most; C3 and C5 (lookups and validation predicates) where they apply 0–80; so 150–300 in all,
which still leaves the upper end at 7 146. But `seacheck`'s remaining work is the smallest of the
front end (850), and with it the pass passes both 9 000 conditions even at the upper end with no
compaction (8 146 and 8 571). Decision 82 therefore treats `seacheck` as Decision 50
treats `sealower`: its 7 000 condition replaced by the two 9 000 conditions, with the C2/C3/C5
compaction as the reserve the measurement after 6c calls for; Decision 81 already moves the
whole-program analyses (about 300–500 lines) to `seaname`, which has the room. (2) **`sealoop` fits
phase 6 but not phase 6 and phase 7's fusion at the stress view** (9 089 > 9 000 at the upper end):
this is exactly the question Decision 56 left to the gate after phase 6 (the fusion seam), and the
gate below decides it; because `sealoop`'s increments have been erratic (§2.7, "Projected for 4h":
4f 271 against 600–900, 4g-2 774 against 315–510, misses of up to +52 % over the upper end), the

pass ahead of `sealoop` would read `sea.hir`, where elemental applications are still `emap` records

gates after 4h no longer limit; its longest line is at the 255-byte limit (no line of it can grow, as

**Reading.** With fusion in `sealoop` (Decision 94 (c)) the gate after phase 7 fails at every end
of the estimate: 8 082–9 392 built, over 7 000 at both ends, and with its fixes over 9 000 at both
ends (9 082–10 392), so §7.3's split rule would fire during phase 7. In the form the gate after
phase 6 used (built after phase 6 + 1.5 × phase 7's estimate, no later remaining) it is 8 867–10 832,
failing the stress line at the upper end by 1 832. A behaviour-neutral compaction first (Decision 94
(b); `sealoop` is written in the `GOSUB` style, 637 `GOSUB`s and no `SUB`, with 617 `REM` lines of
which 287 follow another, so the patterns C1, C2, C4 and C6 that freed 690 lines in `sealower` at
4h-0 apply: an estimated 400–700) still leaves 7 382–8 992, over 7 000 at both ends and over 9 000
with the fixes at the upper end. This is the case Decision 88 wrote its consequence for (fusion
"gets a pass of its own ahead of `sealoop`, and that pass also takes L19"), now reached by the
realistic estimate instead of the 1 500 placeholder; Decision 94 (a) applies it.

With it the margins are smaller than the first draft said: `seafuse` is 4 870–7 150 after phase 7,
**150 over 7 000 at the upper end** (passing both 9 000 conditions with 850 and 350 to spare), and
`sealoop` is 108 under 7 000 at its upper end; every other program is at least 342 under 7 000
(`seagen_x64`, 6 658) and passes the two 9 000 conditions. A historical overrun of 52 % on
`seafuse`'s 7c increment (2 980 → 4 530) would put it at 8 700 built: over 7 000 and, with its fixes,
over 9 000. The estimate therefore does not show that phase 7 fits; it shows that only (a) can fit,
and that `seafuse` needs a checked point after 7c with an agreed relief (Decision 112) before 7e's
code, as below.

### 2.8 Numbers inside the compiler

The passes run as Baysick programs, whose numbers are doubles, which cannot represent ∞ or NaN,
and whose arithmetic stops the program with `OVERFLOW` or `DIVISION BY ZERO` before any check of
the result could run (Baysick LANGUAGE.md §5.4); `SQR` takes `sqrt(|x|)`. Therefore:

* **Float literals** (LANGUAGE.md §3.4) are converted to their exact IEEE bit pattern by pass 1 with exact
  big-integer arithmetic (decimal digits × 10^e as a big integer or rational in arrays of 16-bit
  limbs, then rounding to 53 bits, ties to even), and carried as hex in every later file. The
  assembler only ever sees `.quad 0x…` patterns. Test vectors for the converter come from the
  IEEE definition (hard-rounding cases included), §6.2.
* **Constant folding** (pass 2b, §3.5.7) and the evaluation of constants and constant exponents
  (pass 2a, §3.5.5) compute every `f64` operation with the exact IEEE emulation of
  `passes/lib/f64emu.bas` (`FEADD`, `FESUB`, `FEMUL`, `FEDIV`, `FESQR` on bit patterns held in
  16-bit limbs), never with Baysick's doubles. The emulation is integer arithmetic on limbs, so it
  cannot overflow or divide by zero in Baysick, and it gives the IEEE binary64 result
  (round to nearest, ties to even) for every operand, finite or not: overflow to ±∞, underflow
  to subnormals or ±0, `x ÷ 0` → ±∞ (or NaN for `0 ÷ 0`), every operation on ±∞ or NaN, −0 kept
  (`-0.0 * 1.0` folds to −0.0, `sqrt(-0.0)` to −0.0, as at run time). So no operation is
  guarded: a foldable operation (§3.5.7) folds whatever its operands' values, and every `f64`
  constant expression built from foldable operations folds to one `cf` (constant substitution
  therefore never makes the tree larger than one literal per constant use). No guard is needed
  for exactness either: the emulation is exact by construction, and the only rounding is the
  one IEEE prescribes. (Until phase 1's review the folding was guarded by exponent checks
  because Baysick's doubles could not hold the results; with the emulation those checks are
  gone.) Folding folds only subtrees that are constant on their own (`2 * pi * rpm / 60` folds
  `2 * pi` only, LANGUAGE.md §6.8).
* **NaN bits.** A folded NaN has the bits arm64 produces for the same operation (FPCR.DN = 0,
  the macOS default): if an operand is a NaN, the result is that operand with its quiet bit
  (bit 51) set, the first NaN operand in operand order (a, then b) when both are; otherwise (an
  invalid operation: ∞ − ∞, 0 × ∞, 0 ÷ 0, ∞ ÷ ∞, `sqrt` of a negative number) the default NaN
  `#7FF8000000000000`. Sea's `nan` is `#7FF8000000000000` (§3.5.5), and unary `-` flips the sign
  bit exactly, so the NaNs that occur in folding are `#7FF8000000000000` and
  `#FFF8000000000000`, and every compile-time NaN is quiet. x86_64 (SSE2/AVX2) produces the
  default NaN `#FFF8000000000000` for an invalid operation (and propagates the first NaN
  operand), so run-time NaN bits can differ between the targets and from the folded ones. This is
  never visible: a NaN prints as `NaN`, never signed (LANGUAGE.md §11.1), `write_json` writes
  `null`, comparisons and `isnan` ignore sign and payload, and no Sea operation exposes a value's
  bits (LANGUAGE.md §6.5).
* **`i64` arithmetic** beyond 2⁵³ (literals, overflow checks of folded constants, the magic
  numbers for division by a constant) uses multi-limb integer routines in the pass that needs it.
* **Constant exponents and extents** (pass 2a, §3.5.5) are evaluated with the same emulation
  (and exact `i64`), never with Baysick's floating-point operations; pass 2a writes no folded
  value, only the decision `powk k` (or the extent of a type). A NaN or ∞ exponent is not
  integral, so it is no `powk`.

### 2.9 Self-hosting is not a goal

The Sea compiler stays a Baysick program. Sea is a numerical language: it has no recursive data
structures, no maps, no pointer types — the things a compiler is made of — and adding them for
the compiler's sake would work against the language's purpose. Writing the compiler in Baysick
is also the point of the Baysick project.

### 2.10 Repository layout

| Path | Contents |
|------|----------|
| `driver/sea` | the driver (§2.2), a POSIX `sh` script |
| `passes/lib/io.bas`, `diag.bas`, `tables.bas` | shared pass modules: the header protocol and record reading and writing (§2.2, §3.1–§3.3), diagnostics (§2.6.2), the tables of §2.7 |
| `passes/lib/limb.bas`, `f64emu.bas`, `fltlit.bas` | multi-limb integers, the exact IEEE binary64 emulation and the float-literal conversion (§2.8) |
| `passes/lib/API.md`, `API-arith.md` | the interfaces of the shared modules (§2.6.3): `io`, `diag`, `tables`, `layout` (from 4g-2), `ralloc` (from 5b) and the main-program part `lirrw` (from 5c-2); `limb`, `f64emu`, `fltlit` |
| `passes/seaparse/`, `seaname/`, `seacheck/`, `seaexpand/`, `seafuse/`, `sealoop/`, `sealower/`, `seaopt/`, `sealopt/`, `seavec/`, `seagen_a64/`, `seagen_x64/` | each pass's own Baysick files (§2.1; `seaname/` from phase 4a, `sealoop/` from sub-phase 4e-0, `sealopt/` from sub-phase 5c-2, `seafuse/` and `seavec/` from phase 7), built as §2.6.3 says |
| `tools/gendata.bas` | the `DATA` generator (§2.6.3) |
| `tools/seaval.bas`, `tools/seaval.build.list` | a validator of intermediate files, used by the tests: its standard input names the format (`ast`, `res`, `hir1`, `hir`, `hirf`, `hirl`, `lir1`, `lir2`, `lir3`, `lir`; `lir2`, from sub-phase 5c-2, checked as `lir1` except for the two label rules of §3.6.2 that hold for `lir1` only, numbering by first reference and every defined label referenced, which `lir2` and `lir` do not check, L-bu; a file of format `ast` may hold only the records of §3.4's table, one of format `res` also those of §3.4.1; `hirl` the sets `H HF HL`, §3.5.9, from sub-phase 4e-0); the header, every record's fields against `passes.txt`, the pops and the tree stack (the non-node records are those §3.3 lists), and LIR register numbering and classes; it does not check the first-reference order of types, the ranges of `fid`/`cid`/`iid` references or `rcall` entry names |
| `passes/<pass>/build.list` | the modules and `DATA` blocks of each pass (§2.6.3) |
| `tools/passlines.sh` | the line count of each built pass against Baysick's limits (`make lines`) |
| `tools/math_tables.py` | the generator of `include/math_tables.inc` (§4.10.3, §4.10.6), run with `uv run --with mpmath`; `--check` verifies the committed file |
| `std/std.sea` | the prelude (§2.5) |
| `runtime/arm64_macos/`, `runtime/x86_64_linux/` | the runtimes (§4, §4.7.1); in phases 1 and 2 `rt_main.s`, `rt_out.s`, `rt_err.s`, `rt_fmt.s`, `rt_clock.s`; phase 3 adds `rt_math.s` (§4.10) |
| `Makefile.linux` | on the Linux host: `check-includes`, `all` (`build-x86_64-linux/libsea.a`), `test-rt` (§4.7.1, §6.6.1), `test-math` (`all`, then `tests/math/math_check.c` built with `gcc -O1 -ffp-contract=off` against `build-x86_64-linux/libsea.a` and run on `tests/math`, §4.10.6) |
| `include/` | the contract files (§2.6) |
| `tests/` | the tests (§6.2) |
| `build/` | the build output and installation directory: the pass executables, `sea`, `std.sea`, `errors.inc`, `limits.inc`, `libsea.a` and `libbaysickrt.a` (one of each, for the build's target), and the generated `build/gen/`; never committed |

`make` builds `build/`; `make test` runs the tests of §6.2; `make test-rt`, `make test-stage`,
`make test-math` and `make check-data` run single groups of them (§6.2); `make test-math` builds
`tests/math/math_check.c` with `xcrun cc -O1 -ffp-contract=off` against `build/libsea.a` and
compares all six elementary functions bit for bit over `tests/math/*.vec` (§4.10.6);
`make math-tables` is a developer check that is not part of `make test`: `timeout 120 uv run
--with mpmath python tools/math_tables.py --check`, which verifies the committed
`include/math_tables.inc` against its definitions (§4.10.6); `make lines` reports each built pass's
line count against Baysick's 10 000 lines, and `make check-limits` checks each built pass against
Baysick's other per-program limits of §2.7 (1000 `FOR` statements, 65 536 bytes of string
constants outside `DATA`, 255-byte lines); `make check-includes` and `make check-contracts`
check the contract files (§2.6).

**Status: agreed 2026-10-26.** This section is the specification of phase 6 of §8 (row 6,

more and no fewer (the `write_json` row is part of the library-names row until 6d: `format`,
`print` and `make_dir` leave it in 6b, `write_json` in 6d), in the same change as its tests (the
phase-4 practice); each row still in force keeps one `err_ns_*` test until its sub-phase (6b adds
`err_ns_lib_write_json`, retired in 6d):

| Sub-phase | No longer reported (implemented) | Still reported |
|-----------|----------------------------------|----------------|
| 6b | `named arguments` (every named argument: of user functions, of prelude functions, and names a library function does not take, which are now 224, L-by), `default arguments`, `f64 %`, and the library names `format`, `print`, `make_dir` | `elemental functions`, `ind2sub` (array first argument), `write_json` |
| 6c | `elemental functions` (at the item) and `ind2sub` (at the `call`) | `write_json` |
| 6d | `write_json` | — |

After phase 6 the table in force has exactly the rows of phases 8 and 9 (`@`, `handle types`,

removed rows made unreachable become reachable in the sub-phase that removes the row: 224, 225 and

wrong arguments in 6b; 228, 232, 253, and 202, 217 and 201 at an elemental call in 6c; 243 of `write_json` with a
handle type in 6d (no handle type can be written before phase 8, so its test uses a handle-typed
parameter's type in a signature only from phase 8; until then the `handle types` row reports first,
and the 243 case is tested when phase 8 removes that row). The tests of the removed words are
retired with their rows (`err_ns_lib_format` and the other `err_ns_*` goldens of the removed rows,
§6.2), and no new test names a removed word.

**Readings fixed by phase 6** (front end; lead decisions L-bw, L-bx, L-by, L-cq):

* **Defaults** (L-bx; Decision 91). `seaname` resolves a default's names (§3.4.1, as amended) and
  makes the structural checks, in the signature step of
  "Which program reports it" (§2.6.2), each function's parameters in order: after a parameter with
  a default, a parameter without one is `parameter needs a default value` (236) at its `param`
  node; a `ref` parameter with a default is `ref argument must be a mutable variable, element or
  field` (227) at the default expression (L-bw); the names in a default are resolved like those of
  a `const` item's value. The value checks are `seacheck`'s (Decision 91), made where it checks the
  `const` items (§3.4.1: before the bodies), in item order, each default exactly as the value of a
  `const` item annotated with the parameter's type (LANGUAGE.md §7.2): `not a constant expression`
  (237), `type mismatch` (201), and an evaluation that overflows or divides by zero 260 or 261, each
  at the node the `const` rules name. `sea.res` carries no outcome for a default, so `seacheck`
  evaluates a default's `i64` operations exactly itself, as it does for a `dim:` value (§2.6.2,
  "Readings fixed by 4f"), and detects 260 and 261 there; a default that names a constant uses that constant's outcome
  (Decision 25: a constant without a value, or of the error type, is not evaluated, so the default
  reports nothing more). Every error competes in source order with every other (§2.6.2, "Order
  across the two programs": a default's error on line 50 loses to a constant's on line 1). A default
  without an error is copied into every call that omits it as §3.5.4 says (the expression, with its
  own positions); its value is not written.
* **Named arguments** (L-by, L-bw). A named argument of a user or prelude function names one of its
  parameters (else `unknown parameter`, 224, at the `narg`); a name given twice is 225 at the second
  `narg`; a parameter given neither positionally nor by name and without a default is `missing
  argument` (226) at the `call`, except in a call that reports 224, where 226 is not reported (the
  unknown name may be the missing parameter, L-cy). A library function other than a prelude function takes no named
  argument other than its options (LANGUAGE.md §10, "Options"): any other name is 224 at the `narg`
  (the reading "Readings fixed by 4f" promised). A named argument whose parameter is a `ref`
  parameter is `argument for ref parameter '%s' must be marked ref` (254) at its value, since
  `name: ref x` does not parse (Appendix A's `arg`): a `ref` parameter is given positionally only,
  and LANGUAGE.md §8.1 says so (Decision 93). The arguments are checked in source order (each
  value, then its `narg`), then the call, as in 4f. Pass 2a writes the arguments in parameter order
  with the temporaries of "Evaluation order" (§3.5.5) when that order differs from the source's
  (L-cp).
* **Elemental functions and effects** (L-cq; Decision 81). `seaname` checks an `elemental fn`'s
  signature in the signature step: a `ref` parameter is `effects in elemental function` (228) at its
  `param` node, and a result type other than `f64`, `i64` or `bool` (or a tuple of those) is 253 at
  the `fn` item, after its parameters and result types, and not when a result type is the error
  type (L-dk); an elemental function without results is accepted (Decision 92). After resolving
  every body, `seaname` makes one whole-program pass over the
  resolved bodies (the *call pre-pass*) that computes, for every `fn` item, whether it has effects
  (LANGUAGE.md §8.1: it calls `printf`, `print`, `write_json`, `make_dir`, `save_svg` or a plotting
  function of §12, has a `ref` parameter, or calls a function with effects; `error` is not an
  effect; a fixpoint over the call graph), the cycles of the call graph, and the §8.6 class
  (§2.11.3). Every part of the pre-pass is iterative (a worklist for the fixpoint, an explicit stack
  for the cycle search, both in arrays sized by `SEA_LIM_SYMBOLS` and `SEA_LIM_NODES`), never
  recursive `CALL`s, so Baysick's limit of 1 024 active `CALL`s does not bound the call graph's
  depth. It reports, as body errors through the `rerr` record (§3.4.1, "Order across the two
  programs"), `effects in elemental function` (228) at every `call` inside an elemental function's
  body that calls a function with effects (a library function with effects, or a user function with
  effects; the first in source order is the one reported), and `elemental function cannot be
  recursive` (232) at the first `call`, in source order, between two functions of an elemental
  function E's strongly connected component of the call graph (E reaches the caller and the callee
  reaches E; L-di). Whether 232 is reported agrees with "a cycle through E", but the call named may
  differ: with `b` calling `a` first, `a` calling `b` and `e`, and the elemental `e` calling `a`, 232
  stands at `b`'s call of `a`, on no simple cycle through `e` (finding the first call on such a cycle
  is the directed two-disjoint-paths problem). At one `call` 228 is found before 232 (L-dk); the
  library functions with effects are those of LANGUAGE.md §8.1, every plotting function of §12
  and `save_svg` (L-dj). The pre-pass is the first check a single program makes at a `call` node, so a 228 or
  232 is found before any `seacheck` error at the same position (§2.6.2's condition for moving an
  error into `seaname`); errors earlier in source order still win.
* **Elemental calls** (`seacheck`, LANGUAGE.md §8.5, §6.3). Arguments convert to their parameters'
  types as for any call, element by element for an array argument of an elemental parameter (an
  `i64[]` to an `f64` parameter gets a `cvt`; an array of another element type is 201 at the
  argument with the parameter's type expected, `type mismatch: expected f64, found bool[2]`, L-dm).
  A call whose elemental arguments are all scalars is an ordinary `call`. Otherwise its elemental
  arguments are combined, in parameter order (the order of L19's run-time checks; the arguments are
  still checked in source order) and after the 226 check, by the shape rules of LANGUAGE.md §6.3
  with the static checks of §3.5.5 ("Static shapes"): a vector with a matrix is 202 and a mismatch
  of two compile-time extents 217, both at the `call` (an argument of the error type at an
  elemental parameter makes the call's type the error type, L-dm); its type is the result type (one
  result) or the tuple of result types (several) as arrays of the broadcast shape, fixed-size
  exactly when every array argument of an elemental parameter is fixed-size; uniform parameters
  (`str`, structs, records, arrays) take their arguments unchanged. Pass 2a writes it as a `call`
  (§3.5.6: only `sea.hir1` has a `call` of an elemental function with array arguments).
* **Library calls of phase 6.** `format(fmt, …)`: a formatting call ("Within one formatting
  call", §2.6.2), type `str`. `print(s)`: one `str`, type `void`. `make_dir(path)`: one `str`, type
  `void`. `write_json(path, value)`: `path` a `str`, `value` of any type that is not and does not
  contain a handle type (else 243 at the `call`, LANGUAGE.md §11.4), type `void`. Each with another
  number or type of arguments is 243 at the `call` (a `print` of an `i64` is `no overload of 'print'
  accepts (i64)`); a `ref` argument of `print`, `make_dir` or `write_json` is 255 naming the function (`'write_json' is
  not a ref parameter`, L-dy). `%` with an `f64` operand is `bin mod` of `f64` operands (an `i64` operand
  converted, LANGUAGE.md §6.5), element by element for arrays. `ind2sub(r, k)` with an array `r`:
  `r` and `k` are elemental (`i64` or `i64` arrays), combined as an elemental call's arguments.

#### 2.11.3 Front end and pass 2b

**`seaname`** (Decision 81). Besides the readings above: the `elemental` item is accepted (no
phase-rule error at the item), and the call pre-pass computes the **§8.6 class** of every ordinary
`fn` item of the program's file (the prelude's functions are always inlined by rule 37 and are not
classed), which `seaname` writes in its `rfn` record's `el` (2 for a function that LANGUAGE.md §8.6
(b) or (c) covers; 1 for an elemental function, which §8.6 (a) covers; 0 otherwise). On the source as
written (lead decisions L-ch, L-ci, L-cj):

* (b) **one call site**: exactly one `call` node of the whole stream names the function, counting
  calls in every function of the program's file whether or not `.main` reaches it, calls in the
  function's own body; each `call` node counts once, however often it runs (one inside a loop or in
  an elemental function's body applied to an array) (L-ch; LANGUAGE.md
  §8.6 as amended by 6a);
* (c) **not recursive** (the function lies on no cycle of the call graph of every `call` node of
  the stream, L-cj), **no loop** (its body holds no `while` and no `for` node), and **at most
  `SEA_LIM_INLINE_STMTS` statements**, counted as LANGUAGE.md §8.6 (as amended by 6a) counts them,
  one per Appendix A `statement`: every node of the kinds `let`, `var`, `asg`, `tasg`, `cstmt`,
  `while`, `for`, `match`, `break`, `continue` and `return` counts 1; an `if` counts 1 except an
  `if` that is the `else` child of an `if` (an `else if` of the same `if_stmt` chain), which counts
  0; a `block` counts 1 when it is a statement (a child of a `block`) and 0 as the body of a
  function, loop, `if` branch or `arm`; the statements inside every block count (L-ci).

**`seacheck`** checks named and default arguments, elemental calls and the library calls of phase 6
as the readings say, and writes each function's `fn` record with kind `elem` (an elemental
function), `inl` (an `rfn` with `el` 2) or `fn` (§3.5.4, contract change 2).

**`seaexpand`** implements steps 3 and 4 of §3.5.7 as written (step 4 as amended by 6a: `str` values
and `str` arrays are JSON scalars and vectors, a fixed-size array of JSON scalars is written as
`jvec (dyn e)` or `jmat (dyn e)` so the emitter's entries receive heap arrays only, L-ce, `sealoop`'s
L10 materializing the `dyn`, and a matrix of structs or records with no element is guarded to `[]`);
step 5 keeps the functions that
the kept `emap` instances name (as §3.5.7 says); its G12 validation (§3.5.7) gains, with 6c, an
`inst` record's argument count and types against its function's parameters (an elemental parameter
an array of the parameter's element type or the scalar itself, a uniform one exactly the
parameter's type) and an `emap`'s n and children against its instance, and keeps the `fn` kinds
`inl` and `elem` unchanged. Step 3 as built (L-dl): it runs at `#end` over every function in file
order, before reachability; a `call` becomes an `emap` when an argument of an elemental (`f64`,
`i64`, `bool`) parameter is an array; instances are numbered in order of first reference by an
`emap` across all functions, and step 5 renumbers the kept ones densely in that order, their types
numbered (§3.5.1) before those of the functions; the call's type must be `void` for no result and
else each result as an array of the rank of the array arguments (and two applications with one
instance must have one type), else `BAD_RECORD`; more than `SEA_LIM_SYMBOLS` instances is `program
too large: symbols` at the call. Step 4's capacity as built (L-eb): its new records count against
`SEA_LIM_NODES` (`nodes`), its `.j` locals, counted program-wide, against `SEA_LIM_SYMBOLS`
(`symbols`; a guard for its internal table, not a count of all the symbols, §3.5.9), and the
dynamic types it adds for a `dyn` and the `i64[]` of a matrix's ranges against `SEA_LIM_TYPES`
(`types`), each reported at the last position read, the `eval`'s P.

#### 2.11.4 Pass 3a: `sealoop` (L19, L20)

`sealoop`'s reader accepts, from 6c, the `inst` and `emap` records and the `fn` kind `elem`, from 6b
the kind `inl`, and from 6d the `j*` records of §3.5.5 (it rejects each of them as `BAD_RECORD`
before its sub-phase). Two rewrites are added, and L18 is generalized; none adds a record or field
to `sea.hirl` (only the HIR records `iblk` and `iret` of 4h are used).

* **L20** (LANGUAGE.md §8.6; Decision 83) `call P ty fid n` whose callee F has kind `elem` or
  `inl`: as L18, with these differences. (1) The copied nodes keep their own positions (§3.6.4
  "Sites": code inlined from the program's own functions keeps its own sites); the `xblk`, its
  `tmp`s and the `iblk` take P, and so do the `loc` records of the new `.i` locals (L-cf). (2) A
  `ref` parameter's argument is the `rarg` as written, bound by `tmp Ai = rarg …`; Ai is then a
  *ref local* of the inline block (R31). (3) A `tret C` in the copy becomes `tbind` of k new `.i`
  locals (the function's k result types) of C, followed by `iret P′ k` of their `lv`s (P′ the
  `tret`'s own position). (4) F's result type may be any type: scalars, `str`, dynamic arrays, structs,
  records, fixed-size arrays and tuples of those (an aggregate result: R32). (5) A `call` in the copy
  whose callee has kind `elem` or `inl` is rewritten by L20 again, and one of a prelude function by
  L18, so inlining is recursive; it terminates, because no elemental function lies on a cycle (232),
  an `inl` function of class (c) is not recursive, and a cycle of the reachable program always holds
  a function with two call sites (one from the cycle, one from outside it), which has class 0. When
  every call is rewritten, `sealoop` drops the prelude, `elem` and `inl` functions (their records
  from `fn` to `end`) and renumbers the remaining functions densely in their order, rewriting every
  `fid` field (L-v extended, L-cg); no `inst` or `emap` record is written to `sea.hirl` (L19 has
  replaced every `emap`), so `sealower` never sees the kinds `elem` and `inl`, `inst` or `emap`.
* **L19** (LANGUAGE.md §8.5; Decision 84) `emap P T iid n` with children a1 … an, instance I of
  function F (parameters p1 … pn, k results; an *array argument* is an argument of an elemental
  (`f64`, `i64` or `bool`) parameter whose type in I's list is an array; an argument of a uniform
  parameter, an array parameter included, is passed as `lv Ai` like a scalar one, L-dn): (1) `tmp Ai
  = ai` for every argument in order, so every argument is evaluated once, in full, before any
  element is computed (L-ck); (2) the broadcast extents of the array arguments and their run-time
  `shape mismatch` checks, exactly as rule 22 forms and checks them for an elemental `lib` with
  array operands (the same records, sites and order; the static mismatches were pass 2a's); (3) for
  each result j that the enclosing statement does not discard, a new array `tmp Rj = anew P Tj 0 r`
  of the broadcast extents (Tj the j-th result type of T; for a fixed-size Tj its home, rule 27
  (a)); a result is discarded when its component of the `tbind` or `tasg` holding the `emap` is `-`
  or `skip` (Decision 84; under an
  `eval` every result is discarded; when every result is discarded, k = 1 included, the body of
  step (4) is the inline call as a statement, `eval`, exactly as for k = 0, and nothing is stored);
  (4) rule 22's loop nest over the broadcast extents (column-major:
  the row index innermost, so the element positions run in increasing linear order), whose body reads
  each array argument's element at the position (index 0 in a dimension of extent 1, as rule 22 reads
  a broadcast operand), and calls F (`call P ty1 fid n`, ty1 F's result type) with the element
  values in the elemental positions and `lv Ai` in the uniform ones; L20 inlines that call, every
  site in it the callee's own (an error raised in the body therefore stops the program at the first
  failing element in increasing linear order, with the callee's line, LANGUAGE.md §8.5); for k = 1
  the value is stored by `est` into R1's element at the position; for k ≥ 2 the body is a `block`
  whose first statement is a `tbind` of new `.l` locals E1 … Ek (`-` for a discarded result) of the
  inline call (R8's L12 form) followed by the `est` of every kept Ej; for k = 0 (an elemental
  function without results, Decision 92) no result is allocated and the body is the inline call as
  a statement (`eval`), run for its errors only; (5) the `emap`'s value: for k
  = 1 `lv R1` (owned: T2 moves it out); for k ≥ 2, in place of the `tbind`, `tasg`, `tret` or `eval`
  that holds the `emap`, the statement forms L11 writes for `ind2sub` with k components in place of
  two (the `tbind`'s locals bound from the Rj, a `tasg`'s targets stored by rule 15 (j) with their
  `cv`, `ret k` for a `tret`, nothing kept for an `eval`). An empty broadcast shape gives empty results
  and runs no element (rule 22's guard). L19 then rewrites its output like any code (L4, L7, L10, L12,
  L20). As built (L-do): every kept result's home is allocated first, and a fixed-size broadcast's
  extents (a vector's one, a matrix's rows and columns) are then read from the first kept home; with
  no kept result they are `tmp`s of `ci` of the static extents; an `emap` under an `eval` (any k)
  becomes a new statement `block P n` in place of the `eval`, with no `xblk` of type 1; when the
  holding statement's value is a `seq` whose value is the `emap`, the `seq`'s `bind`s become
  statements of the rewrite and the `seq` is dropped.
* **`ind2sub` with an array `r`** (L-cl): a two-result elemental application of rule 36's scalar
  sequence (`imodf`, `idivf` at P) by L19's steps (1)–(5), with P's site for every check; L11 keeps
  the case of a scalar `r`. The element body (L-dp) is a `block`: `tmp d` = r's element, `tmp g` =
  k's element, `tmp f = bin mod g d`, `tmp h = lib idiv g d`, both always computed (so a discarded
  result's errors are still raised), every node at the `lib`'s position P, then one `est` per kept
  result; as a call statement (`eval`) every result is discarded and both are still computed.
* **`f64 %`**: an element-wise `bin mod` with an `f64` array operand is rewritten by L7 as every other
  element-wise operator; its scalar `bin mod` per element is lowered by rule 39 (`FMOD`, L-cm).
* **`write_json`** (6d): the `j*` records are statements `sealoop` keeps, rewriting their children
  like any expression (`jvec (dyn e)` by L10; a `jopen`'s path and a `jval`'s value as operands);
  the `fore` and `forr` loops of pass 2b's expansion are rewritten by L4 and by the scalar `forr`
  path as any loop. Validation: a `j*` record only where pass 2b writes it (the block of §3.5.7 step
  4: `jopen` first, `jclose` last, `jobj`/`jarr` balanced by `jend` within the block, a `jkey` only
  inside an object, a `jval` child of type `f64`, `i64`, `bool` or `str`, a `jvec` or `jmat` child of
  a dynamic vector or matrix type of those four element types); any violation is `BAD_RECORD`. As
  built (L-dw): a `j*` record only as a statement (a child) of a `block`, and only between a `jopen`
  and its `jclose` in file order, with no `jopen` inside that span; balance is checked per block
  (every `jobj`/`jarr` of a block closed by a `jend` of the same block, a `jkey`'s innermost open
  object opened in the same block, a block's `jclose` its last statement after its `jopen`); between
  a `jopen` and its `jclose` the statements `bind`, `tbind`, `eval`, `asg`, `tasg`, `while`,
  `break`, `cont`, `ret`, `tret`, `match` and `arm` are rejected (only `block`, `if`, `forr`, `fore`
  and the `j*` records remain, as pass 2b writes them); a `jopen`'s child is a `str`; the order of
  keys and values inside an object or array (the value grammar) is not checked.
* **Capacity**: as L18 (§3.5.9 "Capacity"): the nodes L19 and L20 add count against
  `SEA_LIM_NODES` and their `.l` and `.i` locals against `SEA_LIM_SYMBOLS`, a limit reported at the
  position of the `emap` or `call` being rewritten. A program whose inlining multiplies its size
  (an `inl` function calling another `inl` function twice, nested deeply) can reach `program too
  large: nodes`, which LANGUAGE.md §3.1's capacity bound allows.

#### 2.11.5 Pass 3a: `sealower` (rule 39, R31, R32)

* **Rule 39, library calls through the entry table** (Decision 52, specified here; §3.6.6). A node
  of the mapping table below is lowered generically from its entry's record in the `entries` block
  (`rt.inc`'s `SEA_ENTRY_LIST`, §4.8): (1) its operands left to right by rule 1, each already of the
  class the entry's Args letter names (pass 2a typed them); for the formatting entry the `fmt` record
  and the argument slot exactly as rule 8 builds them (`sa S`, the stores, `la F`); (2) `rcall
  <symbol> <site> nr <results> na <arguments>`, the site the node's line when the entry's Site is `S`
  and `-` otherwise, each result into a new register (the last one the destination of rule 2); (3) a
  `p` result is owned (rule 15 (k)), and the owned temporaries among the operands are released right
  after the `rcall` (rule 15 (b)). The rules already written for `printf`, `now`, the elementary
  functions, `error`, `args` and sorting (8, 9, 14, 24, 34, 35) stay as they are, so no earlier golden
  changes (L-cr). `sealower`'s dispatch over node kinds is an `ON … GOTO` line already 215 bytes
  long, so the new kinds (the nine `j*` records) take a second `ON` line rather than lengthening it
  (§2.7's 255-byte limit). Mapping:

  | Node | Entry | Operands |
  |------|-------|----------|
  | `lib format` (its `fmt`) | `FORMAT` | F, S as rule 8 |
  | `lib print(s)` | `PRINT` | s |
  | `lib make_dir(path)` | `MAKE_DIR` | path |
  | `bin mod` of two `f64` | `FMOD` | left, right (no site: the entry cannot fail) |
  | `jopen` / `jclose` | `JSON_OPEN` / `JSON_CLOSE` | the path / none |
  | `jobj` / `jarr` / `jend` | `JSON_OBJ` / `JSON_ARR` / `JSON_END` | none |
  | `jkey v` | `JSON_KEY` | a new `str` data record of v for each `jkey` node (rule 7's `la`; repeated keys share none, L-dv) |
  | `jval` of an `f64` / `i64` / `bool` / `str` | `JSON_F64` / `JSON_I64` / `JSON_BOOL` / `JSON_STR` | the value |
  | `jvec` / `jmat` | `JSON_VEC` / `JSON_MAT` | the array (borrowed) |

* **R31, `ref` arguments of an inline call** (Decision 83). An inline `xblk` (R26) one of whose
  `tmp`s binds a `rarg` is a call for rules 12 and 31 in every respect: the `rarg` is lowered at its
  place in the argument order exactly as for a `call` (a scalar local's slot `sa A` and its store, a
  reference local's `stp`, a struct or fixed-size local's home address, an element or field path's
  checks, cows and address, the deferred case of rule 31 included), and the `tmp`'s local Ai (a *ref
  local*) is then the `p` register holding that address; inside the `iblk` a read of `lv Ai` is the
  callee's read of a `ref` parameter (`ldi`/`ldf`/`ldp` from `Ai - 0 0`, rule 12, 31), an assignment
  to it the callee's store, and its element stores use the cow of the memory location (Ai, 0) (rule
  19); the roots of the inline `xblk` (rule 12) are those of its `rarg`s, so the reads before it are
  protected as before a call (R30 extended); the reloads of rule 12 follow `enddo B`, before R27's
  destination `mov` (as they follow a `call` before `mov x R`). T1's alias does not apply to a ref
  local.
* **R32, aggregate results of an inline call** (Decision 83). An `iblk` whose type is a struct, a
  record or a fixed-size array (or a tuple with such components) gets, before `do B`, a new home H
  of each such result type (rule 27 (a)), as a call's hidden result address is a home the caller
  provides (§3.6.3); an `iret` stores each such value into its H as rule 27 (d) stores into a home
  (the reference fields of a borrowed value retained, an owned value moved), then `exit B`; the
  `iblk`'s value for that component is H, owned as a call's aggregate result is (rule 15 (g)), and a
  destination receives it as rule 27 receives a call's result home. Refined by L-da: H is always a
  new home, allocated before `do B` after the `tmp`s and the R32 homes before the deferred rule-31
  stores; under a `bind` H is moved into the local, under a `tbind`, `tasg`, `tret` or `eval` it is
  copied into the home the parent provides, in R27's place of the `mov`; a struct-literal value goes
  into its own home V, then `li N size; mcopy H V N`, per rule 27 (d).
* **Validation** (in addition to §3.5.9): an `iblk`'s type may be any result type (R32); a ref local
  only as a `tmp` of an inline `xblk` whose child is a `rarg`; a `j*` record's child of the type the
  mapping table requires; no `fn` of kind `elem` or `inl`, no `inst`, no `emap` (L-cg). Any violation
  is `BAD_RECORD`. As built (L-ea): where a `j*` record stands is `sealoop`'s validation (§2.11.4),
  not `sealower`'s; `sealower` checks a `j*` record's child type by the table above and its operand
  count and classes against the entry's Args; no JSON entry has a result; a borrowed operand (an
  `lv`, a field loaded by `ldp`/`ldf`/`ldi`/`ldb`) is neither retained nor released, an owned one
  (L10's `xblk` under a `jvec`, a `str` temporary) is released right after the `rcall`; each `jkey`
  node gets its own new `str` data record (L-dv).

#### 2.11.6 Runtime entries of phase 6

The sixteen entries of phase 6 (Decision 85), ids 23–38, entered `rt.inc`'s `SEA_ENTRY_LIST` and
§4.8's Id-first entry table with WP-CONTRACT (§2.11.1); the table there, with its Contract column,
is their specification (§2.6's contract rule), and this section gives the rules they share. Each
`S` entry takes the site as its last integer argument (§4.8); every returned object is owned,
every argument borrowed; a failing entry calls `_sea_err` and never returns.

Every emitter entry other than `JSON_OPEN` writes into the buffer and flushes it when full. On a
failed flush (or a failed final write or `close` in `JSON_CLOSE`) the entry itself closes the
descriptor if it is still open (ignoring that `close`'s result), sets the descriptor field to −1,
keeps the state and its retained path, and calls `_sea_err` with `CANNOT_WRITE`, the path and the
saved errno; `_sea_err` then finds no open file and does not flush or close again; the path stays
valid until the process exits (`_sea_err` does not return), so the message can use it.
`_sea_err` (§4.5, §4.8), on any run-time error while a JSON file is open (the emitter's state exists
and its descriptor field is not −1), flushes that file's buffer and closes it, ignoring a failure of
that flush (LANGUAGE.md §9.2 step 3; the error it reports is the original one), so `rt_err.s` changes
on both targets (L-ca); an error raised inside `JSON_OPEN` before the descriptor is stored finds no
open file. **Layout** (LANGUAGE.md §11.4; L-bz):
a value at depth d (the top value at 0) is written as follows: a scalar as above; a non-empty object
as `{`, LF, each member on its own line indented 2(d + 1) spaces as `"key": ` and its value at depth
d + 1, every member but the last followed by `,`, then LF, 2d spaces and `}`; a non-empty array
likewise with `[`, its elements and `]`; an empty object `{}`, an empty array `[]`; a matrix of r ≥ 1
rows and c ≥ 1 columns as an array of r arrays of c elements, element (i, j) at position j of row i;
then, after the top value, one LF. A key is written as a string. The emitter keeps one state per
open container (its kind and whether it has an element yet) in a stack on the heap, grown as needed
and freed by `JSON_CLOSE` (L-co: no depth limit, `OUT_OF_MEMORY` if it cannot grow); it trusts the
nesting pass 2b writes, as `sea_printf` trusts its format. The live-object count of `SEA_HEAP_CHECK`
is unchanged by a completed `write_json`.

Where they live (both targets, written alike): `FORMAT` in `rt_fmt.s` (beside `sea_printf` and
`sea_error`, whose formatting and sink it shares) and `PRINT` in `rt_out.s` (beside the
standard-output buffer it writes into); `MAKE_DIR` and the JSON emitter in a new
`rt_file.s`; `FMOD` in `rt_math.s`; the runtime object lists of `Makefile` and `Makefile.linux` gain
`rt_file.s`.

#### 2.11.7 Passes 3b, 3c and 4

No transformation, template or rule changes. `seaopt` and `sealopt` (through `lirrw`) validate the
new `rcall` entry names against the `entries` block as before (their capacity, 399, suffices), and
pass 4 calls the new entries by the calling convention of §4.8 (its capacity raised by
WP-CONTRACT). Phase 5's shapes (§5.2) and the `make test-shape` lines must still hold: the W5 and W4
hot loops are in functions §8.6 does not inline (`lcg_fill` has four call sites and a loop; W4's
loop is in `.main`), while `stack_gap` (one call site in `w5_stats.sea`) is now inlined, which no
shape line names.

#### 2.11.8 The ports and their acceptance

`sea/ports/` is a new directory of the sea repository. `w5_tolerance_mc.sea` is LANGUAGE.md Appendix
D without its figures section and without the `--figures` branch of its option loop (Decision 80);
`w1_shaft_design.sea` is a new port of `w1_shaft_design.m`, written statement by statement as
Appendix D is (operation order kept, LANGUAGE.md §6.8; 1-based indices in its JSON; faithfulness notes
in its header comment), with `shaft_safety` an `elemental fn` called with scalars (`bisect_diameter`),
the 2001-element sweep vector and the 90 × 120 grids (LANGUAGE.md §2.1), and no figure code. Each
accepts only `--export-reference` (any other argument is its `unknown option` error, as Appendix D's
`_` arm). The token maps `sea/ports/<name>.tokens` are written from the MATLAB scripts' `fprintf`
formats and `compare.py`'s `RULES`, never from Sea output (§6.4). `tests/accept.sh` (§6.3, Decision
86) runs them.

As built (6e). `w5_tolerance_mc.sea` drops, besides the figures section and the `--figures` arm,
Appendix D's header line documenting `--figures` and the then-unused `var figures` (L-ed).
`w1_shaft_design.sea` holds `caseMat` 0-based, as Sea indexes (MATLAB's `[2 2 3 1 4]` is `[1, 1, 2,
0, 3]`), with a header note; the bearing index keeps MATLAB's 1-based number internally (`brgIdx`, 0
for none), which is not exported, so the "1-based indices in its JSON" rule above has nothing to
apply to (W1's JSON has no index key); MATLAB's `w1:*` error identifiers are dropped and their
messages kept (none fires); the export record is named `out`, since `ref` is a keyword (L-ee).

### 2.12 Phase 7: fusion and SIMD (sub-phase 7a)

**Status: agreed 2026-10-29.** This section is the specification of phase 7 of §8 (row 7, "Fusion
and SIMD"), written as sub-phase 7a in the way 6a specified phase 6 (§2.11) and revised after two
independent reviews. Its questions are **Decisions 94–113** of §9, each decided by the user as
option (a) (2026-10-29). Its smaller readings are the lead decisions **L-eh – L-fl** (§9, "Lead
decisions of phase 7"), agreed with the text. No code, test or contract file changes with 7a: the contract changes
are listed in "Contract changes" below and are made by the work package WP-CONTRACT of sub-phase
7b, each with its document table in the same change (the contract rule of §2.6). The normative
sections that the text below amends are edited when the user agrees the text (WP-CONTRACT for the
tables that mirror a contract file, the integration of each sub-phase for the rest, as 6b did):
§2.1's pipeline, §2.2's `--emit` kinds, §2.6.3's build lists and line table, §2.10, §3's
introduction (its count of text files: eight today, ten after phase 7), §3.4's file table, §3.5.9
("Locals", "Capacity", L18, L20), §3.6.4, §3.6.5, §4.4 (which still says pass 3b emits each
vectorized loop twice), §4.5 (the heap check's count mode), §4.8, §4.9, §4.10.1, §5.1, §5.3, §5.4,
§6.6.1, and LANGUAGE.md §9.2 (the sentence of §2.12.2 (5), agreed with the text); until each is
edited, this section is the agreed specification and those sections describe the code as built.
At 7c's integration (2026-10-30) §2.12.3 and §2.12.4 were amended with the readings 7c fixed (the
user's D1–D3 of 2026-10-29 and the concatenation decision of 2026-10-30, and the lead decisions
L-fv–L-gj), marked "as built in 7c" where they narrow a rule; they describe `seafuse` as built.

#### 2.12.1 Scope

Phase 7 implements, on both targets, everything row 7 of §8 names and its "done when" needs:

* **Fusion** (§5.1) as the rewrites F1–F5 of §2.12.4: a statement whose value is an element-wise
  tree becomes one loop nest with no temporary array (F1); adjacent element-wise statements over
  one iteration space become one loop nest, and the `let` arrays that are dead after them are never
  stored (F2); a reduction whose operand is an element-wise tree, a view or a same-mask selection
  of such trees runs in that nest with no temporary (F3); views, range and `:` selections and
  same-mask selections are folded into the nest's addressing, and a concatenation copies its
  selection parts straight from their bases (F4); an elemental application is a k-result node of
  the tree (F5). They run in a new program of pass 3a, **`seafuse`** (`sea.hir` → `sea.hirf`, ahead
  of `sealoop`; Decision 94), which also performs L19 (rewritten there, not moved: §2.12.3), as
  Decision 88 foresaw for this seam. `sealoop`'s L18 and L20 learn to copy the fused code of the
  bodies they inline (Decision 110).
* **Buffer reuse** (§5.4, first bullet): a whole-array assignment in a fused nest writes into the
  target's own buffer when it has the result's shape (F2 (6)).
* **Pass 3d, `seavec`** (Decision 78, its open items settled by Decision 98): `sea.lir3` → `sea.lir`,
  sharing `lirrw` (which learns the vector classes, Decision 113); the transformations T11 (full
  unrolling of short constant loops over stack slots), T12 (scalar replacement of slots, §5.3), T13
  (if-conversion of quiet blocks and vectorization of unit-stride innermost loops) of §2.12.6, then
  T10.
* **Vector code in pass 4**: the register classes `x`, `y`, `m` in the shared allocator
  (`passes/lib/ralloc.bas`), NEON code for the 2-lane instructions in `seagen_a64`, SSE2 code for
  the 2-lane and AVX2 code for the 4-lane instructions in `seagen_x64`, the `vfeat` test (§2.12.7).
* **Vector forms of the elementary functions** on both targets: the 2-lane forms on both, the
  4-lane forms on `x86_64-linux`, bit-identical lane by lane to the scalar entries (entries 39–50,
  §2.12.8; Decision 103).
* **W4 complete** (without figures): `sea/ports/w4_heat_plate.sea` with its token map, accepted by
  `tests/accept.sh` like W1 and W5 (§2.12.10), its red-black solver fused; **W1's grid bisection
  fused and vectorized** (the port unchanged); both checked for temporaries by a run-time count
  per iteration (§2.12.10, Decision 105) and for vector code by shape lines (Decision 108).
* Every earlier program's output unchanged bit for bit: standard output, standard error, exit
  status and written files of every `programs/`, `errors/` and acceptance case, on both targets and,
  on `x86_64-linux`, under both kernel variants `sse2` and `avx2` (Decision 104).

Not in phase 7 (§5.1 and §5.4 are amended to say so when the text is agreed): fusion through
prelude calls (`linspace`, `meshgrid` results are materialized as now); struct-array projections
inside a fused tree (L15 stays a leaf); `str` element-wise nodes (barriers: each element allocates);
hoisting a barrier operand's buffer out of a loop (§5.4's third bullet, phase 10 if a benchmark
asks for it); vectorizing `i64` arithmetic, gathers, strided or transposed accesses, blocks other
than T13's quiet ones, carried values other than `sum`'s lanes, `itof` and the rounding
instructions (`xfloor xceil xtrunc xround` and their `y` forms stay records of the contract that no
pass writes in phase 7; pass 4 rejects them as `BAD_RECORD`, Decision 100); pairing the lanes of
fixed-size arithmetic in pass 4 (§5.3's last sentence); the matrix product and factorizations
(phase 8); the speed comparison with MATLAB (phase 10, §6.5). Phase 7 adds no language feature, so
the phase rule (§2.6.2) is unchanged: no row of the after-phase-4 table is removed, and no
`err_ns_*` test changes.

**Contract changes** (WP-CONTRACT, the first package of 7b, alone, before any other 7b code):

1. `include/passes.txt`: the set letters of its header comment: `HL` becomes "`sea.hirf` and

2. `include/rt.inc`: the twelve entries of §2.12.8, ids 39–50, appended to `SEA_ENTRY_LIST`

3. `include/limits.inc`, `include/errors.inc`: no change. Fusion and vectorization report no new

4. LANGUAGE.md §9.2 gains the sentence of §2.12.2 (5) (not a contract file; written with the

#### 2.12.2 The semantic contract of fusion and vectorization

Fusion and vectorization are optimizations LANGUAGE.md does not observe. A fused or vectorized
program has exactly the observable behaviour of the same program compiled without them (by the
rewrites L1–L20 alone, which are the reference: one loop per operation, LANGUAGE.md §6.2's
"element-wise", §5.5's "evaluated completely, then the indices, then the checks, then the stores"):

1. **Values**: every value the program observes (prints, writes, stores into a variable it reads
   later, or uses in a condition) is computed by its element's scalar operation sequence, in the
   order of the parse tree, bit for bit (LANGUAGE.md §6.8); no `f64` operation of that sequence is
   reassociated or contracted. Fusion may compute an element more than once (F3's `variance`) and
   may not compute a result nothing reads (a discarded result, an unstored local); neither changes
   an observed value. The reductions keep their pinned orders (LANGUAGE.md §10.5): `sum`'s eight
   lanes and final tree, the sequential order of `max min argmax argmin nnz any all` and of the
   `i64` sums.
2. **Errors**: which run-time error is reported (message and line), and what was written before it.
   The reference evaluates an element-wise tree node by node in post-order: for each node its
   operands left to right (a leaf in full, with its own checks), then its shape check, its result's
   allocation and its element loop; a statement's store then makes its target's checks. Fusion
   keeps every leaf evaluation and every check in that order, adds none, and moves only element
   computations into one loop after the last check, so it is exact when the moved computations
   cannot fail and have no effect. A *failing node* (below) is fused only where moving its loop
   past the later checks cannot be seen (F1 (2), Decision 95).
3. **Effects**: output (`printf`, `print`, `write_json`, `make_dir`) and calls with effects are never
   moved: a leaf that is such a call is evaluated where the reference evaluates it, and a statement
   with an effect is never part of a fused group (F2 (1)).
4. **Aliasing** (LANGUAGE.md §5.5): an assignment behaves as if its value were computed first; a
   fused nest writes a target in place only when every read of the target's root path in the nest
   is at the element being written and the store visits each element once (F1 (5)); a vectorized
   loop runs only when no store of one lane can reach a load or store of another lane of the same
   iteration (T13 (4)).
5. **Allocation**: fusion and vectorization never add an allocation. A program that the reference
   would stop with `out of memory` may complete, because an intermediate array is not allocated.
   LANGUAGE.md has no rule for this yet (§3.1's capacity bound is about compilation), so the agreed text
   adds to LANGUAGE.md §9.2, after the run-time error table: "*The compiler may evaluate an
   expression without allocating the intermediate arrays its operators would produce (fusion,
   DESIGN.md §5.1). It never allocates more than the operator-by-operator evaluation, so a program
   that runs out of memory may instead complete; it never reports `out of memory` where that
   evaluation would not.*" `SEA_HEAP_CHECK`'s line is unchanged (`heap: 0 live objects` for every
   correct program).
6. **What fusion may not do**: reorder two leaves, two checks, a leaf and a check, or two calls; add
   a check; speculate an element computation that can fail (an `if` arm that can fail is never
   computed for a lane that does not select it, LANGUAGE.md §6.10); fold a value through a variable
   that a statement between its definition and its use assigns; change a dynamic result into a
   fixed-size one or the reverse; change the element order of a store (increasing linear order of
   the selection, the last store winning at a repeated position, LANGUAGE.md §5.5).

**Quiet and failing.** An element computation is *quiet* when its scalar form (the node with its
operands' elements) cannot fail and has no effect: the `f64` operators `+ - * /` and `%` (FMOD),
unary `-` of `f64`, comparisons of `f64`, `i64` or `bool` elements, `& | !` on `bool`,
conversions to `f64` from `i64` or `bool` and between `f64` and `f64`, `powk` and `^` of `f64` (§4.10:
no elementary function fails), `where` of any element type but `str`, the elemental library
functions of LANGUAGE.md §10.4 on `f64` or `bool` operands (`sqrt abs exp log sin cos pow hypot min
max floor ceil round trunc sign isnan`) and `min`, `max`, `sign` on `i64` operands, and an elemental
application whose inlined body is quiet (L-ei). A *failing* element computation is any other
fusible node: `i64` `+ - *`, unary `-`, `%`, `idiv`, `^`, `abs` on `i64` (−2⁶³ overflows), `cvt` to
`i64`, an elemental application whose body is not quiet. Among reductions (F3), `sum` and `mean` of
`i64` elements are failing (each partial sum is checked), and every reduction's `EMPTY_REDUCE`
check is a check (it can fail). `str` element-wise nodes are not fusible (above).

#### 2.12.3 Pass 3a: `seafuse` (program, files, format)

`seafuse` is a new Baysick program of pass 3a, run after `seaexpand` and before `sealoop`
(Decision 94): it reads `sea.hir` and writes **`sea.hirf`**, which `sealoop` reads in place of
`sea.hir`; `--emit hirf` stops after it (§2.2's list of kinds gains `hirf`). Its files are
`passes/seafuse/fu0main.bas` … (in name order) with `passes/seafuse/build.list` = `lib io diag
tables layout`, `data errors exits consts records`; its own lines 100 – 59 999; its `SUB`s, if any,
are prefixed `fu_` (L-eh). The driver runs it as every pass (§2.2 step 5, its `#end` discipline);
`tools/seaval.bas` gains the format `hirf`; `tests/stage.sh` gains the pair `seafuse hir hirf` and
runs `sealoop` on `NAME.hirf` where a test has one (below). `seafuse` rewrites every function of
the file, those of kind `elem` and `inl` and the prelude's included (Decision 110): their bodies'
array code is fused before `sealoop` inlines them, and L18 and L20 copy the fused code.

**`sea.hirf`** holds the records of `sea.hir` (sets `H`, `HF`) and of set `HL` (§3.5.9), with these
semantic rules (checked by `seaval`'s format `hirf` and by `sealoop`'s reader; any violation is
`BAD_RECORD`): (1) no `inst` and no `emap` record (L19 has rewritten every elemental application;
it writes the per-element calls as `call` records of the elemental function, which `sealoop`'s L20
inlines, so the `fn` records of kind `elem` stay, and so do their `call`s); (2) of the `HL` records
only `tptr xblk tmp hloop ext adat eld est anew wbin chkb chk rcnt cow mcpy` (no `cdat`, `iblk`,
`iret`: literals and inlining stay `sealoop`'s); (3) `tptr` records appended to the type table as
§3.5.9 "Types" says, numbered on from `sea.hir`'s last id, and, when F3 writes sum8 and `sea.hir`'s
table has no `tfvec` of `f64` with n 8, the type F8 appended with them (one that `sea.hir` has is
used instead), numbered with the `tptr` records in the same order of first reference (a masked
sum's mask `tptr` therefore precedes F8), so `sealoop`'s reader accepts F8 anywhere among the
appended records and its writer renumbers it with them (L-fw); (4) the locals `seafuse` creates are
`.l` locals, and `sealoop` renumbers every `.l` local of its output in file order (§3.5.9
"Locals"), so `sea.hirl`'s numbering stays canonical whichever program created a local (Decision
109); (5) T1–T3 of §3.5.9 and the refinements R1–R16 hold for every `HL` record of `sea.hirf` as for
`sea.hirl`, and so do R33 and R34 below. **A file holding no `emap` and none of the constructs
F1–F4 rewrite is `sea.hir` byte for byte** (L-ek), so `stage.sh` checks the pair `seafuse hir hirf`
against `NAME.hir` itself when a test has no `NAME.hirf`, and feeds `sealoop` `NAME.hir` then.

**L19 in `seafuse`** (7b). L19 and `ind2sub` with an array `r` (L-cl) are written in `seafuse` as
§2.11.4 specifies them, with one difference of order: as built in `sealoop`, L19 expands each
per-element call with L20 at once; in `seafuse` L19 writes the per-element `call` record, and
`sealoop`'s L20 inlines it later. `seafuse` therefore needs its own copies of the forms L19 uses
(rule 22's checks and nest, L11's and L12's statement forms, the node and local helpers): a rewrite,
not a move of `sealoop`'s code, which shares those helpers with L7, L12 and L20. `sealoop` keeps
L1–L18 and L20 and drops L19's own lines (its shared helpers stay). **7b's neutrality** (Decision
109): over the corpus, `sea.lir1`, `sea.lir2`, `sea.lir3` (the old `sea.lir`), `sea.lir` and every
diagnostic byte-identical before and after (L-p's method), and `sea.hirl` byte-identical (with
`sealoop`'s renumbering in file order, the `.l` names are those of the one-program order); a
difference is a defect of 7b, not a golden to re-derive.

**`sealoop` from 7b**: its reader takes `sea.hirf`; it rejects `inst` and `emap` and validates the
`HL` records it finds as §3.5.9 validates its own output (it rewrites the HIR subtrees under them
like any expression: a leaf `tmp` of `seafuse` may hold a selection, a literal, a reduction, a
prelude call); it writes them unchanged otherwise, and renumbers the `.l` locals on output. **L18
and L20 from 7b** (Decision 110, built in 7b, not 7c, and amended 2026-10-29 by the user: 7b's
`seafuse` already writes L19's `HL` records into `inl` and `elem` bodies): the copy of a body
(§3.5.9 L18, §2.11.4 L20) copies the `HL` records of `sea.hirf` like any record, with each local
field (`tmp`, `hloop` and `rcnt`'s `l` and `e`, and the `lv` reading them) renamed: a callee's
`.l` local becomes a new caller **`.l`** local (not a `.i` local, which would change `sea.hirl`;
one per inlined call, renumbered in declaring-record order with the caller's own; its `loc`
record at position P under L18, at the callee local's own position under L20); the other fields
are copied as they are. **Exception to Decision 109's byte identity** (agreed 2026-10-29): a
`return` of an elemental application (a `tret` of an `emap`) inside an `inl` or `elem` function:
`seafuse` writes L19's `tret` form, a block ending in `ret P k`, at the `emap`'s position, which
L20 copies as `iret`, so `sea.hirl` and the sites of `sea.lir1` differ from before 7b, while
`sea.lir`, the program output and the run-time diagnostics (which report the line only) are
identical.

**R33** (a refinement of R5, no record or field added): an `est` may store into an array whose
`cow` the rewrite has done even when a `bind` of the rewrite holds a second count on it (F2 (6):
`O`, the old value, may be the same object); the store writes the shared buffer, which only the
rewrite's own locals reach. **R34**: a source local whose `bind` F2 dropped keeps its `loc` record,
is declared by no record and read by no node, and rule 16 releases nothing for it.

**Capacity** (Decision 72's rule, L-el): a fusion whose nodes, locals or types would exceed
`SEA_LIM_NODES`, `SEA_LIM_SYMBOLS` or `SEA_LIM_TYPES` is not applied (its statements are written
unfused, for `sealoop` to rewrite one by one), so fusion never makes a compilation fail; L19 reports
its limits as before (`seafuse` counts the whole file as `sealoop` does, §3.5.9 "Capacity"); L18
and L20 count the copied `HL` records and `.l` locals as they count the others. **As built in 7c**
(L-gh): a fused unit (a tree, reduction, concatenation or group) also has an implementation
capacity of 1 180 of its 1 187 slots, counted exactly before the unit is built (1 per fused node
and per leaf, 3 per S, R, A or V selection leaf, per selection target and per concatenation part);
a unit over it is left unfused, and a group stops growing before the statement that would pass it,
like L-el. When `SEA_LIM_NODES`, `SEA_LIM_SYMBOLS` or `SEA_LIM_TYPES` is passed inside a fusion,
that fusion runs to its end on throwaway output, and the walk then re-runs once, with every walk
flag reset, under a threshold: that fusion and every later one in walk order are written unfused.
A limit passed outside any fusion (L19 included), or a second overflow inside a fusion, is reported
as before (the second at the first one's position). A fusion left unfused this way can move a later
capacity position, as below. **Capacity
positions** (agreed 2026-10-29): a "program too large: …" diagnostic keeps its message, but its
position may move, because `seafuse` counts nodes as a pass of its own, without L20's inline cost;
Decision 109's byte identity excludes capacity positions.

#### 2.12.4 The fusion rewrites F1–F5

*Notation* as §3.5.9's (loop(N; K), mloop, lin, vchk, mchk, data(X), ext(X, d)); P is the position
of the rewritten statement, every node a rewrite writes takes P except where said, the nodes of the
program it keeps (leaves, scalar operations in the element expression) keep their own; every site
of a check is the line of the node whose check it is, exactly as in the reference rewrite (L5–L7,
L13), so a fused program reports each check at the line the reference reports it. The *root path*
of an access is its root variable with the field chain to the array (`s.v` in `s.v[1..3]`).

**Element-wise trees.** An *element-wise tree* is a maximal subtree of a statement's value whose
internal nodes are *fusible nodes* and whose leaves are *leaf expressions*. Fusible nodes: `bin`
(not `matmul`, not `cat`, not on `str`), `un`, `cvt`, `powk`, an elemental `lib` (as L7 rewrites
it), `lib where`, and an `emap` (F5); each with at least one array operand (a node with scalar
operands only is a scalar expression inside a leaf or the element expression, rewritten as now).
Leaf expressions: anything else of array or scalar type: `lv` of a local or parameter, a constant,
a field, a call, a literal, a reduction, a concatenation, a selection or a view (F4 says when these
fold instead of being a leaf). **Which trees `seafuse` rewrites** (Decision 111): every tree with
at least two fusible nodes, or one with a folded leaf, or with a matrix space, or that is the value
of an `asg set` to a whole array or a selection, or of a group statement (F2); only a vector tree of
one fusible node with no folded leaf, which is not such a value, is left to `sealoop`'s L7, which
gives exactly F1's form for it (L-em).

* **F1 (statement fusion)** (rules 22 and 21 generalized; Decision 95). A `bind`, `tbind` component,
  `asg set`, `ret`, `tret` component, function argument or other operand position whose value is
  an element-wise tree E of type T (dynamic or fixed-size), when E qualifies by (2):
  1. *Leaf and check phase*: walk E in post-order; at each node, its leaf operands in operand order
     as `tmp Lk = leaf` (scalars too; a folded leaf as F4 says: its base and its index preparation,
     IX 1 and IX 2 of §3.5.9 with their checks), then the node's shape checks exactly as L7 (2)
     writes them for that node (the extents of each array operand loaded once, the combined shape of
     an inner node standing for its operand, vchk/mchk at that node's site); for an `emap`, L19's
     (2) checks at its site. So the leaves and checks occur in the reference order, none is added,
     and the extents of the root are the iteration space (r, or R and C).
  2. *Qualifying*: every node of E is quiet, except that E's **root** may be one failing node N
     when (i) the statement is not in a group, or is its group's last statement (F2 (4)), and (ii)
     nothing that can fail follows N's loop in the reference order: the statement's store has no
     check (a whole-array target, a `bind`, `ret`; not a selection store, whose index and shape
     checks the reference makes after N's loop, L-en). A failing node that is not the root, or a
     failing root that breaks (ii), is a barrier: a leaf of the enclosing tree, rewritten by L7
     later (a failing node below a broadcast could otherwise run over fewer elements than the
     reference's loop, or none in an empty space), and F1 applies to the rest if it still qualifies
     for rewriting (Decision 111).
  3. *Result*: `tmp RES = anew P T 0 k` with the root's extents (fixed-size: `anew P T 0 0`, R1), as
     L7 (3); for the value of an `asg set` to a whole array, the target's buffer by F2 (6)'s reuse
     prologue (a single statement is a group of one for (6)); for a selection target (an L6 store)
     that (5) allows in place, the target's IX 1–IX 3, its shape check and `cow` (L6 steps 2–5, after
     the value's leaf and check phase, as L6's order says) and no RES.
  4. *Nest*: `tmp DR = data(RES)` and `tmp Dk = data(Lk)` for each array leaf, in leaf order; then
     the iteration. A vector space: `loop(N; I)`, every leaf read at I (or its folded map). A matrix
     space has two copies under `if` (`tmp Pl` = the conjunction of `bin eq` of every array leaf's
     extents with the space's, L-ep; a quiet test, not a check): the *plain copy*, `loop(NN; I)` over
     NN = R·C reading every whole-array leaf at I when no leaf is folded, else `mloop(R, C; I, J)`
     reading whole-array leaves at `lin(I, J, R)` and folded ones by their maps (L-eo), so its inner
     accesses are unit-stride for T13; and the *broadcast copy*, `mloop(R, C; I, J)` reading every
     array leaf at L7's index `I·SIk + J·SJk`, and every folded leaf through its own map at row
     I·[rows ≠ 1] and column J·[cols ≠ 1] of the leaf (its SI and t, no SJ; L-fx); when no leaf can
     broadcast (every array leaf fixed-size with the space's static shape) the broadcast copy and
     the test are omitted. `tmp Pl` stands right before its `if`, after the data loads, folding `bin
     band` left to right over every array leaf in leaf order, rows before columns; the plain copy's
     NN is written in its arm before its loop, the broadcast copy's strides (L7 (4)) in its arm
     before its `mloop` (L-ga). The body
     computes the element expression F: E with each array leaf replaced by its element (`eld Ek sk 0
     (lv Dk) index`), each scalar leaf by `lv Lk`, each folded leaf by F4's element read, each inner
     node by its scalar operation (and an `emap` by F5's per-element call); then `est s 0 F (lv DR)
     index` (or the selection's element store of L6 step 7, in the selection's increasing linear
     order).
  5. *Aliasing*: when the tree is stored into a target whose root path E reads, the store is in place
     only when (i) the target is a whole array or a selection of kinds S, R, A, M or MM (never V: an
     index vector may repeat a position, and a later element would read a value the store already
     changed, LANGUAGE.md §5.5), (ii) every read of that root path in E is a whole-array or folded
     leaf read at the element being written (identical index maps: no broadcast, the same selection),
     and (iii) no read of it goes through a call or a field of a different path (L-fe); otherwise E
     is not fused with that store: the value is computed into RES first (fused if it qualifies) and
     stored as before (L6, rule 21). As built in 7c (L-gc), a selection store is in place only when
     its value reads no `lv` of the target's root at all (the strict form of (ii)); a whole-array
     target that its value reads other than as whole-array leaves at the element is never in place
     and starts no group: its tree is fused into RES and stored as before.
  6. *Value*: `lv RES` (owned) as L7's, its owned leaves temporaries of the `xblk` released after
     the nest (T2). Sites: each check at its node's line (1); the `anew` at the root's line.

* **F2 (adjacent-statement fusion)** (Decision 96). In a block, a maximal run S1 … Sn (n ≥ 2) of
  consecutive statements is a *fused group* when:
  1. each Si is a *groupable statement*: a `bind` or `tbind` of new locals, or an `asg set` to a
     whole `var` array or `ref` array parameter, or to an L6 selection target of kind S, R, A, M or
     MM, whose value is an element-wise tree, a folded selection or view (F4), an elemental
     application (F5), or a reduction F3 fuses other than `variance` and `std` (which need the mean
     before their second pass, so they are fused standalone only); or a `bind` of a scalar from such
     a reduction; with no effect anywhere in it (no call with effects, no `printf`, `print`,
     `write_json`, `make_dir`); as built in 7c (L-gc, L-gd), a selection-store statement is fused
     alone (F1 (3), (5)) and is not a group member, a masked reduction does not start a group, and
     every statement of a group has one rank (a statement whose root has another rank ends it; a
     `.flat` reduction's space is a vector of R·C);
  2. *one space, no added check*: each Si keeps exactly its own reference checks (F1 (1)); the
     group adds one quiet run-time test, `tmp Gs` = the conjunction of `bin eq` of every Si's root
     extents with S1's (and of every mask of a masked reduction with S1's root extents): when it
     holds, the fused nest runs; when it does not, the *split copy* runs each Si's own nest over its
     own space, in order, storing every local the group binds (L-eq). A group whose roots are all
     fixed-size with one static shape has no test and no split copy;
  3. *dependences*: a variable or local X assigned or bound by Si is read by Sj (j > i) only as a
     whole-array leaf at the same element, or through a same-shape mask selection that F3 reads at
     the same element (`Tn[colorIn]` in a group over `Tn`'s space); no broadcast, no index of
     another kind, no view, no extent, no reduction of X as a whole outside F3's fused form; a
     target root path V that some Si writes is read by any Sj (j ≤ i or j > i) only at the element
     being written (identical index maps; `T[1..ny-1, :]` written and `T[0..ny-2, :]` read
     conflict), and is written by at most one Si (L-ff); the first statement that would break (3)
     ends the group before it (L-er);
  4. *qualifying*: every node of every Si is quiet, except that the last statement Sn may have a
     failing root (F1 (2)), or be a failing reduction (`sum`, `mean` of `i64`) when nothing that can
     fail follows it.

  The group is rewritten (P S1's position; L-fv, agreed by the user 2026-10-29): (a) each Si's leaf
  and check phase in statement order (F1 (1)), and, for a masked reduction, its mask's count as L5's
  IX 3 and its `EMPTY_REDUCE` check where L13 makes it, and (b) for each stored local its result
  array, bound there (`bind X = anew` at Si's position), then the accumulators of the group's
  reductions (F3), all standing directly in the enclosing block, since a `block` is a scope and a
  local bound inside it would be released at its end while a later statement reads it; then one
  `block P n` holding, for each whole-array target, its reuse prologue (6), and (c) the space test
  (2) and, in its first part, one nest over the space (F1 (4)) whose body computes, per element,
  each Si's element value into a new scalar `.l` local Ei (`bind`), in statement order, a read of X
  bound or assigned by an earlier Si reading Ei instead of memory, then the element stores of the
  targets and stored locals and the reduction steps of F3 (a `tbind` component's element store
  follows its `tbind` in that `tbind`'s block, L-ge); in its second part the split copy; (d) after
  the block, at each reduction Si's position, its final value (F3) bound to its local, and the
  release of the group's own temporaries. **Which results are stored**: a whole-array or
  selection target always; a local bound by Si only when a statement after the group in the same
  block reads it (any node; the block is the local's scope); a local not read after the group is
  never stored in the fused nest (W1's `mid`, `nfv`, `nyv`, `up`), keeps its `loc` record, and its
  `bind` is dropped (R34, L-es); in the split copy every local is stored in an array of its own space
  (the split copy is the reference's per-statement form, with the leaves and checks already made).

  5. *Discarded results*: a `tbind` component `-` and an F5 result the statement discards are not
     computed beyond what the element body needs (L19's rule).
  6. *Buffer reuse* (§5.4): for a whole-array target V (a `var` local or a `ref` array parameter) of
     dynamic type: `tmp E = ` the conjunction of `bin eq` of V's extents with the space's; `if (lv E)
     { cow (lv V) }`; `bind O = lv V` (the old value, held); `if (un not (lv E)) { asg set (lv V)
     (anew P T 0 k extents) }`; the nest reads V's old elements through `data(O)` and stores into
     `data(V)` (R33); O is released at the block's end. A fixed-size V is written in its home in
     place (rule 27; its reads are at the same element by (3)). So `lo = where(up, mid, lo)` in a loop
     writes `lo`'s buffer and allocates nothing once `lo` has the space's shape. Since V is written
     by one statement of the group (3), no second prologue sees O's count.

* **F3 (fused reductions)** (rule 23 over a tree). A `lib` of `sum mean variance std max min argmax
  argmin nnz any all` (no `dim:`) whose vector argument is an element-wise tree, a `.flat` of a
  matrix tree or of a whole matrix (F4), or a masked selection `X[m]` of trees with one mask `lv m`
  (F4): `xblk P T n` with the argument's leaf and check phase (F1 (1)), N the count (the space's
  product; for a masked selection its count by IX 3, then `EMPTY_REDUCE` where L13 checks it), and
  L13's statements for the function with X(K) = the element expression at position K. **Masked**:
  the body stands under `if` of the mask element, and every use L13 makes of the position counts
  selected elements only, through a counter Q of the selected elements so far that replaces K: the
  lane `Q & 7` of `sum`'s sum8 and the index `argmax` and `argmin` return (`argmax(v[m])` with v =
  [9, 1, 5], m = [false, true, true] is 1, the position in the selection) (L-et). `variance` and
  `std` (standalone only, F2 (1)) compute the tree's elements twice (once per sum8, as L13 reads the
  vector twice). `variance` and `std` are fused only when every node of the tree is quiet: a
  failing root is then a barrier, the tree is fused by F1 into RES (which evaluates every element
  and raises its errors in order) and L13 reduces RES (L-gf). In a group the reduction's loop is the
  group's nest; its accumulators are bound before the nest and its final combination follows it.
  A failing reduction (`sum`, `mean` of `i64`) follows F2 (4).

* **F4 (folded views and selections)**. As leaves of a fused tree, a fused reduction or an F2 group:
  `.T`, `.flat`, `.col`, `.row` of an array leaf (rule 28's folding of §3.5.9 "Folded views", with
  the extents of the view); an `idx` whose indices are scalars, ranges and `:` (kinds S, R, A) of an
