#### 2.17.12 Decisions of phase 10

Decisions 162–167 were asked on 2026-11-04 with the outline of this phase and decided by the user the
same day, each as option (a); this text records them with their options. Decisions 168–172 are the
questions the draft left to the user, each with a recommendation (170–172 added after one
independent review of the draft); the user decided them on 2026-11-04 with the agreement, each as
option (a). Mirrored in §9 ("Decisions of phase 10").

162. **Which benchmarks phase 10 runs.** Options: (a) **the seven workloads against MATLAB (§6.5),
     the existing micro-benchmarks (§5.9), and a small set of Sea-level matrix benchmarks written in
     Sea: GEMM (`@`), `solve` and one fused element-wise loop, compared with Apple Accelerate on the
     Mac and OpenBLAS on Linux by C harnesses in `bench/` only, never linked into Sea, with stated
     sizes and methodology; their results are reported, and the only pass rule is §6.5's workload
     rule**; (b) the workloads and the micro-benchmarks only; (c) a full kernel suite like Baysick's
     (every kernel, every size, peak loops). Recommended: (a). Affects §2.17.6, §2.17.7, §5.7 (its
     list of measured kernels, with the agreement). **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).
163. **Who takes the final measurement.** Options: (a) **an agent, in one go, unniced, on the idle
     M2 Pro, when the user says "go"; it records the load average before and after, the machine,
     the OS and the commit**; (b) the user runs the `make` target and pastes the output.
     Recommended: (a). Affects §2.17.3, §2.17.10, row 10c. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).
164. **What follows a miss.** Options: (a) **if any workload misses on either measure, a targeted
     optimisation sub-phase, agreed with the user, follows, and then everything is re-measured**;
     (b) the miss is recorded and v1 waits. Recommended: (a). Affects §2.17.11 (row 10o), §2.17.9
     (the kept attempts), Decision 168. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).
165. **Linux numbers.** Options: (a) **Linux x86_64 numbers are measured on the ssh host `desktop`
     (Intel Core i7-4790) and reported, compared with nothing**; (b) no Linux numbers. Recommended:
     (a). Affects §2.17.4, §2.17.6, §2.17.7, `make bench-cross`, `BENCH.md` §8. **Decided: (a)**
     (the user, 2026-11-04).
166. **The version after the pass.** Options: (a) **when §6.5 passes, Sea's version becomes 1.0.0
     (Decision 79) wherever it is recorded: the driver's `--version` text (`driver/sea`, the only
     place in code), §1.2 and §2.2, `sea/CLAUDE.md`'s status and version line, and `README.md`**;
     (b) the version stays 0.y. Recommended: (a). Affects row 10d. **Decided: (a)** (the user,
     2026-11-04).
167. **NumPy timings.** Options: (a) **the NumPy reference timings are an extra reported column,
     never judged**; (b) MATLAB only. Recommended: (a). Affects §2.17.5, `BENCH.md` §4.
     **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).
168. **What an optimisation sub-phase may change** (Decision 164's 10o). Options: (a) **the
     compiler passes, the runtimes and the prelude only; a port changes only where it departs from
     its MATLAB script's algorithm (a defect of the port), never to restructure an accepted port for
     speed**; (b) also port rewrites that keep the MATLAB script's algorithm and outputs but change
     how the Sea code is written (for example a hand-vectorized loop or a preallocated buffer), each
     still accepted by `tests/accept.sh`; (c) anything that keeps acceptance, a different algorithm
     included. Recommended: (a): a gain in the compiler or runtime holds for every Sea program, the
     ports stay the programs that were accepted, and the comparison stays "the same program written
     plainly in each language"; (b) measures how well the port was tuned as much as Sea; (c) would
     no longer compare like with like. Affects row 10o. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).
169. **The README after 1.0.0.** Options: (a) **10d adds to `README.md` a short "Performance"
     table (per workload, Sea's best of 5 and MATLAB's best on both measures, and the machine),
     generated by `report.py` from the committed results, with a link to `docs/BENCH.md`**; (b) the
     README only states the version and links `docs/BENCH.md`. Recommended: (a): the speed goal is
     Sea's first goal (§1.1), and a generated table cannot drift from the measurement. With (a),
     `report.py` has a `--readme` option printing that table (written in 10b), and row 10d's
     WP-VERSION pastes it. Affects row 10d, §2.17.9. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).
170. **The start condition of each measurement.** An independent review saw this Mac at a 1-minute
     load average of 1.68–2.28 while idle with an agent session open, so the draft's limit of 1.0
     could not be reached. Options: (a) **a separate build step before any timed run, then before
     each tool's measurement a cool-down of at least 120 s, then a wait (15-minute timeout) until the
     1-minute load average is at most 2.0; the wait and the load are recorded; on timeout the driver
     stops and the agent reports instead of measuring**; (b) the same with the limit 1.0; (c) no load
     condition: the load is only recorded. Recommended: (a): the build's heat and the agent's own
     background load are allowed for, a measurement on a busy machine is still refused, and every
     wait is in the record; (b) would in practice never start; (c) could publish numbers taken on a
     loaded machine. Affects §2.17.3, §2.17.10, L-po, L-pl. **Decided: (a)** (the user,
     2026-11-04).
171. **What `axpby` measures, and how hoisting is excluded.** In a loop, `w = 0.75 * x - 1.25 * y`
     reuses `w`'s buffer and allocates nothing per call (§5.4, §2.12's F2 (6)), so an allocation
     count cannot show that each call ran. Options: (a) **the natural Sea form, reusing `w`'s
     buffer, guarded for every implementation by an input that changes with the call number (r mod
     2, so the checked result is that of the last call) and by the rule that a batched call may not
     be more than twice as fast as a single one**; (b) a form that allocates a fresh result on every
     call (for example a function returning the expression), so the heap count of the first draft
     works. Recommended: (a): it measures what a Sea user's loop costs, the input change makes
     hoisting impossible rather than merely detectable, and the guard is the same for Sea and C; (b)
     measures an allocation the language avoids in practice. Affects §2.17.6, L-pg. **Decided: (a)**
     (the user, 2026-11-04).
172. **NumPy's threads.** Options: (a) **NumPy's default threads, as MATLAB's pass baseline ran
     with its default threads: no thread variable is set, and the BLAS and thread settings NumPy
     reports are recorded**; (b) single-threaded (`VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS=1`,
     `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1`), like Sea. Recommended: (a): the column sits beside MATLAB's default
     baseline and is not judged; (b) would make it comparable with the single-threaded MATLAB file
     instead. Affects §2.17.3, §2.17.5. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).

#### 2.17.13 Lead decisions of phase 10

Readings taken because one answer is clearly right, agreed by the user with the text and Decisions
168–172 on 2026-11-04 (§9, "Lead decisions of phase 10"):

* **L-ow** (no warm-up run, one measurement) Nothing runs a port between its build and run 1, so run
  1 is the first run, as MATLAB's first repetition is; best of 5 includes it (§5.7). The pass is
  decided within one final measurement; runs of different attempts are never combined.
* **L-ox** (the printed compute time) The ports print the compute time with three decimals because
  the MATLAB reports do and the reports are compared (§6.4); the check therefore compares the largest
  value the printed number can stand for, printed + 0.0005, strictly below MATLAB's best at full
  precision. This can only make the check stricter, never pass a slower run.
* **L-oy** (every timed run is correct) Run 1 of each workload is judged as acceptance judges it, and
  runs 2–15 must give the same bytes (the `Compute time` line aside), the same status and an empty
  standard error, and leave only `NAME.json` and the fixtures. Judging happens after the timed runs,
  so the `uv` processes never run between two timed runs.
* **L-oz** (scheduling) No QoS class, affinity or nice value is set for any measured process on
  either system, so every implementation runs under the same default scheduling as MATLAB did; this
  departs from Baysick BENCH.md §3.1 (which sets a QoS class and pins on Linux) for the sake of that
  equality. The drivers refuse to run niced. Because a shell started by an agent may inherit a
  lowered scheduling class that no tool can portably query, `spawn_time` records each workload
  run's user + system CPU time (`wait4`), and `report.py` flags runs whose CPU time is below 0.8 of
  their wall time as runs that waited for a CPU; a flag is reported, not a failure.
* **L-pa** (power) The baseline machine `Mac14,9` is a portable; in final mode the drivers refuse to
  measure on battery or in Low Power Mode, which lower the clock, and record the power source.
* **L-pb** (what the check accepts) Only final-mode results of a clean tree, whose summary agrees
  with its runs file: the check can then be re-run by anyone on the committed files, and the
  measured binaries are those of the recorded commit.
* **L-pc** (the machine) §1.2's comparison is valid only on the baseline's machine, so a model or CPU
  name different from the MATLAB files' is a failure of the check, not a warning.
* **L-pd** (NumPy) Timed in-process (`main()` with `perf_counter`, five runs in one interpreter, the
  module imported untimed), the committed `.py.json` protected by redirecting `common.REF_DIR`, and
  run 1 judged by `compare.py`'s own NumPy-mode function; Mac only, because the column exists to sit
  beside MATLAB's and the host has no MATLAB baseline. Five runs, as the MATLAB files hold, not 15:
  the column is not judged, and the slowest scripts make 15 runs costly. The redirection of file
  descriptor 1 and the flush before it are outside the timed region, the flush after `main()`
  inside it; `numpy.sh` writes the record, with the facts only Python knows (versions, BLAS,
  threads, the load after the last timed run) from `numpy_time.py`'s `info.txt`.
* **L-pe** (exact kernel data) Integer and dyadic data make every correct implementation's result
  identical, so validation is an equality against `expect.c`'s `int64_t` values, as Baysick's tests
  use exact products; the cost of these operations does not depend on the values.
* **L-pf** (one protocol for all implementations) Each implementation is an executable with the same
  arguments and output, timed by itself around the calls, one process per repetition, with the same
  calibration and batching, so Sea and the vendor are measured identically; a Sea program cannot
  time a repetition loop of the runner's choosing any other way.
* **L-pg** (no hoisting) A loop-invariant `a @ b` could in principle be moved out of the timed loop,
  and the fused `axpby` allocates nothing per call, so an allocation count proves nothing for it.
  Instead every implementation changes one input by the call number's parity before each call, so
  no call is loop-invariant and the checked result is the last call's (exactly checkable for both
  parities), and a batched call may not be more than twice as fast as a single one (Decision 171
  (a)). The Sea programs' text is fixed in §2.17.6 so the guard's premises cannot drift.
* **L-ph** (vendor calls) `cblas_dgemm` with β = 0 into a preallocated matrix; `dgesv_` with its
  copies inside the timed call, because `solve` must also not change its arguments; `vDSP_vsmsmaD`
  as Accelerate's one-pass out-of-place a·x + b·y, and on Linux `cblas_dcopy` + `cblas_daxpby` as a
  labelled two-pass proxy, since OpenBLAS has no out-of-place form (Baysick BENCH.md §2 labels its
  `add` proxy the same way).
* **L-pi** (no peak loops) The Sea-level benchmarks measure the language over the kernels; GEMM's
  quality against the instruction-set peak is Baysick's measurement (Baysick BENCH.md §3.4), and
  Decision 162 chose a small set over a full suite.
* **L-pj** (micro-benchmarks re-measured) The compiler changed after 5d (phases 6–9, L, W8), so the
  micro-benchmarks are re-measured at the measured commit, with the current compiler and C only; the
  5d files stay as the record of phase 5.
* **L-pk** (kept attempts) A failed measurement is committed and then moved to
  `bench/results/p10-attempt-K/`, so the record shows every attempt and `BENCH.md` §10 lists them.
* **L-pl** (order) On the Mac everything is built first, then the workloads (the pass rule) are
  measured, then the kernels, the micro-benchmarks and NumPy (the longest), each after its own start
  condition (Decision 170 (a)), so no build and no previous tool's heat precedes a measurement
  without a cool-down; the Linux run follows the Mac measurement so its `ssh` traffic never overlaps
  a Mac measurement.
* **L-pm** (Linux) The ports are compiled on the Mac and linked on the host as the cross tests do;
  workloads and Sea kernels run under both x86_64 variants; run 1 of each is judged on the Mac with
  the same `compare.py` and `compare_report.py` commands (the host need not have `uv`); no compile
  time is reported for Linux.
* **L-pn** (generated tables) Every number in `BENCH.md` §2 and §4–§8 comes from `report.py`, and
  the lead checks that by re-running it; no measured number is typed by hand.
* **L-po** (load) Under Decision 170 (a) a driver measures only after the cool-down and once the
  1-minute load average is at most 2.0, and stops with exit 2 when that does not happen within 15
  minutes; the final measurement's agent then reports instead of retrying, so the user can make the
  machine idle. The wait and the loads before and after every driver are recorded, and `check.py`
  warns (never fails) when the workloads' load exceeded 2.0.
* **L-pp** (no re-measurement after 10d) The version is a string in the POSIX-sh driver only; the
  compiled programs do not contain it, so 10d changes no measured binary.
* **L-pq** (Python tools) `check.py` and `report.py` read JSON and TSV; Python's standard library does
  that reliably where sh and awk would not, and `uv` is already required by acceptance. They never
  import NumPy.
* **L-pr** (§5.7's kernel list) §5.7 lists Sea's own kernels (GEMV, LU, Cholesky, triangular solve,
  sort, the vector elementary functions) as measured "this way"; under Decision 162 (a) phase 10
  measures the three Sea-level benchmarks of §2.17.6 instead, which run GEMM, LU with its triangular
  solves, and a fused vector loop through the language, in §2.17.9's TSV format rather than
  Baysick's and against the vendor library only, with no instruction-set peak (L-pi). With the
  agreement §5.7 says so (§2.17.14).
* **L-ps** (one session) `make bench` creates a session id that every record carries; a final-mode
  driver never replaces a result file and `session.sh` needs an empty directory, and `check.py`
  requires one session and one `sea_commit` across every record present, so the committed results
  are one measurement and cannot mix runs of different sessions or commits.
* **L-pt** (C call barrier) Each timed C call goes through a `noinline` function ending in `asm
  volatile("" ::: "memory")`, so `-O2` can neither inline it into the timing loop nor hoist or merge
  identical calls; with the per-call input change of L-pg this makes the C and the Sea loops do the
  same work.
* **L-pu** (build, then measure) Separate `build` and `measure` commands, with `measure` refusing stale
  or missing builds, keep every compiler and linker out of the measured interval and give the start
  condition a machine that is no longer building; the cross remote script follows the same order on
  the host.
* **L-pv** (the printed wall) Walls are written with nine decimals, so the check compares the best
  wall + 5·10⁻¹⁰ strictly, as L-ox does for the compute time; the summary's medians of 10 carry one
  decimal more and are recomputed exactly in decimal.
* **L-pw** (cross outputs) On Linux, W2 and W3 (class R) are judged by `compare.py`'s rules only, as
  `make cross` defers and judges them; W1, W4, W5, W7 and W8 must also give the Mac's bytes (the
  `Compute time` line aside), which `make cross` already guarantees, so a host run that differs is
  wrong even if it passes the rules.
* **L-px** (NumPy pinned) The NumPy column names its version, so the version is pinned
  (`numpy==2.5.4`, the release `uv` resolves today) rather than whatever `uv` picks on the day of the
  measurement; the run-1 check confirms it reproduces the cross-check's outputs.
* **L-py** (clean trees) Cleanliness excludes `bench/results`, which the measurement itself writes,
  and is checked from the driver's own root; Baysick's tree is recorded and required clean too
  (outside its `sea` submodule path), because its runtime is linked into every measured binary.
* **L-pz** (overrides) `PORTS` and `KERNELS` let 10b inject failing programs without touching the
  tree, as `tests/accept.sh`'s `PORTS` does; final mode accepts only their defaults, so a final
  result always measures the committed programs.
* **L-qa** (fixed program texts) The three Sea programs are written verbatim in §2.17.6, so their
  input change, check computation and output format are part of the agreed text; a text the
  compiler rejects is corrected in the document with the lead, never silently in `bench/`.

Added in 10b (2026-11-04): the readings the 10b tools took where the agreed text left a detail
open, written into §2.17 where it says "as built in 10b"; the lead confirms them with the 10b
verification before committing:

* **L-qb** (the machine line's baseline) `check.py` prints the distinct models and CPUs of the
  MATLAB files joined by `/`, so a mismatch inside the baseline itself is visible on the line
  instead of being hidden behind one file's values (§2.17.8).
* **L-qc** (reading a load average) The 1-minute load is the first number of the recorded field,
  so the record's exact spacing and separators never make the check fail (§2.17.8).
* **L-qd** (report headings) `report.py` prints BENCH.md's section numbers and titles with `###`
  subsections, so 10c pastes the output unchanged (§2.17.9).
* **L-qe** (micro precision) The micro tables print times to 3 decimals and rates as `%.2f`, the
  formats of every other generated table (§2.17.9).
* **L-qf** (a bare README table) `report.py --readme` prints no heading, so the README keeps its
  own heading levels (§2.17.9).
* **L-qg** (micro variants) The micro record's `variants` is `none`: the micro-benchmarks call no
  kernel, and every record keeps the same fields (§2.17.7).
* **L-qh** (micro loads) The micro record writes the loads as the other records do, three numbers
  separated by single spaces (§2.17.7).
* **L-qi** (micro `--out`) A relative `--out` is taken from the Sea repository, as `BENCH_OUT` is,
  so `make` and a direct call write to the same directory (§2.17.7).
* **L-qj** (micro rules in final mode) Final mode forces §5.9's 1.0 s and 5 repetitions whatever
  the environment holds, so an exported quick setting can never shorten a final measurement
  (§2.17.7).
* **L-qk** (the micro cross stamp) `micro.sh --current --cross` builds and measures in one call, so
  it compares the stamp taken before the remote run with the one taken after it instead of a
  `stamp.txt` from an earlier `build` (§2.17.3, C1).
* **L-ql** (marker placement) The attempt marker is made after the checks that need no
  measurement and just before the first step that measures or could leave a partial result: for
  workloads `--cross` after the bundle is packed, for micro `--cross` before the compile (§2.17.3,
  C2).
* **L-qm** (nice in quick mode) Nice 0 is required in final mode only; the nice value is recorded
  in both modes, so a quick trial may run niced without blocking development (§2.17.3).
* **L-qn** (check order) The output-file, session and mode checks run before the preconditions,
  so a mistaken invocation is refused before anything is built or measured (§2.17.4).
* **L-qo** (build without a session) `workloads.sh build` needs no session: it depends only on the
  trees, which its stamp records (§2.17.4).
* **L-qp** (`ports.txt`) The build records its resolved ports directory, and `measure` refuses
  binaries built from another one, so an injected `PORTS` can never be measured as the committed
  ports (§2.17.4).
* **L-qq** (the mirror refusal) `workloads.sh` and `numpy.sh` also refuse a final-mode run into a
  quick session's directory, so a final measurement is never mixed with quick records; C3 itself
  requires only the quick-into-final refusal, and `kernels.sh` and `micro.sh` do not add the
  mirror (§2.17.3, C3).
* **L-qr** (the OpenBLAS header) `kernels.sh --cross` probes the include directory with
  `pkg-config` and then the Debian/Ubuntu paths, and accepts a directory only when the vendor
  harness's `config` line confirms `openblas_get_config`, so a wrong header is never linked
  silently (§2.17.6).
* **L-qs** (minimum of three) The reference time is the minimum of three validated runs, the
  least disturbed estimate of one call's cost (§2.17.6).
* **L-qt** (the reference batch) The kernel calibration times a batch of b ≥ 2 calls, growing ×4
  until it lasts 10 µs, instead of one call, because one call is below the macOS clock's tick and
  carries the first-call cost; the guard then allows a factor of 2 against that reference
  (§2.17.6).
* **L-qu** (starting the final run) The final run is started in the foreground or through
  `/bin/sh -c '… &'`, because zsh's `BG_NICE` gives a background job nice 5 and final mode
  refuses it (§2.17.3).

## 3. Intermediate files

The passes of §2.1 communicate through ten text files in the temporary directory (six before
sub-phase 4e-0, which adds `sea.hirl`; eight before phase 7, which adds `sea.hirf` and `sea.lir3`). This section
fixes their exact formats; `sea/include/passes.txt` (§3.9) is the same information in a form the
passes' generated `DATA` blocks are made from (§2.6), and the two change only together.

| File | Written by | Read by | Content |
|------|-----------|---------|---------|
| `sea.ast` | 1 `seaparse` | 2a `seaname` | the syntax tree as parsed, untyped (§3.4) |
| `sea.res` | 2a `seaname` | 2a `seacheck` | the same tree with names resolved, declarations checked and constants evaluated (§3.4.1) |
| `sea.hir1` | 2a `seacheck` | 2b | the resolved, typed tree (§3.5) |
| `sea.hir` | 2b `seaexpand` | 3a `seafuse` (from phase 7; before it `sealoop`) | the same after constant substitution and folding, elemental instantiation, `write_json` expansion and reachability (§3.5) |
| `sea.hirf` | 3a `seafuse` | 3a `sealoop` | `sea.hir` after fusion and the elemental applications (§2.12.3; from phase 7), with `HL` records of §3.5.9 |
| `sea.hirl` | 3a `sealoop` | 3a `sealower` | the same with the array constructs made explicit as scalar loops over element accesses (§3.5.9; from sub-phase 4e-0) |
| `sea.lir1` | 3a `sealower` | 3b | loop-level code over virtual registers (§3.6) |
| `sea.lir2` | 3b `seaopt` | 3c `sealopt` | the same after T1–T4 and T10 of §5.8 (§3.6; from sub-phase 5c-2, Decision 74; before it `seaopt` wrote `sea.lir`) |
| `sea.lir3` | 3c `sealopt` | 3d `seavec` | the same after T5–T10 of §5.8 (§3.6; from phase 7, where `sealopt` writes this file; before it `sealopt` wrote `sea.lir`) |
| `sea.lir` | 3d `seavec` | 4 | the same after scalar replacement and vectorization (§2.12.6, §3.6; from phase 7, Decisions 78, 98) |

The pass-1 input stream (§2.2) uses the header records of §3.2; pass 4 writes `sea.s`, which is
assembly text and has no records. `sea build --emit X` copies `sea.X` unchanged (§2.2), so a
dump is the file itself; §3.8 says how dumps are tested.

### 3.1 Lines, fields and field encodings

* A file is a sequence of **records**, one per line, each line ended by LF. Every byte of a file
  is LF or in `0x20`–`0x7E`: strings are escaped (below), so no other byte occurs.
* A record is a sequence of **fields** separated by exactly one space, with no leading or
  trailing space and no empty field. The first field is the record's **opcode** (lower-case
  letters and digits, or `#` + a name for a header record, §3.2); the fields after it are fixed
  by the opcode, in the order of the tables below and of `passes.txt`.
* A line is at most 65 536 bytes (`SEA_LIM_RECORD_BYTES`), Baysick's input-line limit
  (Baysick LANGUAGE.md §12, §15.2), so every record is read with one `LINPUT #k`. Every record
  stays far below it:
  * a record holds at most one string field, and a string field is at most 12 288 bytes: a
    string literal lies on one source line of at most 4096 bytes (LANGUAGE.md §3.1, §3.5), its
    value has at most as many bytes as its source text, and escaping writes each byte as at most
    3 bytes; a `#file` path is at most 4096 bytes (the operating systems' path limit); names and
    keys are identifiers of at most 63 bytes. No record carries a variable number of strings
    (the patterns of an `arm` are child `str`/`cs` nodes, §3.4, §3.5.5), except `rerr` of
    `sea.res` (§3.4.1): at most three substitutions of one error, each at most 4 096 bytes;
  * the records with a variable number of fields (`rtup`, `rfn`, `ttuple`, `inst`, `tbind`,
    `func`, `call`, `rcall`, `ret`, `chk`) repeat numbers or registers, each at most 7 bytes with its separator,
    and their counts are bounded by the limits of §2.6.1: at most `SEA_LIM_PARAMS` parameters
    and `SEA_LIM_RESULTS` results per function, plus one hidden address per result (§3.6.3),
    and the fixed arities of the runtime entry points and error codes (§4.8, §2.6.2); so such a
    record has fewer than 200 fields and 1 400 bytes.
* The last record of every file is `#end` (§2.2, end-of-input discipline).

**Field types.** Each field has one of these types (the names are those of `passes.txt`):

| Type | Written as | Read by a Baysick pass with |
|------|-----------|-----------------------------|
| `u` | an unsigned integer 0 … 999 999 999 in decimal, no sign, no leading zeros (`0` for zero) | `VAL` (at most 9 digits, Baysick LANGUAGE.md §6.1) |
| `i` | an `i64` value: if −10⁹ < v < 10⁹, an optional `-` and decimal digits as for `u` (zero is `0`, never `-0`); otherwise `#` and the 16 upper-case hexadecimal digits of its two's-complement 64-bit pattern (`#FFFFFFFFC4653600` is −1 000 000 000) | `VAL`, or four 16-bit limbs of 4 hex digits |
| `f` | always `#` and the 16 upper-case hexadecimal digits of the IEEE-754 binary64 pattern, sign bit first (`#3FB999999999999A` is 0.1, `#8000000000000000` is −0.0) | four 16-bit limbs (§2.7, table `C`) |
| `s` | a byte string, escaped (below) | `CHANGE` to codes, then decoding |
| `pos` | a source position `F:L:C`: `F` the index of the `#file` record (0 for the first, in header order), `L` the line in that file (from 1), `C` the column (from 1, counting bytes), each a `u` | `POS` of `:`, `VAL` |
| `site` | a run-time error site `F:L`: file index and line as in `pos` | as `pos` |
| an enumeration | one of the words `passes.txt` lists for it (`add`, `f64`, `arm64-macos`, …) | comparison with `DATA` words |
| a reference | a `u` number naming a table entry of the same file: `ty` a type (§3.5), `lid` a local, `fid` a function, `cid` a constant, `iid` an elemental instance, `blk` a structured LIR construct; or a prefixed token: `d`*n* a LIR data label, `s`*n* a stack slot, and the LIR registers `i`*n*, `f`*n*, `p`*n*, `x`*n*, `y`*n*, `m`*n* (§3.6) | `SEG$`, `VAL` |
| `fl` | `printf` flags: `-` for none, else the letters `l` (flag `-`), `p` (`+`), `s` (space), `z` (`0`), `a` (`#`), each at most once, in this order | codes |

A field is written `name:type`, then optionally `?`, then optionally `*` and a count. With `?`
(`u?`, `lid?`) the field may instead be the single character `-`, meaning "absent". With
`*count` (`ty*n`) the field is repeated as many times as the value of the earlier `u` field
`count`, each repetition a field of its own; both may be combined (`lid:lid?*n`: n fields, each a
local or `-`). In the tables of this section a bare reference type (`ty`, `lid`, `fid`, `cid`,
`iid`, `lab`, `slot`, `blk`), possibly with `?` or `*count`, stands for the field of that name and
type (`lid?*n` is `lid:lid?*n`); `passes.txt` writes every field as `name:type`.

**String escaping.** A string field holds the bytes of the string, each byte `b` written as the
character `b` itself if `0x21 ≤ b ≤ 0x7E` and `b ≠ 0x25` (`%`), and otherwise as `%` followed by
two upper-case hexadecimal digits: space is `%20`, `%` is `%25`, LF is `%0A`, the UTF-8 bytes of
`é` are `%C3%A9`. The **empty string** is the field `%` alone (a `%` not followed by two
hexadecimal digits occurs nowhere else). `#` and `-` in a string are ordinary characters: a field's
type is known from its position, and only the first field of a record can be a header opcode.

**Why these encodings.** Numbers are exact for Baysick: `VAL` reads at most 9 digits and doubles
cannot carry an `f64` pattern or an `i64` beyond 2⁵³, so everything else travels as hexadecimal
limbs (§2.8). A field never contains a blank and is never empty, so records split with `POS` on
`" "` and `SEG$`, Baysick's `PRINT #` writes every field unchanged (its lazy spaces never drop a
trailing blank, because there is none: Baysick LANGUAGE.md §8), and `=` compares two whole fields
exactly: the trailing-blank rule of §2.7 cannot apply to strings that contain no blank. A decoded
string value (which may contain blanks, or be empty) is never compared with `=`; passes compare
its codes or its length first (§2.7).

### 3.2 Header records

| Record | Fields | Meaning |
|--------|--------|---------|
| `#sea` | `ver:u` | the format version; `1` for the formats of this section |
| `#target` | `t:target` | the compilation target (enumeration `target`: `arm64-macos`, `x86_64-linux`) (`--target`, §2.2) |
| `#file` | `path:s` | one source file, in stream order: `std.sea` first (absent with `--no-prelude`, §2.2), then the program, its path as given to `sea`. File index `F` of positions counts these records from 0 |
| `#end` | — | the last record of the stream or file |

* **Pass-1 input stream** (written by the driver, §2.2): `#sea 1`, `#target`, then for each file
  its `#file` record followed by its source lines, then `#end`. A source line is written as `|`
  and its bytes, unescaped, then LF; a last line without LF is written the same way. Baysick's
  `LINPUT` removes one CR before the LF (Baysick LANGUAGE.md §15.2), which is the CR rule of
  LANGUAGE.md §3.1.
* **Intermediate files**: `#sea 1`, `#target`, all `#file` records in stream order, then the body
  records, then `#end`. Pass 1 writes this header (it writes its output after reading its whole
  input); every later pass copies the header records of its input unchanged.
* A pass stops with status 11 (§2.2) if its input lacks a header record, has them out of order,
  has a version other than 1 or an unknown target, or has a body record before the header ends.

### 3.3 Trees in post-order

`sea.ast` and `sea.hir*` hold trees. A tree is written in **post-order**: every node is one
record, written after the records of all its children, the children in source order (left to
right). Each node record **pops** a number of nodes, fixed by its opcode or given by one of its
fields (the "pops" column below and in `passes.txt`): those nodes are its children, the
earliest-written first. A reader therefore needs one stack: for each node record it pops that
many entries, builds the node with them as children in order, and pushes the node. Records never
refer to other nodes by number; the structure is given by the order alone. The header records,
the declaration records of §3.4.1 (`rerr`, `rtup`) and those of §3.5 (`t…` type records: `tvec tmat tfvec tfmat tstruct trec ttuple` and
`tptr` of §3.5.9; `fd`, `inst`, `fn`, `par`, `loc`) are not nodes and do not touch the stack; this list, not `passes.txt`, says which records are not nodes, and tools
take it from here. The records that end a section (`prog`, `cn`, `end`) pop their nodes and
push nothing, and the stack must then be empty; anything else is an internal error (status 11).

**Positions.** Every node of `sea.ast` and `sea.hir*` carries a `pos`: the position of the first
token of its source text. Parentheses are not nodes and are not part of the text of the node they
enclose, but they are part of the text of an enclosing node that starts with them: in
`(a + b) * c` the `+` node is at `a` and the `*` node at `(`. A node that a later pass creates
takes the position its rule names. Diagnostics (LANGUAGE.md §9.1, §9.2) report the position or
line of a node; which node each message reports is part of the error table (§2.6).

**Why post-order.** A pass reads its whole input into its tables (§2.7) and builds every tree
with one stack, without forward references; the stack never holds more entries than there are
nodes. The parser's recursion (bounded by the nesting limit 64, §2.7) produces post-order
naturally, and later passes iterate over post-order records (§2.7).

### 3.4 `sea.ast`

The syntax tree of the whole compilation unit, prelude first, exactly as parsed by the grammar of
LANGUAGE.md Appendix A: no names are resolved and nothing is typed. The body is the post-order of
each top-level item and statement in stream order, followed by `prog n`, the last record before
`#end`, which pops all n of them and is the one record without a position.

**Records** (every record except `prog` has `pos` as its first field after the opcode; the
"Pops" column is the number of child nodes as `passes.txt` writes it, §3.9, and "Children" names
them in order):

| Record | Fields after `pos` | Pops | Children (in order) | Source |
|--------|--------------------|------|---------------------|--------|
| `prog` | `n:u` (no `pos`) | `n` | n items and statements | the compilation unit |
| `const` | `name:s t:u` | `1+t` | [type if t = 1], expr | `const name [: type] = expr` |
| `struct` | `name:s n:u` | `n` | n `field` | `struct name { … }` |
| `field` | `name:s` | `1` | type | `name: type` in a struct |
| `fn` | `name:s el:u np:u nr:u` | `np+nr+1` | np `param`, nr types, block | `[elemental] fn name(…) [-> result] { … }`; el = 1 for `elemental`; nr = 0 (no result), 1 (`-> T`) or the number of types of a tuple result |
| `param` | `name:s rf:u d:u` | `1+d` | type, [default expr if d = 1] | `[ref] name: type [= expr]`; rf = 1 for `ref` |
| `type` | `base:s shape:shape nd:u` | `nd` | nd dims (each an `int` or `name`) | `base` is `f64`, `i64`, `bool`, `str` or an identifier; shape `s` (no brackets, nd 0), `v` `[]` (0), `m` `[,]` (0), `fv` `[d]` (1), `fm` `[d, d]` (2) |
| `let`, `var` | `t:u` | `2+t` | pattern, [type if t = 1], expr | `let`/`var pattern [: type] = expr` |
| `pname` | `name:s` | `0` | — | a name in a pattern |
| `pskip` | — | `0` | — | `_` in a pattern or as a tuple-assignment target |
| `ptuple` | `n:u` | `n` | n `pname`/`pskip` | `(p1, p2, …)` |
| `asg` | `op:asgop` | `2` | target, expr | `target op expr`; op `set add sub mul div` for `= += -= *= /=` |
| `tasg` | `n:u` | `n+1` | n targets (expressions or `pskip`), expr | `(t1, …, tn) = expr` |
| `cstmt` | — | `1` | a `call` | a call statement |
| `if` | `e:u` | `2+e` | cond, block, [else if e = 1: a `block`, or an `if` for `else if`] | `if` statement |
| `while` | — | `2` | cond, block | |
| `for` | `name:s npos:pos` | `2` | iterable (a `range` for a range loop, else an expression), block | `for name in … { … }`; `pos` is that of `for`, `npos` that of `name` (the loop variable); fields in this order |
| `match` | `n:u` | `n+1` | scrutinee, n `arm` | |
| `arm` | `k:u` | `k+1` | k `str` patterns, block | `"a" \| "b" => { … }`; k = 0 for `_` |
| `break`, `continue` | — | `0` | — | |
| `return` | `k:u` | `k` | k expressions | k = 0 `return`, 1 `return e`, ≥ 2 `return (e1, …, ek)` |
| `block` | `n:u` | `n` | n statements | `{ … }`, at the `{` |
| `int` | `v:i` | `0` | — | an integer literal's value (unsigned, ≤ 2⁶³; 2⁶³ is `#8000000000000000` and occurs only as the operand of `neg`) |
| `float` | `v:f` | `0` | — | a float literal, converted by pass 1 (§2.8) |
| `str` | `v:s` | `0` | — | a string literal's bytes after escape processing (LANGUAGE.md §3.5) |
| `true`, `false` | — | `0` | — | |
| `name` | `name:s` | `0` | — | an identifier |
| `dollar` | — | `0` | — | `$` |
| `neg`, `not` | — | `1` | operand | unary `-`, `!` |
| `bin` | `op:binop` | `2` | left, right | op `add sub mul div mod pow matmul eq ne lt le gt ge band bor and or` for `+ - * / % ^ @ == != < <= > >= & \| && \|\|` |
| `call` | `n:u` | `n+1` | callee, n arguments | `callee(a1, …, an)` |
| `narg` | `name:s` | `1` | expr | a named argument `name: expr` |
| `ref` | — | `1` | target | a `ref target` argument |
| `conv` | `t:cvtype` | `1` | expr | `f64(e)`, `i64(e)`, `str(e)` (there is no `bool(e)`: LANGUAGE.md Appendix A) |
| `index` | `n:u` | `n+1` | base, n indices (each an expression, `all` or `range`) | `base[i]`, `base[i, j]` |
| `all` | — | `0` | — | `:` as an index |
| `range` | `incl:u st:u` | `2+st` | lo, hi, [step if st = 1] | `lo..hi` (incl 0), `lo..=hi` (incl 1), `step` |
| `rangev` | — | `1` | a `range` | `( range )`, a range used as a value |
| `dot` | `name:s` | `1` | operand | `x.name`: field, projection or view, decided in pass 2a |
| `array` | `r:u` | `r` | r `row` | `[ … ]`, at the `[`; r = 0 for `[]` |
| `row` | `n:u` | `n` | n expressions | one row of an array literal |
| `slit` | `name:s n:u` | `n` | n `init` | `Name { … }` |
| `rlit` | `n:u` | `n` | n `init` | `{ … }` |
| `init` | `name:s` | `1` | expr | `name: expr` in a struct or record literal |
| `ifx` | — | `3` | cond, then-expr, else-expr (an `ifx` for `else if`) | `if` expression |

**What pass 1 has checked.** Every error of LANGUAGE.md §3 and every violation of the grammar of
LANGUAGE.md Appendix A and its disambiguation rules is reported by pass 1, so a written `sea.ast` is
syntactically valid: the child of `cstmt` is a `call` (otherwise `expression statement has no
effect`), `dollar` occurs only inside the index list of an `index` node (array-literal brackets
do not count, LANGUAGE.md §5.3), the operand `#8000000000000000` of `int` occurs only directly
under `neg` (parentheses produce no node, so `-(9223372036854775808)` is accepted too),
and
`a < b < c` has been rejected (comparisons are non-associative; a parenthesized comparison is an
ordinary operand). Everything that depends on names or types is reported by pass 2a.

**Example** (`ex.sea`, compiled with `--no-prelude`, so the program is file 0):

```sea
struct P {
    x: f64
    n: i64
}
fn scale(p: P, k: f64 = 2.0) -> f64 {
    return p.x * k ^ 2 * (0.5 * 3)
}
let p = P { n: 3, x: 1.5 }
var t = 0
for i in 0..p.n {
    t += scale(p, k: i)
}
t += scale(p)
printf("%.3f\n", t)
```

`sea build --emit ast --no-prelude ex.sea`:

```
#sea 1
#target arm64-macos
#file ex.sea
type 0:2:8 f64 s 0
field 0:2:5 x
type 0:3:8 i64 s 0
field 0:3:5 n
struct 0:1:1 P 2
type 0:5:13 P s 0
param 0:5:10 p 0 0
type 0:5:19 f64 s 0
float 0:5:25 #4000000000000000
param 0:5:16 k 0 1
type 0:5:33 f64 s 0
name 0:6:12 p
dot 0:6:12 x
name 0:6:18 k
int 0:6:22 2
bin 0:6:18 pow
bin 0:6:12 mul
float 0:6:27 #3FE0000000000000
int 0:6:33 3
bin 0:6:27 mul
bin 0:6:12 mul
return 0:6:5 1
block 0:5:37 1
fn 0:5:1 scale 0 2 1
pname 0:8:5 p
int 0:8:16 3
init 0:8:13 n
float 0:8:22 #3FF8000000000000
init 0:8:19 x
slit 0:8:9 P 2
let 0:8:1 0
pname 0:9:5 t
int 0:9:9 0
var 0:9:1 0
int 0:10:10 0
name 0:10:13 p
dot 0:10:13 n
range 0:10:10 0 0
name 0:11:5 t
name 0:11:10 scale
name 0:11:16 p
name 0:11:22 i
narg 0:11:19 k
call 0:11:10 2
asg 0:11:5 add
block 0:10:17 1
for 0:10:1 i 0:10:5
name 0:13:1 t
name 0:13:6 scale
name 0:13:12 p
call 0:13:6 1
asg 0:13:1 add
name 0:14:1 printf
str 0:14:8 %25.3f%0A
name 0:14:18 t
call 0:14:1 2
cstmt 0:14:1
prog 7
#end
```

`k ^ 2` binds tighter than `*` and `*` is left-associative (LANGUAGE.md §6.1), so the
`return` expression is `(p.x * (k ^ 2)) * (0.5 * 3)`; both outer `*` nodes start at `p`
(column 12), the parenthesized product at `0.5` (column 27). The float literals are 2.0
(`#4000000000000000`), 0.5 (`#3FE0000000000000`) and 1.5 (`#3FF8000000000000`); the format
string's bytes are `%.3f` and LF.

#### 3.4.1 `sea.res`

The syntax tree of `sea.ast` with its names resolved and its declarations checked: the output of
`seaname` and the input of `seacheck`, the two programs of pass 2a (§2.1, Decision 17). Nothing
in it is typed except what the declarations fix. Its records are those of `sea.ast` (§3.4) and
the records of this section (codes 50–63 of set `A` in `passes.txt`, §3.9), which occur only in
`sea.res`.

**Body**, in this order: at most one `rerr`; the `rtup` records, in id order; then the tree: the
records of the body of `sea.ast`, in the same order, each copied unchanged except the
replacements below. A replacement record is a node at the same position with the same children
(the same pops); its fields are those of the record it replaces, in the same order, followed by
its new fields (`rpowk` drops the operator field, always `pow`). So both programs build the same
tree and number its nodes alike, and every position, child count and error position of `sea.ast`
is unchanged in `sea.res`.

**Entered items and resolved regions.** An *entered* item is a top-level item that becomes a
symbol: every `fn`, `const` and `struct` item except one whose name an earlier item already has
(the later one is `redefinition of '%s'` and is not entered; an item with a predeclared name is
entered, after its `redefinition of predeclared name`, which from 4h an item of the prelude, in
file 0 of a stream with more than one `#file` record, does not get, lead decision L-s). The *resolved regions* are the body block
of every entered `fn`, the top-level statements of the program's file (the body of `.main`),
and the expression (not the type annotation) of every entered `const`, without the *skipped
regions*: every `match` statement and every `for` whose iterable is not a `range` (each whole
statement, the iterable and the body included), which the single program never walks while the
phase rule reports them (`not supported yet: match`, and `not supported yet: arrays` at the
`for`; until phase 4 implements them, which then removes them from this list). Then:

* every entered `fn`, `struct` and `const` item record is replaced by `rfn`, `rst`, or one of
  `rcni rcnf rcnb rcne rcn` respectively; a not-entered item is copied unchanged;
* every `int` record of the file becomes `rint`;
* in the resolved regions, every `name` becomes `rname` (the subtree of a `type` node is not
  part of a resolved region: its `int` and `name` dims stay as they are, apart from `rint`), every `pname` `rpname`, every `for`
  `rfor`, and every `bin` with operator `pow` that is a `powk` by the rule below becomes `rpowk`;
* from phase 6 (Decision 91, L-bx) a parameter default is a resolved region too: its `name`
  records become `rname` (resolved like those of a `const` item's value) and its `bin pow` records
  `rpowk` by the rule below; `seaname` writes no outcome for it (no `rcn…` record), and `seacheck`
  evaluates and checks it (§2.11.2);
* nothing else changes: `type` records (also those of signatures), struct fields (and, until phase
  6, parameter defaults), and everything outside the resolved regions (the bodies of not-entered
  functions among it) are copied unchanged apart from their `int` records.

**Declaration records** (not nodes, §3.3):

| Record | Fields | Meaning |
|--------|--------|---------|
| `rerr` | `pos:pos code:u k:u a:s*k` | the first error `seaname` found ("Errors" below): its position, its code (§2.6.2) and its k substitutions in text order, spelled as §2.6.2 says (k ≤ 3, the most `args` letters an error has; each a name, a word or a type, at most 4 096 bytes); the one record with more than one string field (§3.1) |
| `rtup` | `id:u n:u t:ty*n` | a tuple type (§3.5.1 `ttuple`): the results of a function with n ≥ 2 results; ids from 10, dense, in order of creation (the signatures of the entered functions in item order, a tuple already created reused) |

A `ty` field of `sea.res` is 0 (a type that has an error, already reported), 1–9 (the predefined
types of §3.5.1) or the id of an `rtup` of the same file. `seacheck` adds the types it infers and
numbers all types again when it writes `sea.hir1` (§3.5.1).

**Replacement records:**

| Record | Fields after `pos` | Pops | Replaces | Meaning |
|--------|--------------------|------|----------|---------|
| `rfn` | `name:s el:u np:u nr:u fid:u rty:ty t:ty*np` | `np+nr+1` | `fn` | an entered function: `el` 0 for an ordinary function, 1 for an elemental one and 2 for an ordinary function that LANGUAGE.md §8.6 (b) or (c) requires inlined (§2.11.1, §2.11.3); its `fid` (§3.5.4: `.main` is 1, the entered `fn` items follow from 2 in stream order), its result type `rty` (1 for none, the type of one result, the `rtup` of several; 0 when a result type has an error) and its parameters' types `t` in order (0 for a parameter whose type has an error, among them a `str` parameter while strings are `not supported yet`, §2.6.2) |
| `rst` | `name:s n:u sid:u` | `n` | `struct` | an entered struct: its number `sid`, from 1 in stream order among the entered structs |
| `rcni` | `name:s t:u cid:u v:i` | `1+t` | `const` | an entered constant (`cid` from 1 in stream order among the entered constants, as `cn`, §3.5.2) whose value is the `i64` v |
| `rcnf` | `name:s t:u cid:u v:f` | `1+t` | `const` | … whose value is the `f64` v |
| `rcnb` | `name:s t:u cid:u v:u` | `1+t` | `const` | … whose value is the `bool` v (0 or 1) |
| `rcne` | `name:s t:u cid:u e:cerr epos:pos` | `1+t` | `const` | … whose evaluation fails: e `ovf` (`integer overflow`, code 260) or `div0` (`integer division by zero`, 261) at the operator node at `epos` |
| `rcn` | `name:s t:u cid:u` | `1+t` | `const` | … for which `seaname` has no value ("Constants" below) |
| `rpname` | `name:s lid:lid` | `0` | `pname` | the local the name declares |
| `rfor` | `name:s npos:pos lid:lid` | `2` | `for` | the local of the loop variable |
| `rint` | `v:i fv:f?` | `0` | `int` | `fv`: the bits of the literal's value as an `f64` when that value is exact in `f64`, else `-`; for the literal 2⁶³ (only the operand of a `neg`, §3.4) the bits of −2⁶³, `#C3E0000000000000`, because the two are written as one constant (§3.5.5) |
| `rname` | `name:s k:nkind ref:u` | `0` | `name` | what the name denotes where it stands: k `loc` a local or parameter of the current function (ref its lid), `cst` an entered constant (its cid), `fn` an entered function (its fid), `st` an entered struct (its sid), `pd` a predeclared name (LANGUAGE.md Appendix C; ref 0; from 4h every name of Appendix C except `linspace`, `meshgrid`, `setdiff` and `bincount`, which only an entered item names, lead decision L-s), `none` nothing (ref 0) |
| `rpowk` | `k:i` | `2` | `bin` (`pow`) | a `^` whose exponent is a constant integer k with \|k\| ≤ `SEA_LIM_POWK` (below); both children are kept |

**Names.** Each name is looked up by the scope rules of LANGUAGE.md §3.3, §7.2 and §7.7: the
locals and parameters of the current function that are in scope (innermost first), then the
entered items, then the predeclared names (from 4h without the four prelude names `linspace`,
`meshgrid`, `setdiff` and `bincount`, which only an entered item names: with `--no-prelude` they
resolve as `none`, lead decision L-s). In the body of a prelude function (file 0 of a stream with
more than one `#file` record) the entered items are only those of the prelude: an item of the
program, even one that redefines a predeclared name (212), is never found there, so a program item
cannot capture a call inside the prelude (lead decision L-s). Locals are numbered as §3.5.4 says (the parameters
1 … np, then the declared names in source order; a shadowing declaration is a new local), and
the lids of `rpname`, `rfor` and `rname loc` are those numbers, so they are the lids of the
`loc` records `seacheck` writes. The expression of a constant sees no locals. A skipped
region keeps its `sea.ast` records: it declares no local, so its `pname`s and its `for` carry no
lid and take no number, and the locals after it are numbered as if it were absent (as the single
program numbered them). `seacheck` takes every lid from `sea.res`; it never derives a lid from a
counter of its own and never compares such a counter with the lids of `sea.res` (it checks only
what "What `seacheck` validates" lists).

**The `symbols` limit** is `seaname`'s. It counts cumulatively, as the single program entered its
symbols: 1 for `.main`, then each entered item in stream order, then for each entered function
in fid order its parameters and then the locals of its body, then the locals of `.main`, each
function's locals in the order of their lids; skipped regions count nothing. The declaration
that would make the count exceed `SEA_LIM_SYMBOLS` is reported (`program too large: symbols`,
at the position §2.6.2 gives for it).

**Reading `sea.res` in `seacheck`.** Its reader is that of the single program with these
requirements: a record has up to 72 fields with its opcode (`rfn` with 64 parameters: 71 after
the opcode; `rtup` with 64 components: 66), and every `u`, reference and enumerated field of a
record is kept (up to 69 for `rfn`, 66 for `rtup`), not only the first three, so the splitting
of a record into at most 12 fields and the three `u` slots of a node row must change; `rerr` and
`rtup` are not nodes and are never pushed on the tree stack; the strings of `rerr` are not
interned (they count against no limit); an `fv` creates no row of the constants table (a
literal's row comes from its `v`, as for `sea.ast`); and the count of types for the `types`
limit starts at the number of `rtup` records.

**Constants.** Both programs take the entered constants in one *constant order*: for each
entered constant in stream order that is not yet visited, it is visited: marked *waiting*, then
the nodes of its expression are scanned in file order, and each `rname cst` among them that
names a constant not yet visited is visited first, recursively (an explicit stack, no Baysick
recursion); when a constant's scan ends it is *checked* (`seacheck`) or *evaluated*
(`seaname`) and marked done. In `seacheck`, a name of a waiting constant met during a check
closes a cycle: it is `not a constant expression` (code 237) at that name.

`seaname` evaluates each entered constant, in the constant order, on the well-typed path only:
it types the expression by the rules of LANGUAGE.md §4.2 and §6 (untyped integer constants,
the conversion to an annotated `f64`, `i64` → `f64` where an operator converts), decides the
`powk` of every `^` in it (below), and evaluates it as §3.5.2 says (`FEPOW` for the other `^`
and for `pow`). It reports no error and checks no rule: where it cannot type or evaluate the
expression (a node other than a literal, `true`, `false`, `neg`, `not`, `bin`, `rpowk`, a name
of a constant or of `pi inf nan eps`, or a call whose callee is an `rname pd` naming `pow` or
`sqrt`, with positional arguments only (a call of a function item named `pow` or `sqrt`,
entered after its `redefinition of predeclared name`, is none of these); operand types the rules
do not accept; an annotation it cannot use; a name of a waiting
constant), and wherever the rule of LANGUAGE.md §7.2 leaves a constant unevaluated (it names a
constant without a value, Decision 25), it writes `rcn`. Its outcome is written in the item's
record: `rcni`, `rcnf`, `rcnb` a value; `rcne` an evaluation that fails (the first failing
operation in evaluation order); `rcn` none of these (no value). A constant with an `rcne` or
`rcn` outcome has no value for the constants after it.

`seacheck` checks every entered constant itself, in the constant order, as the single program
does, reports its errors, and then decides its value (§3.5.2, Decision 25):

1. if the check found an error, the constant has no value, and the outcome is ignored;
2. otherwise, if its expression names a constant without a value, or its type is the error type
   (0), or a node of its expression has the error type, or its expression holds a node `seaname`
   does not evaluate (one outside the list above: in a constant without an error of its own this
   is a call of a function item named `pow` or `sqrt`, or a node below an error-typed one), it has
   no value and no error, and the outcome is ignored (Decision 25 as refined: "a part of the
   expression whose type is in error");
3. otherwise the outcome must be a value of the kind of its derived type (`rcni` for `i64`,
   `rcnf` for `f64` (a constant `f64` `%`, `5.5 % 2.0`, is evaluated, L-dd), `rcnb` for `bool`), which becomes its value, or an `rcne` whose `epos` is
   the position of a `bin` or `neg` node of that constant's expression, `ovf` only at an `add`,
   `sub`, `mul` or `neg` and `div0` only at a `mod`: `seacheck` then reports `integer overflow`
   or `integer division by zero` at `epos` at that moment, so it takes its place in its find
   order, and the constant has no value. Any other outcome (`rcn` among them) is `BAD_RECORD`
   (status 11).

So a program without errors has a value for every constant, and `seacheck` reports
`BAD_RECORD` if it would write `sea.hir1` with a constant that has none. `seacheck` adds each
value to its constants table (`C` rows, §2.7) and enforces the `constants` limit for the
values of constants, at the constant's item (§2.6.2); `seaname` does not count them. A constant
without a value is read as a poisoned value (§3.5.2): it makes no `powk` and no further error.

**Constant exponents.** A `^` in a resolved region becomes `rpowk k` when, were it well typed,
§3.5.5's rule ("Constant exponents") would make it `powk k`: the exponent typed by the rules of
LANGUAGE.md §4.2 and §6 as `seacheck` types it (an untyped exponent taken as `f64`, an `i64` one
converted), its names resolved as above, and evaluated exactly; an exponent that names a
constant without a value is not constant. `seacheck` writes `powk k` for an `rpowk` whose `^` it
finds well typed, exactly where the phase-1 rule did (§3.5.5), and checks and writes nothing of
the exponent's value itself.

**Errors.** `seaname` reports the errors of the declaration checks only: those of the items (in
stream order) and then those of the signatures of the entered functions (in item order), the
codes §2.6.2 assigns to it ("Which program reports it"). It keeps the first of them in source
order (of two at one position, the first found), writes it as the `rerr` record, and still
writes the whole file and ends with status 0, so that `seacheck` checks the rest; with no such
error there is no `rerr`. A capacity limit `seaname` enforces (§2.7) is reported by `seaname`
itself at once, status 10 (the driver then uses no output). `seacheck` starts its own search
with the `rerr` error as the first error found, so of two errors at one position `seaname`'s is
reported (it was found first, by the order of §2.6.2).

**Protocol** (§2.2 steps 5–7). `seaname` reads `sea.ast` (Baysick file 1) and writes `sea.res`
(file 2); `seacheck` reads `sea.res` (file 1) and writes `sea.hir1` (file 2). Each copies the
header records of its input (§3.2), reads its input only with `LINPUT #1` after `IF END #1`,
requires the final `#end` (else `<program>: internal error: truncated input`, status 11, where
`<program>` is `seaname` or `seacheck`), writes `#end` last, and writes nothing to standard output.
The driver runs `seacheck` only on a `sea.res` that ends with `#end` (§2.2 step 6), and also when
it holds an `rerr`. `seaname` validates `sea.ast` as the single program did (a record of codes
50–63 in `sea.ast` is `BAD_RECORD`), and reports its errors and capacity errors as §2.6.2 says.

**What `seacheck` validates** (before checking anything; any violation is `BAD_RECORD`, status
11): every record against `passes.txt` (every enumerated field one of its words, every `pos`
well formed, only bytes 0x20–0x7E); `rerr` and `rtup` only before the tree, at most one `rerr`,
its `code` a code of phase `C2` with k equal to the number of its `args` letters; `rtup` ids
dense from 10 and every `ty` field 0, 1–9 or a defined id; no record of codes 50–63 outside the
places listed above, and none of `fn`, `const`, `struct`, `name`, `pname`, `for` or `int` where a
replacement is required; `fid`, `sid` and `cid` dense from 2, 1 and 1 in stream order; in each
function the lids of `rpname` and `rfor` dense from np + 1 in the source order of their
declarations (a loop variable before the locals of its body, although post-order writes its
`rfor` after them) and every `rname loc` naming a lid of that function; every `rname cst`, `fn` and `st` naming an entered item. The
constant guards above.

**Example** (`rs.sea`, compiled with `--no-prelude`):

```sea
const N = 2 * 3
fn parts(x: f64) -> (f64, i64) {
    let k = i64(x)
    return (x ^ 2, k + N)
}
let (a, b) = parts(pi)
for i in 0..b {
    printf("%g\n", a)
}
```

`sea build --emit res --no-prelude rs.sea`:

```
#sea 1
#target arm64-macos
#file rs.sea
rtup 10 2 4 3
rint 0:1:11 2 #4000000000000000
rint 0:1:15 3 #4008000000000000
bin 0:1:11 mul
rcni 0:1:1 N 0 1 6
rtype 0:2:13 f64 s 0 4
param 0:2:10 x 0 0
rtype 0:2:22 f64 s 0 4
rtype 0:2:27 i64 s 0 3
rpname 0:3:9 k 2
rname 0:3:17 x loc 1
conv 0:3:13 i64
let 0:3:5 0
rname 0:4:13 x loc 1
rint 0:4:17 2 #4000000000000000
rpowk 0:4:13 2
rname 0:4:20 k loc 2
rname 0:4:24 N cst 1
bin 0:4:20 add
return 0:4:5 2
block 0:2:32 2
rfn 0:2:1 parts 0 1 2 2 10 4
rpname 0:6:6 a 1
rpname 0:6:9 b 2
ptuple 0:6:5 2
rname 0:6:14 parts fn 2
rname 0:6:20 pi pd 0
call 0:6:14 1
let 0:6:1 0
rint 0:7:10 0 #0000000000000000
rname 0:7:13 b loc 2
range 0:7:10 0 0
rname 0:8:5 printf pd 0
str 0:8:12 %25g%0A
rname 0:8:20 a loc 1
call 0:8:5 2
cstmt 0:8:5
block 0:7:15 1
rfor 0:7:1 i 0:7:5 3
prog 4
#end
```

`parts` is function 2 with the result type `(f64, i64)`, the tuple type 10, and one parameter of
type 4 (`f64`); `N` is constant 1, of value 6, evaluated in `i64`.
In `split`, `x` is local 1 (the parameter) and `k` local 2; in `.main`, `a`, `b` and `i` are
locals 1, 2 and 3. The exponent `2` of `x ^ 2` is an untyped constant, taken as `f64` and
integral, so the `^` is `rpowk 2`. The type nodes of the signature are `rtype` records with their
types (4, 4, 3), as `sea.res` writes them from sub-phase 4d on (§3.4.2); before 4d they stayed
`type` records. The
`int` values 2, 3 and 0 are exact in `f64` (`#4000000000000000`, `#4008000000000000`,
`#0000000000000000`).

#### 3.4.2 `sea.res` in phase 4

Phase 4 (§8) extends `sea.res` so that `seaname` resolves every type and every struct literal and
`seacheck` keeps no type resolution of its own (Decision 17's division: names and declarations in
`seaname`, typing in `seacheck`). Everything of §3.4.1 holds, with these additions (codes 64–72 of
set `A`, which occur only in `sea.res`). Sub-phase 4d brings the array types, 4g-1 the `str`
constants, 4g-2 the struct types and the struct literals (Decision 47); until a sub-phase lands,
the records it brings are not written and §3.4.1 applies unchanged to what they would cover.

**Skipped regions.** A `for` whose iterable is not a `range` stops being a skipped region in 4d
(element loops, LANGUAGE.md §7.5) and a `match` in 4g-1; both are then resolved regions like any
other statement (their loop variable takes its lid in the order of §3.4.1, "Names": a `for` loop
variable before the locals of its body). After phase 4 there are no skipped regions.

**Type nodes.** Every `type` node of an entered item (the parameter and result types of an
entered `fn`, the field types of an entered `struct`, the annotation of an entered `const`) and
of a resolved region becomes `rtype`, which carries the resolved type; its dims stay its children,
an `int` dim as `rint` and a `name` dim as `rname`. A dim name is looked up like any name (§3.4.1,
"Names"), except that in a signature, a struct field or a constant's annotation no local is in
scope (only the entered items, then the predeclared names). A `type` node of a not-entered item
stays as it is.

**Struct literals.** Every `slit` of a resolved region becomes `rslit`, whose `sid` is the entered
struct its name denotes where it stands, looked up as names are (a local of that name hides the
struct), or 0 when the name denotes no entered struct; `seacheck` reports `unknown struct type`
(229) at an `rslit` with `sid` 0 (§2.6.2, at word `type`). Record literals (`rlit`) are unchanged.

**`str` constants** (4g-1). A constant whose value is a `str` (LANGUAGE.md §7.2: a string literal, a
constant naming one, or `+` of such) is written `rcns` with its bytes, evaluated by `seaname` on
the well-typed path as §3.4.1 says; `seacheck`'s step 3 of "Constants" accepts `rcns` exactly for
the derived type `str`. Two lead decisions of 4g complete it (§0):

* **L-g.** A comparison (`==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`) of two `str` constant expressions is a
  `bool` constant expression, evaluated by `seaname` byte-wise and unsigned with a proper prefix
  the smaller (the order of rule 32's `sea_str_cmp`, LANGUAGE.md §4.4); a constant whose value it is
  is written `rcnb` like any `bool` constant (`const B = "a" < "b"` is `rcnb` with the value 1).
* **L-f.** Every `str` value `seaname` computes while evaluating a constant (the value of a
  literal, of a named constant, of each `+`) has at most `SEA_LIM_LINE_BYTES` (4 096) bytes; a longer
  one is `program too large: strings` (400) at the constant's item (§2.6.2, `here`), reported by
  `seaname` at once like its other capacity errors. So every `rcns` value, the `cs` leaf of its `cn` (§3.5.2) and
  every `cs` that constant substitution puts in place of a `cref` (§3.5.7) stay within §3.1's 12 288-byte string field, as a
  literal does; no limit is added (`SEA_LIM_LINE_BYTES` is the bound of one source line, which
  bounds every literal).

**The type table** of `sea.res` holds the `rtup` records of §3.4.1 and the type records below; ids
are dense from 10 over all of them, given in order of creation, and the table is written in id
order before the tree (after the `rerr`, if any), each `rtst` followed directly by its `rtfd`
records. `seaname` creates the types in this order, a type that already exists never being created
again (arrays and tuples are the same type when structurally equal, structs by declaration,
§3.5.1), and a type with an error never being created (its uses take 0):

1. one struct type per entered struct, in `sid` order (so the struct with `sid` s has id 9 + s);
2. the types of the fields of the entered structs, in `sid` order, each struct's fields in
   declaration order;
3. the types of the signatures of the entered functions, in item order, each function's
   parameters in order and then its result types (a tuple after its components, §3.4.1);
4. the type of every other `rtype` node, in file order (the annotations of constants and of
   `let`/`var` among them).

An array type's element type always exists when the array type is created (it is predefined or a
struct type of step 1).

| Record | Fields | Meaning |
|--------|--------|---------|
| `rtvec` | `id:u elt:ty` | `T[]` (§3.5.1 `tvec`) |
| `rtmat` | `id:u elt:ty` | `T[,]` |
| `rtfvec` | `id:u elt:ty n:u` | `T[n]` |
| `rtfmat` | `id:u elt:ty r:u c:u` | `T[r,c]` |
| `rtst` | `id:u name:s sid:u n:u`, followed by n `rtfd` records | the type of the entered struct `sid` (its name, its n fields in declaration order) |
| `rtfd` | `name:s ty:ty` | one field: its name and type (0 if the field's type has an error) |

| Record | Fields after `pos` | Pops | Replaces | Meaning |
|--------|--------------------|------|----------|---------|
| `rtype` | `base:s shape:shape nd:u ty:ty` | `nd` | `type` | a resolved type node: the fields of `type`, then its type (0 if it has an error) |
| `rslit` | `name:s n:u sid:u` | `n` | `slit` | a struct literal and the struct it names (0: none) |
| `rcns` | `name:s t:u cid:u v:s` | `1+t` | `const` | an entered constant whose value is the `str` v |

**Resolving a type node** (`seaname`; for one node first the base, then the dims left to right,
then the shape; the first error found is the node's, and the node's type is then 0):

* the base: `f64`, `i64`, `bool`, `str` are types 4, 3, 2, 5; `Figure`, `Axes`, `Lu`, `Chol` the
  handle types 6–9; an identifier that denotes an entered struct (looked up as a name, in the
  scope above) its struct type; anything else is `unknown struct type` (229) at the node;
* a dim: an `rint` is its value; an `rname` of an entered constant with an `rcni` outcome is that
  value, with `rcnf`, `rcnb` or `rcns` the error `type mismatch: expected i64, found f64` (`bool`,
  `str`; 201) at the dim, with `rcne` or `rcn` (no value: §3.4.1) the type 0 without an error (the
  constant's own error is reported by `seacheck`); an `rname` of kind `none` is `undeclared name
  '%s'` (200) at the dim, and of any other kind `not a constant expression` (237) at the dim;
* the shape: `s` is the base type; `v`, `m` the dynamic vector and matrix of the base, `fv`, `fm`
  the fixed ones with the dims as extents. An extent below 0 is `invalid array size %d` (263) at
  the first such dim, with its value; extents whose product exceeds `SEA_LIM_FIXED_ELEMS` are
  `fixed-size array too large: use a dynamic array` (216) at the node; an array of a handle type
  is `arrays cannot hold %s` (258) at the node, with the handle type's name;
* the phase rule (§2.6.2): while a sub-phase of §8 does not implement them, a fixed-size array
  type (until 4e), a struct type (until 4g-2), a fixed-size type of `str` elements (from 4e until
  4g-2: `strings`) and a handle type (until phases 8 and 9) are `not
  supported yet` (259: `arrays`, `structs`, `strings`, `handle types`) at the node, found after every
  error above. From 4g-1 a type node with the base `str` and a shape `s`, `v` or `m` has its type
  wherever it stands (in a signature too: `str` is 5, `str[]` and `str[,]` their array types) and
  no phase-rule error. Before 4g-1 `str` follows the rules of §2.6.2 at the nodes they name, and the type written
  depends on where the node stands: in a signature (a parameter or result type of an entered
  `fn`) a type node with the base `str`, of any shape, has the type 0 and creates no type (its
  `rtype` has `ty` 0, and so has its slot in `rfn`; `seaname` reports `strings` at the `param`
  node or the result's type node, §2.6.2); everywhere else (a constant's annotation, a struct
  field, a `let`/`var` annotation) `str` is the type 5 and `str[]`, `str[,]` create their array
  types of element 5 like any other; `seacheck` then reports `strings` at the local's declaring
  node (`let x: str[] = …`: at the `pname`) or at the constant's annotation (its type node), and a
  struct field's `str` is covered by the struct item's 259 `structs` until 4g.

`seaname` resolves the type nodes in this order: the annotations of the entered constants whose
shape is `s` (the constant evaluation of §3.4.1 needs them), then the constants are evaluated,
then the struct fields (step 2), the signatures (step 3) and every other type node in file order.
The capacity limit `types` (400) for a type `seaname` creates is reported at the type node being
resolved, except for a type of a signature, which is reported at the `fn` item.

**Before 4g-2** no struct type exists: step 1 creates nothing, no `rtst` or `rtfd` record is
written, and a type node whose base denotes an entered struct is 259 `structs` with the type 0.
The field types of an entered struct are nonetheless resolved in step 2 (the struct item itself
reporting 259 `structs`, §2.6.2): they are `rtype` nodes, their errors are reported, and their
array types are created (`struct P { v: i64[] }` creates `rtvec 10 3`).

**Struct declarations** (`seaname`, 4g-2), for each entered struct in stream order: `redefinition of
'%s'` (235) at the later of two fields of one name (at word `binding`); `field name reserved for
views` (222) at a field named `T`, `flat`, `col` or `row`; the errors of each field's type node
(above); and `recursive struct` (221) at the `struct` node of every struct whose type contains
itself, through the types of its fields, of the fields of the structs they contain, and of the
elements of fixed and dynamic arrays among them, however deep. `seacheck` checks struct
literals against the fields of the `rtst` records: `missing field` (204), `duplicate field`
(205), `unknown field` (206); and `no field '%s' in %s` (249) at a `dot`.

**`seacheck` reading and validation**, in addition to §3.4.1: the type records occur only in the
type table, `rtst` records exactly once per entered struct in `sid` order at ids 10, 11, …, each
followed by exactly n `rtfd` records; every `ty` field is 0, 1–9 or an id of the table (a field
may name an id defined later in the table); no `type` record remains in an entered item or a
resolved region and no `slit` in a resolved region; the `types` limit's count starts at the size
of the type table. `seacheck` takes every annotation's type from its `rtype` and adds only the
types it infers.

**Example** (`rt.sea`, `--no-prelude`; after phase 4):

```sea
const N = 2
struct P {
    v: f64[N]
}
fn first(ps: P[]) -> f64 {
    return ps[0].v[0]
}
let a = [P { v: [1.5, 2.5] }]
printf("%g\n", first(a))
```

`sea build --emit res --no-prelude rt.sea`:

```
#sea 1
#target arm64-macos
#file rt.sea
rtst 10 P 1 1
rtfd v 11
rtfvec 11 4 2
rtvec 12 10
rint 0:1:11 2 #4000000000000000
rcni 0:1:1 N 0 1 2
rname 0:3:12 N cst 1
rtype 0:3:8 f64 fv 1 11
field 0:3:5 v
rst 0:2:1 P 1 1
rtype 0:5:14 P v 0 12
param 0:5:10 ps 0 0
rtype 0:5:22 f64 s 0 4
rname 0:6:12 ps loc 1
rint 0:6:15 0 #0000000000000000
index 0:6:12 1
dot 0:6:12 v
rint 0:6:20 0 #0000000000000000
index 0:6:12 1
return 0:6:5 1
block 0:5:26 1
rfn 0:5:1 first 0 1 1 2 4 12
rpname 0:8:5 a 1
float 0:8:18 #3FF8000000000000
float 0:8:23 #4004000000000000
row 0:8:18 2
array 0:8:17 1
init 0:8:14 v
rslit 0:8:10 P 1 1
row 0:8:10 1
array 0:8:9 1
let 0:8:1 0
rname 0:9:1 printf pd 0
str 0:9:8 %25g%0A
rname 0:9:16 first fn 2
rname 0:9:22 a loc 1
call 0:9:16 1
call 0:9:1 2
cstmt 0:9:1
prog 5
#end
```

`P` is struct 1, type 10 (step 1); its field `v` has the type `f64[2]`, id 11 (step 2: the dim `N`
is constant 1 with the value 2); the parameter of `first` has the type `P[]`, id 12 (step 3), its
result `f64` (4). The literal `[P { … }]` has `str`/struct elements, so it is a dynamic `P[]`
(LANGUAGE.md §6.9, Decision 20); that is `seacheck`'s typing and does not show here.

### 3.5 `sea.hir1` and `sea.hir`

Both files have the same records; §3.5.6 lists what may appear in which (`sea.hirl`, the third HIR
file, from sub-phase 4e-0, is §3.5.9). The body has up to four
parts, in this order: the **type table**, the **constants** (`sea.hir1` only), the **elemental
instances** (`sea.hir` only) and the **functions**.

#### 3.5.1 Types

Every type of the program has one id. Ids 1–9 are predefined and never written: 1 `void` (no
value: statements, functions without a result, format pieces), 2 `bool`, 3 `i64`, 4 `f64`,
5 `str`, 6 `Figure`, 7 `Axes`, 8 `Lu`, 9 `Chol`. Every other type has one record, ids from 10:

| Record | Fields | Type |
|--------|--------|------|
| `tvec` | `id:u elt:ty` | `T[]` |
| `tmat` | `id:u elt:ty` | `T[,]` |
| `tfvec` | `id:u elt:ty n:u` | `T[n]` |
| `tfmat` | `id:u elt:ty r:u c:u` | `T[r,c]` |
| `tstruct` | `id:u name:s n:u`, followed by n `fd` records | a declared struct, fields in declaration order |
| `trec` | `id:u n:u`, followed by n `fd` records | an anonymous record type (LANGUAGE.md §4.6) |
| `fd` | `name:s ty:ty` | one field |
| `ttuple` | `id:u n:u t:ty*n` | the results of a multiple-result function (n ≥ 2) |

Two types have the same id exactly when they are the same type: arrays, records and tuples
structurally (LANGUAGE.md §4.6 for records), structs by declaration. Fixed extents are the values
pass 2a computed for them (a `const` extent is evaluated exactly in integers by pass 2a, because
types need it; LANGUAGE.md §4.5). The range nodes of loops, indices and range values all have the
type `i64[]` (`tvec` of 3).

**Numbering.** Ids from 10 are given in order of first reference in the records after the type
table (file order, fields left to right); when a type is numbered, its component types that are
not yet numbered are numbered first, in order (element type; field types in declaration order;
tuple components), recursively. Types no record after the table refers to (directly or as a
component) are not written. The table is written in id order.

#### 3.5.2 Constants (`sea.hir1`)

| Record | Fields | Pops | Children |
|--------|--------|------|----------|
| `cn` | `cid:u name:s ty:ty pos:pos` | `1` | the constant's expression |

One `cn` per `const` item, in stream order, numbered from 1, each preceded by its value: pass 2a
evaluates every constant (LANGUAGE.md §7.2) exactly, as it evaluates constant exponents (§3.5.5,
with the emulation of §2.8 for `f64` and exact `i64`), and writes the result as **one leaf**: a
`ci`, `cf`, `cb` or `cs` of the constant's type, at the position of the expression's root. So the
child of a `cn` is always a single leaf, and constant substitution (§3.5.7) puts one leaf in place
of each `cref`. An evaluation that overflows `i64` or divides an `i64` by zero is the compile
error 260 or 261 (§2.6.2) and writes nothing. A constant that names a constant without a value
(one with an error, a failed evaluation or none of its own), whose type is the error type (after
another error), any node of whose expression has the error type, or that calls a function item
named `pow` or `sqrt` (entered after its `redefinition of predeclared name`), is not evaluated at all and reports nothing of its evaluation
(LANGUAGE.md §7.2, Decision 25); a use of a constant without a value reads a poisoned value
(no `powk`, no further error). `pos` is that of the `const` keyword. A use of the
constant is a `cref` node. From phase 4a `seaname` evaluates the constants and hands each value, or
the outcome without one, to `seacheck` in the constant's `sea.res` record (`rcni` … `rcn`,
§3.4.1); `seacheck` writes the `cn` leaf from it.

#### 3.5.3 Elemental instances (`sea.hir`)

| Record | Fields |
|--------|--------|
| `inst` | `iid:u fid:fid rty:ty n:u t:ty*n` |

An instance is an elemental function (`fid`) applied with one particular list of argument types
(`t`, one per parameter, after the conversions of LANGUAGE.md §4.2; at least one of the
elemental parameters has an array type); `rty` is the type of the application's value (an array
of the broadcast shape, LANGUAGE.md §6.3, or a tuple of such arrays). Applications with the same
`fid` and argument types share one instance. Instances are numbered from 1 in order of first
reference by an `emap` record and written in id order.

#### 3.5.4 Functions

```
fn <fid> <name> <kind> <rty> <np> <nl> <pos>
par <name> <ty> <mode>                       np records: locals 1 … np
loc <name> <ty> <mut> <pos>                  nl records: locals np+1 … np+nl
<the body's records>
end                                          pops the body (one block)
```

| Record | Fields | Pops | Meaning |
|--------|--------|------|---------|
| `fn` | `fid:u name:s kind:fkind rty:ty np:u nl:u pos:pos` | `0` | kind `main` (the implicit main function of the top-level statements, LANGUAGE.md §7.2, named `.main`), `fn`, `elem` (an `elemental fn`) or `inl` (an ordinary function that LANGUAGE.md §8.6 (b) or (c) requires inlined, from an `rfn` with `el` 2; `sealoop` removes it, §2.11.4); `rty` the result type (1 for none, a `ttuple` for several); `pos` the `fn` or `elemental` keyword, for `.main` line 1, column 1 of the program's file |
| `par` | `name:s ty:ty mode:pmode` | `0` | a parameter; mode `val` or `ref` |
| `loc` | `name:s ty:ty mut:lmut pos:pos` | `0` | a local; mut `let`, `var` or `for` (a loop variable, LANGUAGE.md §7.5); `pos` its name in the declaration (for a loop variable the `npos` of its AST `for`) |
| `end` | — | `1` | the end of the function; pops its body block |

Functions are numbered from 1: `.main` first, then every `fn` item in stream order (the prelude's
first); in `sea.hirl` the prelude's functions are dropped and the rest renumbered densely in their
order (§3.5.9 L18, from 4h). Locals are numbered per function: the parameters in order, then the locals in the order
of their declaring names in the source (the names of a `let`/`var` pattern from left to right, a
loop variable at its `for`), then the temporaries `.t1`, `.t2`, … that pass 2a creates
("Evaluation order", §3.5.5), then the locals `.j1`, `.j2`, … that pass 2b creates (§3.5.7), and
in `sea.hirl` then the locals `.l1`, `.l2`, … that `sealoop` creates (§3.5.9) and, from 4h, then
the locals `.i1`, `.i2`, … that its rewrite L18 creates for the locals of inlined prelude bodies
(§3.5.9, lead decision L-u).
Each group is numbered in the order of its declaring records in the function's body (file order:
the `bind` of a `.t` local, the `bind`, `forr` or `fore` of a `.j` local, the `tmp`, `bind`,
`rcnt` or `hloop` of a `.l` local, the `bind`, `tbind`, `forr` or `tmp` of an `.i` local), so the
numbering is a property of the written file, and the names count
from 1 in each function. A shadowing declaration (`var lo = lo`) is a new local. The body of
`.main` is a `block`, at the position of `.main`, holding the top-level statements of the
program's file in order (the prelude has items only). Default arguments, named arguments and the
`ref` marks of calls are resolved: a call's arguments are written in parameter order (their
evaluation order is kept by the rule "Evaluation order" of §3.5.5), a missing argument is a copy
of the parameter's default expression with the default's own positions, and a `ref` argument is
an `rarg` node.

#### 3.5.5 Nodes

Expression records have the fields `pos ty` first: `ty` is the expression's static type after
every implicit conversion, which pass 2a has made explicit (`cvt`, `dyn`, `fix`, and for the
components of a tuple assignment the `cv` flags of `tasg`, which pass 2a sets, pass 2b carries
unchanged and `sealoop` realizes by L12 (§3.5.9) or carries (a scalar 1), since a component has no
expression node to put a `cvt`, `dyn` or `fix` on); untyped integer
constants (LANGUAGE.md §4.2) are written with their decided type (`ci` for `i64`, `cf` for
`f64`). Statement records have `pos` first and no type.

| Record | Fields after `pos` | Pops | Children | Meaning |
|--------|--------------------|------|----------|---------|
| `ci` | `ty v:i` | `0` | — | an `i64` constant |
| `cf` | `ty v:f` | `0` | — | an `f64` constant (also `pi` `#400921FB54442D18`, `inf` `#7FF0000000000000`, `nan` `#7FF8000000000000` (the quiet NaN that LANGUAGE.md §10.1 leaves unspecified), `eps` `#3CB0000000000000`, LANGUAGE.md §10.1) |
| `cb` | `ty v:u` | `0` | — | `false` (0) or `true` (1) |
| `cs` | `ty v:s` | `0` | — | a `str` constant |
| `lv` | `ty lid` | `0` | — | a local or parameter of the current function |
| `cref` | `ty cid` | `0` | — | a named constant (`sea.hir1`) |
| `dol` | `ty dim:u` | `0` | — | `$`: the extent of dimension `dim` (0 or 1) of the base of the innermost enclosing `idx` (LANGUAGE.md §5.3) |
| `cvt` | `ty` | `1` | operand | `i64` → `f64`, of a scalar or element by element (LANGUAGE.md §4.2) |
