```
                      check-includes`; POSIX sh and awk): every SEA_* name and value and every
                      error, errno and entry record of the .inc files equals the tables of §2.6.1,
                      §2.6.2 and §4.8, and every record format of passes.txt equals the tables
                      of §3.2–§3.6 (§3.9), in both directions
  run.sh              Mac runner of programs/, errors/ and the passes/ dumps (it compiles with
                      the test's directory as working directory, so diagnostics name NAME.sea);
                      cross.sh, cross_pack.sh, cross_run.sh: the x86_64-linux cases on the
                      Linux host (§6.6.1, `make cross`, `make cross-pack`)
  NAME.status         the expected exit status: a decimal number and LF
  harness/            Baysick test programs of the shared modules (limb, f64emu, fltlit) that
                      read the committed vectors
  arith_check.sh      runs harness/ on vectors/ (exact arithmetic and float literals)
  lib_check.sh        checks passes/lib against the contract (e.g. the BAD_DATA copy, §2.6.2)
  driver_check.sh     the driver's options, messages and statuses (§2.2)
  passes/NAME.out     (optional, beside a dump test) the program's expected standard output when
                      built and run
  passes/NAME.lir     with neither NAME.sea nor NAME.lir1: a pass-4 test, LIR written by hand
                      (the input of seagen_a64, §3.6); + NAME.out (the expected standard output)
                      [+ NAME.err, NAME.status]. stage.sh runs seagen_a64 on it, assembles the
                      sea.s with `as`, links it with libsea.a and libbaysickrt.a as the driver
                      does, runs the program with standard input /dev/null and compares
                      standard output with NAME.out, standard error with NAME.err (else empty)
                      and the exit status with NAME.status (else 0)
  NAME.meta           (optional, beside a programs/ or errors/ test) `key=value` lines for the
                      runner: `stdout=epipe` connects standard output to a pipe whose reading
                      end is closed before the program starts (for `cannot write '<stdout>':
                      Broken pipe`, LANGUAGE.md §9.2); `stdout=closed` starts the program
                      with standard output closed (`>&-`, for `cannot write '<stdout>': Bad
                      file descriptor`); with either key NAME.out is not compared
  rt/arm64_macos/NAME.s, rt/x86_64_linux/NAME.s (§4.7.1) a runtime test: an assembly program, in
                      Baysick's assembly style, that calls runtime entry points through rt.inc
                      and is linked with libsea.a; + NAME.out [+ NAME.err, NAME.status], the
                      expected bytes derived from LANGUAGE.md and §4 (`make test-rt`)
  stage.sh            runs one pass on the committed golden output of the previous pass
                      (passes/NAME.ast → seaname → compare with NAME.res, NAME.res → seacheck →
                      compare with NAME.hir1, and so on; from 4e-0 the pairs NAME.hir → sealoop
                      → NAME.hirl and NAME.hirl → sealower → NAME.lir1 replace NAME.hir →
                      sealower → NAME.lir1), so each pass is tested on its own (`make test-stage`); a passes/NAME.lir with
                      neither NAME.sea nor NAME.lir1 is the input of a pass-4 test (above), a
                      passes/NAME.hirl with neither NAME.sea nor NAME.hir that of a sealower test
  protocol.sh         the pass-protocol tests (truncated inputs, missing #end, §2.2), for every
                      pass program (seaname on a truncated sea.ast, seacheck on a truncated
                      sea.res, …)
  check_data.sh       checks the generator (§2.6.3) on the contract files: every generated
                      line ≤ 255 bytes, every record present (`make check-data`)
  vectors/NAME.py     generators of exact test vectors (float-literal bits, printf digits),
                      run with `uv run`; their outputs are committed beside them, and the tests
                      read only the committed outputs (Python is never needed to run a test)
```

Test names carry the spec area: `lex_*`, `res_*` (`sea.res`, §3.4.1), `type_*`, `idx_*`, `op_*`, `stmt_*`, `fn_*`, `elem_*`,
`err_*`, `lib_*`, `fmt_*`, `json_*`, `plot_*`, `la_*`, `perf_*`.

* **Format tests** compare `printf` output for chosen values against the bytes the C99 rules give
  (the expected bytes are worked out from the exact binary values, including tie cases).
* **Literal-conversion tests** pin the bits of hard decimal-to-binary cases.
* **Folding tests** check that expressions near the limits of §2.8 (overflowing products,
  division by zero, `sqrt` of a negative constant, `inf`/`nan` operands) compile, are not
  folded, and give the IEEE results at run time.
* **Elementary-function tests** (`math/`) check the ≤ 1 ulp bound against reference values
  computed at high precision (the reference generator is a script run with `uv run --with
  mpmath`; Python is only ever run through `uv`), check that results which are exactly
  representable (`pow(2, 10)`, `exp(0)`, `log(1)`) are exact, and check that scalar and vector
  forms and both targets give identical bits.
* **Plot tests** (`plots/`): a `.struct` file lists, per SVG, the expected counts of plot areas,
  polylines, markers, bars, images and `<line>` contour segments, and the exact texts (titles,
  labels, legend entries, tick labels) — all derivable from LANGUAGE.md §12 by hand for tiny figures — and
  the runner checks well-formed XML, the structure, and identical bytes on both targets.
* **Linear-algebra tests** use exact data (small integer matrices with exact factorizations and
  solutions), as Baysick's product tests do, so even class-R results are exact and identical,
  plus ∞/NaN propagation tests and empty-operand tests.
* **Pass-protocol tests** feed each pass a truncated input (no `#end`) and check status 11 and
  the one line `<pass>: internal error: truncated input` on standard error, and check that the
  driver rejects a pass output without `#end` (§2.2).
* **Tests of the pass-2a split** (phase 4a, §3.4.1, §2.6.2 "Which program reports it"): a
  `NAME.res` beside every `NAME.hir1` dump test, hand-derived from §3.4.1; the example `rs` of
  §3.4.1 (`rs.sea`, `.ast`, `.res`, `.hir1`); `res_*` dump tests (`NAME.sea`, `.ast`, `.res`) for
  every replacement record and every outcome: `rname` of each kind (a local shadowing an outer one,
  `var lo = lo`, a loop variable, a block scope, a struct name, an undeclared name), `rint` with
  `fv` `-` and the 2⁶³ literal, `rcni rcnf rcnb`, `rcne` (`ovf`, `div0`), `rcn` (an expression
  `seaname` cannot type or evaluate, and a constant naming one without a value), a cycle, a
  skipped region (a `match`, a `for` over an array) copied unresolved, `rpowk` from a constant and none
  where a local shadows the constant, a not-entered function copied unchanged, `rtup` reused;
  and an `rerr` of each error `seaname` reports, the first of two by position, and the first
  found of two at one position; `errors/` tests of the merge: a `seaname` error after and before
  a `seacheck` error in source order, two at one position (`not supported yet: elemental
  functions` and `missing return` at one `fn` keyword: the first is reported), a constant's
  `integer overflow` before and after another error. Every test of the corpus (`programs/`,
  `errors/`, the dumps, `rt/`, `math/`) passes unchanged; the scripts `driver_check.sh`,
  `protocol.sh` and `stage.sh` change as §8 (4a) lists.
* **Tests of the pass-3a split** (sub-phase 4e-0, §3.5.9, Decisions 26–30). Every test of the corpus
  passes unchanged (all `programs/`, `errors/` with byte-identical diagnostics, every `.ast .res
  .hir1 .hir .lir1 .lir` dump, `rt/`, `math/`, the W4 acceptance, the heap check). Every dump test
  with a `.sea` and a `.lir1` gains a `NAME.hirl`, the input stage.sh gives `sealower` (17 files):
  for the 11 tests without a rewritten construct (`fn_multi fn_printf fn_ref fn_ref_order lx
  math_lower op_shortcircuit stmt_loops stmt_tasg type_ifx_arm arr_rule36`) it is the `.hir` byte
  for byte (§3.5.9, "Unchanged functions"); for the 6 tests that use `zeros`, `ones`, `len` or a
  `for` over a vector (`arr_rule16 arr_rule17 arr_rule18 arr_rule19 arr_rule30 arr_rule31`) it is
  written by hand from §3.5.9 (L1–L4, types, locals, positions) by the generator that writes their
  other files (`tests/vectors/dump4d_cases.py`, or a `dump4e0_cases.py` in its style, every record
  written by hand, the copy cases asserted equal to the `.hir`), never printed by a pass. The two
  stage pairs check each hand-written file from both sides: `sealoop` must write it from the
  `.hir`, and `sealower` must lower it to the unchanged `.lir1`. New dump tests (`.sea .ast .res
  .hir1 .hir .hirl .lir1 .out`, the `.lir1` from the unchanged rules 17 and 30): `loop_fore_exits`
  (`break`, `continue` and `return` inside a `for` over a vector, nested element loops, `for x in
  ones(3)` over an owned vector, a `for` over a `ref` parameter of array type, a `for` over an `if`
  expression of two vectors, and, from the sub-phase whose programs can write one, a `for` over a
  `seq` vector with `.t` locals: the three cases of L4's `bind`, §3.5.9), `loop_fill` (`filled` of
  `f64`, `i64` and `bool` vectors and matrices, `ones` and `zeros` of a matrix, a count that is a
  `ref` parameter, `filled(k, g(ref k))` whose value is copied by rule 12, `ones(if c {2} else
  {3})` and `filled(a && b, n)`: T1's `ifx`/`and` child), `loop_ext` (`len rows cols numel` of
  locals and of temporaries, `numel(zeros(2, 3))`, `numel(if c {m1} else {m2})`); `protocol.sh` with `sealoop` on a truncated
  `sea.hir` and `sealower` on a truncated `sea.hirl` (and `sealoop` in the fake-pass chain);
  `driver_check.sh` with `--emit hirl` and the usage line `--emit ast|res|hir1|hir|hirl|lir1|lir`;
  `lib_check.sh` with `seaval` accepting the `arr_rule30.hirl` golden as format `hirl` and rejecting
  mutated copies (an `HL` record under format `hir`, a `tmp` with a missing field).
* **Constants without a value** (Decision 25, sub-phase 4a-0; LANGUAGE.md §7.2): `errors/` tests,
  the lines below are lines 1, 2 (and 3) of each file (a comment, if any, follows them), and
  the expected output is derived from the rule:
  `err_const_noval_overflow`: `const B = 9223372036854775807 + 1 + A` / `const A: i64 = 1 + x`
  prints `err_const_noval_overflow.sea:2:20: error: undeclared name 'x'` (before the rule
  `1:11: integer overflow`); `err_const_noval_pow`: the same with `const A: i64 = pow(2.0)`,
  `…:2:16: error: no overload of 'pow' accepts (f64)`; `err_const_noval_errtype`: `const B = A +
  1 % 0` / `const A = f()` / `fn f() -> str { return 1 }`, `…:3:11: error: not supported yet:
  strings` (`A` has the error type and no value, so `B` is not evaluated and its `1 % 0` reports
  nothing; before the rule `1:15: integer division by zero`); all with status 1.
  For the refinement of Decision 25 (§9), also with status 1: `err_const_noval_calltype`:
  `const A: f64 = f()` / `fn f() -> str { return 1 }` prints `…:2:11: error: not supported yet:
  strings` (as before); `err_const_noval_shortcircuit`: `const D = B || 9223372036854775807 + 1 >
  0` / `const B: bool = false && f() == 1.0` / `fn f() -> str { return 1 }` prints `…:3:11:
  error: not supported yet: strings` (`B` has no value, so `D` is not evaluated; the single
  program printed `…:1:16: error: integer overflow`); `err_const_noval_userpow`: `const C =
  pow(2.0, 3.0)` / `fn pow(x: f64, y: f64) -> f64 { return x }` prints `…:2:1: error:
  redefinition of predeclared name` (as before); and `res_*` dump tests of these three programs
  (their constants written `rcn`, their `rerr`).

* **Phase-4 tests** (sub-phases 4c–4h, §8). Expected outputs are derived from LANGUAGE.md and,
  for dumps, from §3.4.2, §3.5.5 and §3.6.6 by hand; the examples of those sections are dump
  tests with their exact text (`rt`, the rule examples of §3.6.6 that are whole programs). New
  name prefixes: `arr_*` (dynamic and fixed arrays, construction, scalar indexing, `$`, copy on
  write), `sel_*` (selections, masks, views, selection stores), `ew_*` (element-wise operators
  and broadcasting), `red_*` (reductions), `sort_*` (sorting and searching), `str_*`, `struct_*`,
  `match_*`, `heap_*` (reference counts), `lir4_*` (hand-written LIR of the new records),
  `prel_*` (the prelude). Mechanisms added in 4c:
  * **The heap check in every program run.** From 4c `tests/run.sh` and `cross_run.sh` run every
    program of `programs/`, `errors/` and `passes/` with `SEA_HEAP_CHECK=1` in the environment
    (§4.5). When the program exits with status 0, its standard error must end with the line
    `heap: 0 live objects` and LF, which the runner removes before it compares standard error
    with `NAME.err` (so no expected file mentions it); a missing line or any other count is a
    FAIL (`leak: <the line>`). With any other status the line must be absent (the runner
    compares standard error unchanged). A `NAME.meta` key `heap=off` runs that one program
    without the variable, and a key `env=SEA_HEAP_CHECK=<value>` (below) replaces the runner's
    value; in both cases the runner expects and removes the line only when the value is exactly
    `1` (the tests of the variable itself: `heap_env_unset` with `heap=off` and `heap_env_other`
    with `env=SEA_HEAP_CHECK=2`, each checking that nothing is written).
  * **`env=NAME=VALUE`** in a program case's `NAME.meta` (as in `rt/`, §6.6.1) sets one more
    environment variable for the run; only `SEA_HEAP_CHECK` is allowed in a program case.
  * **`NAME.prelude`** (an empty marker file beside a `passes/NAME.sea`): the dumps of that test
    are built with the prelude (no `--no-prelude`; §3.6.6 rule 37), and stage.sh feeds the
    passes the same way (its pairs read the committed goldens; from 4h it skips the pair `hir1 →
    hir` when `NAME.hir1` is absent and the test has no `NAME.sea` or has a `NAME.prelude`
    marker (a `.sea` test without the marker still fails on a missing golden), and the pair `hir → hirl` when `NAME.hir` is absent and
    `NAME.prelude` exists, so that a dump starting at `.hir` or `.hirl` is not a missing golden
    input). From 4h (Decision 57) allowed
    beside `.hir`, `.hirl` and `.lir1` dumps and an optional `.out`, and beside no other kind (no
    `.lir` in phase 4, §3.6.6 "Phase-4 dump tests"); `run.sh` and `cross_pack.sh` build such a
    test without `--no-prelude` and compare the `#file` record of file 0 of its dumps as `#file
    std.sea` (the goldens are written so; the driver still writes the install path, §2.2).
  * **`tests/accept/`** (§6.3): the phase-4 acceptance programs, run by `tests/accept4.sh`
    (Mac) and as cross cases (§6.6.1).

    and `not a constant expression`; `argmax`/`argmin` ties (first index) and NaN; `sort` and
    `argsort` of `f64` (−0/+0 order kept, NaN placement ascending and descending, stability with
    ties in both directions) and `i64`; `find`, `find_first`, `find_last` with no `true`. In detail
    (every expected output from LANGUAGE.md and the rules, through a `tests/vectors/` script run with
    `uv` whose output is committed, never from a run of the compiler):
    * `red_sum_*`: `f64` sums of 7, 8, 9 and 17 elements with values chosen so that the 8-lane result
      differs from the left-to-right one (possible from 4 elements on; up to 3 the lane tree adds in
      index order), and of 0 and 1 elements (the empty sum, `sum([x]) = x`), printed with `%.17g` and compared with `==` to exact literals; `sum([-0.0])`
      prints `-0`, the empty sum `0`; NaN and ±∞ operands; `i64` sums whose every partial sum fits
      (totals at −2⁶³ and 2⁶³ − 1), and `[4611686018427387904, 4611686018427387904,
      -4611686018427387904]`, whose total fits but whose second partial sum overflows
      (`errors/r_red_sum_ovf`: `integer overflow` at the call's line, status 1; LANGUAGE.md §10.5: the
      partial sums in index order are checked), and the same vector under `mean` (`r_red_mean_ovf`).
    * `red_mean_var`: `mean` (empty: NaN), `variance` (n = 0: NaN; n = 1: 0; a case where the
      two-pass result differs from a one-pass formula), `std`, each of `f64` and `i64` vectors.
    * `red_maxmin`: `max min argmax argmin` with ties (the first index), NaN first, in the middle,
      last and everywhere (NaN, index 0), −0/+0 in both orders (the sign printed), `i64`; the empty
      vector (`errors/r_red_max_empty`, `r_red_argmin_empty`: `max of an empty array`, `argmin of an
      empty array` at the line, status 1).
    * `red_bool`: `nnz any all` of empty (0, `false`, `true`), all-true and all-false vectors.
    * `red_dim`: `dim: 0` and `dim: 1` on 3 × 4 matrices for the nine functions (`f64`, and `i64`
      where allowed), on 0 × 3 and 3 × 0 (with `dim: 0`, 0 × 3 gives `sum` three zeros and `max` the empty error and 3 × 0
      empty results; with `dim: 1`, 3 × 0 gives `sum` three zeros and `max` the empty error and 0 × 3
      empty results),
      and on a fixed `f64[3,4]` (a fixed-size result, Decision 39).
    * `find_*`: none true, all true, mixed; `find(M.flat)` (column-major); `find_first`/`find_last`
      returning −1.
    * `sort_*`: `f64` with −0/+0 interleaved (order kept, signs printed), NaN with both signs and
      several payloads ascending and descending, ties in both directions (with `argsort`), ±∞, `i64`
      at −2⁶³ and 2⁶³ − 1, empty, one element, a fixed-size argument (a dynamic result, Decision 39),
      `desc:` as a run-time `bool` expression, and a 1 000-element LCG vector with many ties (the
      model's checksums); sizes on both sides of 32 (insertion sort and radix paths).
    * `heap_red_*`: owned operands (`sum(v * 2.0)`, `sort(v[0..3])`, `max(A.flat)`, `argsort` of a
      fixed vector) and `v[argsort(w, desc: true)] = 0.0` (an owned index vector of L6, released at the end of

      supported yet: named arguments`), `sort(v, true)` (243), `sum(v, dim: 0)` of a vector and `sum` of a `bool` vector (243, with

* **Phase-5 tests** (sub-phases 5b–5d, §8; Decisions 66 and 69). Phase 5 changes no program's
  behaviour, so the first test is the whole corpus: every `programs/`, `errors/`, `passes/` and `rt/`
  case, the acceptance programs and `make cross` pass unchanged after each sub-phase. Expected outputs
  of the new tests are derived from LANGUAGE.md and, for dumps, from §5.8 by hand. New name prefixes:
  `opt_*` (programs whose output would change if a transformation were inexact), `opt5_*` (dumps of
  pass 3b), `ra5_*` (hand-written LIR for pass 4).
  * **`opt_*` programs** (T1 of 5c-1 and 5c-2, `tests/programs/opt_*`, `tests/errors/r_opt_*`):
    a loop that prints a line per iteration and then indexes out of bounds at a known iteration (the
    lines before, then the error with the exact index, dimension, extent and line); an overflow and
    an out-of-bounds index in the same iteration, in both orders; a check inside an `if` arm that never
    runs (no error), and inside an arm whose condition is loop-invariant and false (T8 and T9 must not
    move it); `j ± 1` over `1..n-1` and over `0..n` (the second fails at its last iteration); a range
    ending at `2^63 - 1` with `i + 1` in the body (`integer overflow` at the last iteration: T1 must
    keep that check); negative steps and `step 2`; facts that hold only inside a guard or a loop and
    must not be used after it (`a[n - 1]` after an empty `for i in 0..n` with `n = 0`, and an index
    narrowed by two `break` tests inside a `do` loop, used after the loop with a value the tests
    excluded: both report their errors); a `while` loop assigning an invariant value to a variable
    printed after it, run zero times (the old value is printed); a `ref` scalar updated in a loop,
    read by the caller afterwards, and the same with a run-time error part-way (the output before the
    error is what counts) and with a `continue` of an enclosing loop and a `return` inside the loop; a
    `ref` to an element (`f(ref v[3], v2)`) with both arrays printed afterwards; copy on write in
    loops: a loop storing into an array that another variable shares (the other one keeps its values),
    a loop whose stores are all skipped, a `ref` array parameter updated in a loop, a loop that stores
    into an array it also passes to a function (no versioning: the cow stays), and a loop that stores
    into an array after a copy made before the loop is passed to a function inside it; `%` and `idiv`
    by the constants 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 10, 11, 2147483647, 2^62 and 2^62 + 1 on −2⁶³, −2⁶³ + 1, −1, 0, 1,
    2⁶³ − 1 and multiples of the divisor ± 1; `% 0` and `idiv(x, 0)` with a constant 0
    and `idiv(x, -1)` with x = −2⁶³ (the errors unchanged, at their lines); a negative constant divisor;
    `f64` division by 4.0, 0.5, −2.0, 2^1023, 2^-1022 and 3.0 on values giving normal, subnormal,
    overflowing and signed-zero results, printed with `%.17g` (which round-trips) and as their
    `str()` text; an `if` with one `mov` per arm, as a value (T4); `f64` comparisons `==`, `!=`, `<`,
    `<=`, `>`, `>=` with a NaN operand in an `if`, as a selected value and as a loop exit (only `!=`
    holds); values live across calls inside loops (a value computed before a loop and read after a
    `printf` in it). Each has a hand-derived `.out` (and `.err`, `.status`); the cross runner runs
    them on the host.
  * **`opt5_*` dumps** (T2 of 5c-1 and 5c-2, `tests/passes/opt5_*.sea` with `.lir1` and `.lir`, and
    the generator `tests/vectors/dump5_cases.py`): for each transformation at least one program whose

    its pair `seaopt lir1 lir2` and skips the pair `sealopt lir2 lir` whenever `NAME.lir` is absent

    targets; every line also requires no frame access in that range (arm64 `[sp`, `[x29`; x86_64
    `(%rsp)`, `(%rbp)`), no `bl` or `call`, and the stated number of branches to cold blocks

    lir` of the program, the function's number f and the block numbers b of its innermost `loop` and

    10 registers, and only the order of §4.9.2's scan (smallest deepest loop depth, then ends last)
    keeps the spilled ones outside those loops (§5.2, L-bo).

### 6.3 Workload acceptance

`sea/ports/w1_shaft_design.sea` … `w5_tolerance_mc.sea` and `w7_drivetrain.sea` are the ports. `sea/tests/accept.sh`
(both targets) for each port:

1. builds it; runs it in a fresh directory with `--export-reference`, capturing stdout;
2. checks the JSON against `sea/workloads/reference/<name>.json` with `compare.py`'s rules, run
   as `uv run --no-project --with numpy python reference_py/compare.py --candidate <dir>
   <name>`. The `--candidate` option (a change to `sea/workloads/`, Decision 7 in §9)
   compares `<dir>/<name>.json` instead of the NumPy file with the same `RULES`, with one
   stricter rule for the near-tie keys: for an `argmax_tol`/`argmin_tol` key (W2's `r_worst`,
   `e_crit0`), the candidate's index must be **exactly** the first 1-based position of the
   extremum of the candidate's own exported array (`util_removed`, `fos0`), NaN ignored, and the
   MATLAB array's value at that index must be within the rule's `rel` of the MATLAB extremum.
   The first condition is structural: a port that forgot to add 1 points at the element before
   its own extremum and fails even if that element is a near-tie of MATLAB's;
3. checks the report (§6.4);
4. with `--figures`, checks that the SVG files exist, are well-formed XML and have the panels and
   series of the MATLAB figure (one structural file per port, written from the MATLAB script);
   their content is not compared with MATLAB's PNGs.

Indices in the JSON must be MATLAB's 1-based numbers (the port adds 1, LANGUAGE.md Appendix D); the keys
with `exact` rules (`rank`, `k_worst`, `i_best`, `lcg_final`, counts, …) check this.

**Phase-6 acceptance** (Decisions 80 and 86; the "done when" of phase 6, §8 row 6). The
ports of phase 6 are `sea/ports/w1_shaft_design.sea` and `sea/ports/w5_tolerance_mc.sea`, without
figures (§2.11.8), each with its token map `sea/ports/<name>.tokens` (§6.4). **`tests/accept.sh [-v]
[--save-out DIR] [PATTERN...]`** (Mac; run by `make test` in the group `test-accept`, after
`tests/accept4.sh`, whose programs stay because the shape tests and the phase-4 keys use them): for
each `sea/ports/NAME.sea` (NAME a workload name), in a `mktemp -d` directory T, `sea build -o
T/run/NAME` under `accept4.sh`'s compile timeout (`SEA_COMPILE_TIMEOUT`, default 120 seconds; W1's
compile time is measured and recorded in §6.3 at 6e, so a port near the limit is seen), then run in
the working directory `T/run` with
`--export-reference`, `SEA_HEAP_CHECK=1` and standard input `/dev/null` under a 120-second timeout
(`SEA_ACCEPT_TIMEOUT` overrides it), standard output to `T/report.txt` and standard error to
`T/stderr.txt` (both outside the run directory); the status must be 0, `T/stderr.txt` exactly
`heap: 0 live objects` and LF, and `T/run` must then hold `NAME.json` and nothing else but the
executable; then `uv run --no-project --with numpy python <workloads>/reference_py/compare.py
--candidate T/run NAME` (every key of the MATLAB reference) and `uv run --no-project --with numpy
python <workloads>/reference_py/compare_report.py NAME T/report.txt sea/ports/NAME.tokens
--candidate-json T/run/NAME.json` must both exit 0. Output
format, exit statuses, `--save-out` (which also copies `NAME.json`), `BUILD`, `SEA` and `WORKLOADS`
as `accept4.sh`'s. Steps 1–3 of the list above are this script as of 6e; step 4 (`--figures`)
came with 9d, which also changed the run as §2.14.9 and "Phase-9 acceptance" below say (one run
with `--export-reference --figures`, the run directory holding `output/NAME.svg` too, L-mc).
**On the Linux host** each port is a cross case (§6.6.1) built and checked on the Mac by
`cross_pack.sh` through `accept.sh --save-out`: the host runs it with `--export-reference` and
compares its standard output with the Mac's byte for byte after removing, on both sides, every line
that matches `^Compute time: .* s$` (the one line §6.4 and §6.6 exclude), and its `NAME.json` byte
for byte through the case's `NAME.expect/` (L-cn); `compare.py` is not needed there (Decision 86).
The line filter is new code in `tests/cross_pack.sh` and `tests/cross_run.sh`: a port case is marked
by a `.meta` line `filter=compute-time` (a new case attribute, §6.6.1), which `cross_run.sh` applies
with `grep -v` to both outputs before comparing, and the Mac side applies when it saves the expected
output; both are WP-ACCEPT's files (§8 row 6e). As built (L-ef): each port is a case of a new
case kind `ports` (§6.6.1), whose `NAME.args` (`--export-reference`) and `NAME.meta`
(`filter=compute-time`) `cross_pack.sh` generates; a port that fails `accept.sh` on the Mac is a pack
failure (`NAME.packfail`).

*Measured at 6e* (2026-10-29, Apple M2 Pro, the shared 6e build). Compile times (`build/sea build -o
… ports/NAME.sea`, wall clock): `w1_shaft_design` 13.8 s, `w5_tolerance_mc` 7.1 s, both far under
`SEA_COMPILE_TIMEOUT`'s 120 s. Both ports pass `tests/accept.sh` (22.7 s for the two): `compare.py
--candidate` passes every key, W1's 31 keys mostly bit-identical to MATLAB's with the largest
relative difference 3.8e-16, W5's largest relative difference about 1.8e-14; `compare_report.py`
finds both reports equivalent, and each report text is byte-identical to MATLAB's but for its
`Compute time` line. On the Linux host both ports' standard output is byte-identical to the Mac's
but for that line, and their JSON byte-identical (§8 row 6e).

**W7 acceptance** (decided 2026-10-29, Decision 114; accepted at 7g, 2026-11-01, "Measured at
7g" below; port-only by Decision 120). The port is `sea/ports/w7_drivetrain.sea` without figures,
written from `sea/workloads/w7_drivetrain.m` (a port defect found in a pass is reported, not
worked around in the port), with its token map `sea/ports/w7_drivetrain.tokens` (§6.4).
`tests/accept.sh` takes it with no change, as it takes every `sea/ports/NAME.sea`: built under
`SEA_COMPILE_TIMEOUT`, run with `--export-reference` under `SEA_HEAP_CHECK=1`, `compare.py
--candidate` passing every key of `workloads/reference/w7_drivetrain.json` by W7's `RULES`
(indices, tooth counts, face widths, counts and the gear table exact; times and speeds 1e-9
relative; step counts ±1, region counts ±2, the first upshift one 1 ms step; top speed 2e-6 m/s;
refined reductions 1e-7 relative) and `compare_report.py` finding the report equivalent; `make
cross` runs it as a `ports` case (byte-identical to the Mac's output but for the `Compute time`
line) under both x86_64 variants. The MATLAB reference `reference/w7_drivetrain.json` and `.txt`
exist (§1.2). The port must keep MATLAB's operation order in the time step (the linearly implicit
wheel step, the CVT ratio update, the vehicle update), the clutch and CVT branches, the tire slip
curve, both bisections, the parabola vertex and the gear search (each written out in the script;
the README's tolerance table gives the decision margins measured on the NumPy cross-check). It
writes its own linear interpolation for MATLAB's `interp1` (LANGUAGE.md has none, see the gaps
below): with the pinned formula `(1-s)*y0 + s*y1`, which matches MATLAB's `interp1` bit for bit
(measured 2026-10-29; `np.interp`'s formula differs by 1 ulp on about 25% of inputs), so only the
last bits of `sin`, `cos` and the real power differ from MATLAB's, which the rules above absorb.
W7's compile time is recorded here when it is accepted, as W1's was at 6e.

*Measured at 7g* (2026-11-01, Apple M2 Pro). The port is `ports/w7_drivetrain.sea` (874 lines) with
`ports/w7_drivetrain.tokens`; neither changed any pass, runtime, prelude, include file or golden
(Decision 120). `tests/accept.sh` passes W1, W4, W5 and W7 (`passed: 4`). For W7, `compare.py
--candidate` passes every key of `reference/w7_drivetrain.json`, each identical to MATLAB's or
differing by 0 (bit for bit); `compare_report.py` finds the report equivalent, byte-identical to
`reference/w7_drivetrain.txt` apart from the `Compute time` line; `SEA_HEAP_CHECK=1` gives `heap: 0
live objects`. The token map was checked by perturbation: changing a time, a region count by 3,
stage 1's centre distance, an err[%] or a backlash maximum each fails with exactly its rule.
W7's compile time (`sea build`, wall clock): 17.4–20.8 s (20.8 s on the first, cold run), far under
`SEA_COMPILE_TIMEOUT`'s 120 s. Its compute time is 0.134–0.135 s, against MATLAB's best compute of
8.602 s (the W7 baseline file); this figure is a record, not a measurement by §5.7's methodology.
The lead decisions of 7g are L-ic–L-ii (§9).

**Feature gaps W7 meets** (the list that 7g took up; none was a phase-7 work item, and a
LANGUAGE.md change needs the user's agreement; Decision 120 decided (a), the port meets every gap
itself, and the candidates below stay for a later phase). (1) `interp1` (linear table lookup; about
2.2M calls per run for the engine torque and 33k for the Lewis form factor) is in neither
LANGUAGE.md nor §10.13: the port writes it as a function (as Appendix D writes `prctile_mid`) with
the formula above; a library `interp1(x: f64[], y: f64[], xq: f64) -> f64`, class E with that
formula pinned and NaN outside the table (as MATLAB), is the candidate. (2) Growing arrays
`v(end+1) = x`: Sea has no in-place append; today the port preallocates to the 326,700 candidates
and keeps a count (or concatenates `[v, x]`, O(n) per append), and `push(ref v, x)` with
amortized growth (§10.13) is the candidate if the MATLAB idiom should be fast. (3) `diff`
(§10.13 "later"): a loop or slices today. (4) Floating-point ranges `1.5:0.25:3.5`: Sea's ranges
are `i64` (§5.1); `linspace(1.5, 3.5, 9)` gives the same values. (5) Rank-3 arrays
(`tDist(nCfg, nG, nCrr)`): a v1 non-goal (LANGUAGE.md §1.3), one matrix per rolling-resistance
case today (`t_dist`, `t_dist_lo`, `t_dist_hi` are the exported keys). Not gaps: `argsort`
(stable) with index selection, `argmin`, `find_last`, `inf` with `min(a, b)`, early `return` in a
multi-result function, and each `printf` format written as one string literal.

time (`sea build`) 31.1 s, within `SEA_COMPILE_TIMEOUT`'s 120 s. Compute time, best of 3: 0.150 s,
against MATLAB's best of 0.617 s (§1.2). All 55 keys pass `compare.py --candidate`, every float
bit-identical (max abs diff 0); the report is EQUIVALENT under `compare_report.py` and byte-identical
to `reference/w8_ev_can.txt` apart from the `Compute time` line; `plot_struct.py` passes; `heap: 0
live objects`. The run with `--log workloads/w8_ev_can/bench_serial.txt` exits 0 (its report is
recorded, not compared: 2 055 frames on `twai0`, 507 overlaps, as expected for handling times). No
compiler or runtime defect was found. `sh tests/accept.sh -v w8` passed 1 (31.8 s); `make test`
passes (accept 2 + 7, the other groups as after Lc); `make cross`: 1 341 cases packed, 0 failed to
compile; default variant 1 054 passed and 0 failed, `sse2` 1 054 and 0, once-only 285 and 0; host
2 393 passed, 0 failed, 4 deferred; Mac 4 passed, 0 failed. W8 is byte-identical to the Mac apart
from the `Compute time` line, its 3.6 MB log carried as `NAME.files/`. The lead decisions of W8d are
L-oo–L-ov (§2.16.14, §9).

**Phase-4 acceptance** (Decision 19; the "done when" of phase 4, §8). Until phase 6 brings
`write_json`, the acceptance programs write a JSON subset with `printf` and are checked on the
named keys only:

* `tests/accept/w4_sor.sea` (4d) computes W4's scalar SOR solve (`w4_heat_plate.m`'s grid,
  hole, boundary conditions and the lexicographic SOR loop with its convergence test, written
  with scalar loops over `f64[,]` and `bool[,]` arrays, the largest temperature found by a
  scalar loop); the script's two configuration checks, which call `error` (4g) and
  never fire on its grid, are not ported, and `tests/accept/w5_stats.sea` (4h) W5's sampling and
  statistics (the LCG, the `Dim` struct array of Appendix D, the deviations, the cold-case
  statistics and the histogram by `bincount`). Each writes to standard output exactly one JSON
  object and nothing else: `{`, then for each key in the order of its `.keys` file `"<key>": `
  and the value, the pairs separated by `, `, then `}` and LF; an `i64` value is written with
  `%d`, an `f64` with `%.17g` (which round-trips; a non-finite value is a failure of the
  program, never written), a vector as `[`, its elements as above separated by `, `, and `]`,
  and a matrix as MATLAB's `jsonencode` writes one, an array of its rows: `[`, then row 0, row
  1, … each written as a vector (its elements in column order), separated by `, `, then `]`
  (a 2 × 3 matrix: `[[a00, a01, a02], [a10, a11, a12]]`).
  `w4_sor.sea` writes `it_sor` (the iteration count, `i64`) and `T_max` (the largest
  temperature, `f64`); `w5_stats.sea` writes `first_dev` (`f64[10,7]`: the first 10 rows of the
  deviation matrix `dev`, MATLAB's `dev(1:10, :)`, written as a matrix: 10 rows of 7),
  `mean_cold`, `std_cold` (`f64`) and `hist_counts` (`i64[60]`). Indices and counts are MATLAB's (1-based where they
  are indices, LANGUAGE.md Appendix D).
* `tests/accept/NAME.keys`: one line, the keys separated by commas without spaces, in output
  order (`it_sor,T_max`; `first_dev,mean_cold,std_cold,hist_counts`); `tests/accept/NAME.wl`:
  one line, the workload name (`w4_heat_plate`, `w5_tolerance_mc`).
* **`tests/accept4.sh [-v] [--save-out DIR] [PATTERN...]`** (Mac; run by `make test` from 4d as the group
  `test-accept`): for each `tests/accept/NAME.sea`, in a `mktemp -d` directory, `sea build` (in
  `tests/accept/`, as `run.sh` builds), run with `SEA_HEAP_CHECK=1` and standard input
  `/dev/null` under a 120-second timeout; the status must be 0, standard error exactly `heap: 0
  live objects` and LF, and standard output is written to `<dir>/<wl>.json`; then `uv run
  --no-project --with numpy python <workloads>/reference_py/compare.py --candidate <dir> --keys
  <keys> <wl>` must exit 0. The output format is `run.sh`'s (`FAIL NAME: <reason>`, `----`,
  `passed: P  failed: F`); exit 0, 1, or 2 on a setup error (no `uv`, no `compare.py`, no driver).
  `<workloads>` is `sea/workloads`, a plain directory of the sea repository (not a submodule; `WORKLOADS` overrides it).
  `--save-out DIR` also copies the standard output of each passing case to `DIR/NAME.out`
  (`cross_pack.sh` uses it); `SEA_ACCEPT_TIMEOUT` (seconds, default 120) overrides the timeout of
  the run and of the comparison, and `BUILD`, `SEA` the build directory and the driver.
* **On the Linux host** the acceptance programs are cross cases (§6.6.1) whose expected
  standard output is the Mac's: `cross_pack.sh` builds and runs each on the Mac, checks it as
  above, and packs its standard output as the case's `NAME.out`; the host compares byte for
  byte (Decision 19: the same bits on both targets, so `compare.py` is not needed there).

**`compare.py --keys K1,K2,…`** (a change to `sea/workloads/reference_py/compare.py`, a file of the sea repository, made with
sub-phase 4d, the first that runs it; §8). With `--candidate DIR` and exactly one workload name,
it compares only the listed keys: a listed key must be present in both files and passes by its
`RULES` entry exactly as in candidate mode (the near-tie rule included); a key of the candidate
file that is not listed is a failure (`FAIL <key> not requested`), and the MATLAB file's other
keys are ignored; the report lists the compared keys in sorted order as the full mode does. A
listed key's candidate value must have the MATLAB value's nesting before its elements are
compared: a number against a number, a flat list against a flat list of the same length, a list
of rows against a list of the same number of rows, each of the same length as the MATLAB row
(`FAIL <key> shape <candidate shape> vs <MATLAB shape>` otherwise); the elements are then
flattened in row order and judged by the key's rule, as the full mode judges them. The shape
texts are `scalar`, `vector[n]`, `matrix[r x c]` (a list of rows of one length), `rows[l0,l1,…]`
(rows of different lengths) and `nested` (deeper than two levels); nestings must be equal
exactly. In keys mode an unlisted candidate key fails also when it starts with `_` (the full and
candidate modes still skip such keys); a key listed twice is compared once.
Usage errors, each a message on standard error and exit 2: `--keys` without `--candidate`, with
no or more than one workload name, with `--self-test`, or with no value; an empty list or an empty element; a key
that is not in the workload's MATLAB reference; an `argmax_tol`/`argmin_tol` key whose array key
is not listed; an unknown workload name. The two checks that read the MATLAB reference (an
unknown key, an unlisted array key) are made only when that file exists; when it does not, the
comparison reports the missing file as in candidate mode (exit 1). Exit status otherwise as
before (0 when every listed key passes, 1 if not).
`--self-test` gains these cases: the MATLAB file reduced to the listed keys passes; a listed key
missing from the candidate fails; an unlisted extra key fails; a matrix key (`first_dev`) with
its rows written as one flat list, with a row missing and with a row one element short fails,
and written as rows passes; each usage error exits 2; a
corrupted listed key fails with exactly that key; and the full mode's behaviour is unchanged
(the existing cases pass unchanged).

### 6.4 Report equivalence

**Reference text.** The MATLAB report texts are stored (Decision 7 in §9, sea commit c1736f7):
`run_all.m` captures each script's report with `diary` on the last repetition into
`sea/workloads/reference/<name>.txt`, committed for the five workloads from the user's rerun
(M2 Pro, MATLAB R2026a).

**Token map.** Each port has a file `sea/ports/<name>.tokens` that says how each numeric token
of the report is judged. One line per report-line pattern:

```
<line regex>  <token number>  <rule>
```

where the regex matches the report line (POSIX extended, anchored), the token number counts
blank-separated tokens from 1, and the rule is one of `compare.py`'s rule kinds applied to the
two tokens read as numbers. `compare_report.py` splits a map line into its fields on whitespace, so
a regex contains no blank: a blank of the report line is written `[[:space:]]`, never `[ ]` (which
the split would cut in two) (L-eg). Where a JSON key's tolerance is below one printed unit of the
report token, the map converts that tolerance to the report's units (as the `Rejects:` yield below
converts 4e-6 of a fraction to 4e-4 percent) and adds no rounding slack (L-eg).

**Reading a token.** Before a token is parsed, three characters are stripped, in this order: one
trailing `,`, `;` or `:`; then one trailing `)`; then one leading `(`. Each stripped character, or
its absence, must be the same on both sides (otherwise the lines differ). A stripped token that
contains `..` is split at its first `..` into two parts, each judged as a token of its own (so
`(0.1000,` is the number `0.1000`, and `0..5` the numbers `0` and `5`). A token or part is
**numeric** if it then parses as a decimal number (optional sign, digits with an optional
decimal point, optional exponent `e`/`E` with sign); a non-numeric token or part must be identical
as text on both sides. A token-map entry that names a token split at `..` applies its rule to
both parts.

The rules are: `exact`, `int n`, `num atol rtol`, or `json <key>`. A `num atol rtol` rule
passes when |c − r| ≤ atol + rtol·|r|, where r is the reference token's number and c the
candidate's (`rtol` is scaled by the magnitude of the reference token). A `json <key>` rule uses
the rule of that JSON key; for a key whose rule is relative to the key's largest magnitude, the
scale is taken from the reference JSON; for a key whose JSON rule is `argmax_tol` or
`argmin_tol`, the token passes when the reference token equals the MATLAB JSON value of that key,
the candidate token equals the candidate JSON value of that key, and the candidate JSON passes the
own-extremum rule of §6.3. A numeric token not listed is judged by the **default rule** (a value
within one unit of the last printed digit): the two tokens pass if they are equal as text, or if
|a − b| ≤ u, where a and b are their values and u is the larger of their two **units**; the unit of
a token is 10^(e − d), where e is its printed exponent (0 if it has none) and d the number of
digits after its decimal point (0 if it has none). The comparison is exact decimal arithmetic on
the printed digits, never floating point. So `9.99e-05` against `1.00e-04` (u = 10⁻⁶),
`9.9999` against `10` (u = 1) and `0.999` against `1.000` (u = 10⁻³) pass, and `1.5` against
`1.7` (u = 0.1) fails. Example (W5; the report lines are those of LANGUAGE.md Appendix D):

```
^Rejects:              2   int 2
^Rejects:              5   int 2
^Rejects:              8   int 2
^Rejects:             14   num 4e-4 0
^Histogram:            8   int 2
^Histogram:           10   int 2
^Histogram:           13   int 2
```

(`Rejects:` token 14 is the yield in percent, whose JSON rule `yield` is 4e-6 absolute on the
fraction; `Histogram:` tokens 8, 10 and 13 are the underflow, overflow and fullest-bin counts,
judged like `hist_counts`.)

**Equivalence.** A Sea report is equivalent to the MATLAB report when both have the same number
of lines and, line by line: the line `Compute time: … s` is skipped on both sides; the lines
have the same number of tokens; non-numeric tokens are identical; numeric tokens pass their
rule. The token maps are written from the MATLAB scripts' `fprintf` formats and the JSON rules,
never from Sea output (§6.1), and reviewed with the port.

### 6.5 Workload benchmarks

`sea/bench/workloads.sh`, on the machine of the MATLAB baseline:

* builds each port once (compile time reported separately);
* runs it 5 times, then 10 more times, each with `--export-reference` in a fresh directory,
  measuring whole-process wall time with a small exec-and-wait harness
  (`clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)` around `posix_spawn` + `waitpid`), and reading the program's
  own `Compute time` line;
* reports, per workload: the first run, the best of the first 5 (the pass/fail number, the same
  rule as MATLAB's baseline, §5.7) and their median, and the median and range of the 10 further
  runs; compute and whole-process; next to MATLAB's
  first, median and best from `baseline_timings_matlab.json` (§1.2) and the single-threaded
  first, median and best from `baseline_timings_matlab_1thread.json`, and the ratios; plus machine model, macOS version, kernel variant, load average before and after
  (BENCH.md conventions);
* **passes** when, for every workload, Sea's best-of-5 whole-process time < MATLAB's best
  `total_seconds` and Sea's best-of-5 compute time < MATLAB's best `compute_seconds` (§1.2).

The MATLAB rerun of Decision 7 is committed (sea commit c1736f7): `baseline_timings_matlab.json`
(default thread count, the pass criterion, as Decision 7 chose) and
`baseline_timings_matlab_1thread.json` (`maxNumCompThreads(1)`, reported), five repetitions
each. The same script also compares Sea's medians with the default baseline's medians and
reports the single-threaded MATLAB numbers beside them. The same script runs on the Linux host
for the x86_64 numbers (reported, not compared with MATLAB, which has no Linux baseline).
The tools, the run directory, the correctness check of every timed run, the exact pass check and
the output files are §2.17.4 and §2.17.8; the seven workloads' pass criteria are the four MATLAB
files of §1.2 (W7 and W8 from their own files).

### 6.6 Cross-target identity

* **Spec tests**: standard output, standard error, exit status and written files are
  byte-identical on `arm64-macos` and `x86_64-linux` (and for every kernel variant, run with
  `SEA_KERNELS=<variant>`). Tests involving class-R operations use exact data (§6.2).
* **Ports W1, W4, W5** use no class-R operation: their reports (except the compute-time line),
  JSON and SVG files must be byte-identical across targets and variants.
* **Port W3** uses class-R operations in exactly two places: `eig_sym` for the natural
  frequencies (`f_nat`) and the 3 × 3 `solve` of the parabolic refinement (`c_best`). Its road
  (`sin(argR) @ Ak`, a class-E matrix-vector product) and its whole RK4 simulation are class E.
  So all of W3's outputs except `f_nat` and `c_best` (and the report tokens that print them)
  must be byte-identical across targets; those two are compared with the acceptance rules.
* **Port W2** solves with `chol`/`lu` (class R) throughout; its outputs are compared across
  targets with the acceptance rules (§6.3–§6.4), not byte for byte, and its SVG by Decision 138 (a)
  (the same text but for numbers within a hundredth, `tests/svg_skeleton.py`, L-mb; since 9d). Its `K @ u0` reactions
  are class E given the same `u0`.
* W2 and W3 are judged across targets by Decision 127 (a): the host defers their runs and the Mac's
  `tests/cross_accept.sh` compares them (§2.13.9, §6.6.1 "As built in 8d"); W3's `f_nat` line is
  compared byte for byte, its tokens having no `json f_nat` rule (L-jz).
* `x86_64-linux` output is produced by the cross scripts as Baysick's are (`sea/tests/cross*.sh`
  on the ssh host, default `desktop`; §6.6.1).

#### 6.6.1 Cross testing x86_64-linux

As in Baysick (Baysick DESIGN.md §8.3), compiling happens only on the Mac (the passes are macOS
Baysick programs) and the run half on the Linux host. Three POSIX `sh` scripts and two make
targets do it; every spec test that runs a program is a cross case, and the expected files are
the same files the Mac uses (one set for both targets).

**Cases.**

* `programs/NAME`: every program test.
* `errors/NAME` whose program compiles: the run-time error tests. A test whose `sea build`
  fails with status 1 and exactly `NAME.err` on standard error (and `NAME.status` 1) is a
  compile-time test, target-independent (it never reaches pass 4), checked on the Mac only, and
  skipped silently; any other failure is a pack failure.
* `passes/NAME` with a `NAME.out`: the program built with `--no-prelude` and run (§6.2).
* `passes/NAME.lir` pass-4 tests (hand-written LIR, §6.2): the file with its `#target` record
  replaced by `#target x86_64-linux`, run through `seagen_x64` on the Mac (not a `NAME.lir` beside a
  `NAME.lir3`: that is a `seavec` golden, as in `stage.sh`, L-fc).
* `passes/NAME.lirx64` with a `NAME.out` and no `NAME.sea` (7e, L-fc, L-hj): the x86_64-linux-only
  pass-4 tests. Without a `NAME.lir3` the file is the input of `seagen_x64` as it is (`gen7_y*`,
  `gen7_vfeat`); with a hand-written `NAME.lir3` the case is `seavec` on the `.lir3` retargeted to
  `x86_64-linux`, then `seagen_x64` on that live output (the `.lirx64` golden is `stage.sh`'s). A
  `NAME.lirx64` without a `NAME.out` is only a golden and no case.
* `accept/NAME`: every phase-4 acceptance program `tests/accept/NAME.sea`, built and checked on
  the Mac by `tests/accept4.sh --save-out`, its standard output packed as `NAME.out` (§6.3).
* `ports/NAME`: every phase-6 port `ports/NAME.sea` (from 6e, L-ef): `cross_pack.sh` runs
  `tests/accept.sh --save-out` on it (build, run, heap check, `compare.py`, `compare_report.py`);
  when that passes, it compiles the port as any case and packs its standard output without the lines
  matching `^Compute time: .* s$` as `NAME.out`, its `NAME.json` as `NAME.expect/NAME.json`, and the
  generated sidecars `NAME.args` (the one argument `--export-reference`) and `NAME.meta` (the one
  line `filter=compute-time`); when `accept.sh` fails, `NAME.packfail` holds `status <n>` and
  `accept.sh`'s standard output and standard error (exit 2 of `accept.sh` is a setup error of
  `cross_pack.sh`). The host runs it under `SEA_ACCEPT_TIMEOUT` (default 120 seconds), as an
  `accept/` case.
* `fusion/NAME` (7f, L-hx, L-hy): every `tests/fusion/NAME.sea`, compiled like a program case, with
  the sidecar `NAME.fusion` (`k=`, `per_iteration=` from its header lines `// fusion K: N` and
  `// Allocations per iteration: N.`; a program without both lines is a setup error of
  `cross_pack.sh`); the host builds it once and runs it with K and K + 1 under `SEA_HEAP_CHECK=count`
  under both variants (in a fresh empty working directory, stdin `/dev/null`; each run must exit 0
  with exactly the count-mode heap line on standard error and leave no file; its standard output is
  not compared) and requires the difference of the allocation counts to equal `per_iteration`,
  with 0 live objects (§2.12.10). A passing variant prints `ok   fusion/NAME: A allocations at
  K=K, A′ at K=K+1`, and a failure `FAIL fusion/NAME: reason`, the second variant labelled ` [sse2]`
  after the name and the first unlabelled, as for a program case; a pack failure is counted once.
* `plots/NAME` (9b, §2.14.8 "Cross", L-la, L-lq): every `tests/plots/NAME.sea`. `cross_pack.sh` runs
  `tests/plots.sh --save-out DIR --only NAME` on the Mac (`--only` runs exactly that case, since a
  pattern is a substring): the build, the run under the heap check and `plot_struct.py` on
  `NAME.struct`; a Mac failure is a pack failure (`NAME.packfail` with `plots.sh`'s output; its exit
  2 is a setup error of `cross_pack.sh`). The case is then compiled like a program case and packed
  with `NAME.out` (the Mac's standard output, possibly empty) and `NAME.expect/PATH` for every file
  the `.struct` names (subdirectories included; the existing `NAME.expect/` mechanism). The host
  runs it like a program case under both variants (heap check, status 0, standard error empty but
  the heap line) and checks `NAME.out` and `NAME.expect/` byte for byte: the output, each expected
  SVG, and no other file. The `.struct` check runs on the Mac only. Plot error tests (`r_plot_*`,
  `err_plot_*`) are ordinary `errors/` cases.
* `rt/NAME`: every `tests/rt/x86_64_linux/NAME.s` (§4.7.1). Its `.meta` may hold
  `stdout=epipe`, `stdout=slowpipe` and `env=NAME=VALUE` lines (`SEA_KERNELS` and
  `BAYSICK_KERNELS` otherwise unset) and nothing else: no `requires=` (§4.7.1). A program case's
  `.meta` may hold only `stdout=epipe` and `stdout=closed` (§6.2), and `filter=compute-time`
  (L-cn, L-ef; written only for `ports/` cases): with it, `cross_run.sh` removes the lines matching
  `^Compute time: .* s$` from both the expected and the actual standard output before comparing;
  from 8d also `compare=accept` and `compare=accept except=KEY,…` (Decision 127; written only for
  `ports/` cases whose source has the `// cross:` header line, "As built in 8d" below).
  `cross_run.sh` stops with exit 2 on any other line, an empty line excepted.

**An extra case, `math/math_check`.** Besides the program cases, `make cross` runs one case on the
host: `cross_pack.sh` copies `tests/math/math_check.c` and `tests/math/*.vec` into
`<bundle>/tests/math/` (a setup error if there is no `.vec` file), and `cross_run.sh` builds the
harness there with ` -O1 -ffp-contract=off` against `build-x86_64-linux/libsea.a` (`-lm`;
any compiler output is a FAIL) and runs it on `<bundle>/tests/math` under the case timeout
(60 seconds); it passes when the exit status is 0 and standard error is empty (§4.10.6). The
pattern `math/math_check` selects it.

**Two more once-only cases, `la/la_check` and `la/la_link`** (from 8b; §2.13.8, L-ja, L-jd).
`cross_pack.sh` copies `tests/la/gen_consts.sh`, `la_check.c` and `la_link.sh` into
`<bundle>/tests/la/` with a marker file per selected case, and for `la/la_link` its own compilation
of `tests/programs/la_mm_exact.sea` as `cases/la/la_mm_exact.s`. On the host `cross_run.sh` writes
`sea_consts.h` with `gen_consts.sh` from the bundle's `include/`, builds `la_check.c` with `gcc
-std=c11 -O2 -Wall -Wextra -ffp-contract=off` against `libsea.a` and `libbaysickrt.a` (any compiler
output is a FAIL) and runs it once under a 300-second limit (it selects every usable variant
itself); it passes with exit status 0 and an empty standard error. `la/la_link` runs `la_link.sh -s`
on the packed assembly (`as --64`, the `gcc` link with `-Wl,--trace`). Both are counted with the
once-only cases, and a full bundle without either is a FAIL; the patterns `la/la_check` and
`la/la_link` select them.

The dump tests (`--emit`) and the other Mac groups (`stage.sh` dumps, `protocol.sh`,
`lib_check.sh`, `arith_check.sh`, `driver_check.sh`, `check_data.sh`) are target-independent and
run only on the Mac (`make test`).

**Bundle** (a self-contained directory made on the Mac, consumed on Linux):

```
<bundle>/BUNDLE                       one line: "sea-x86_64-linux-bundle 1"
<bundle>/Makefile.linux               Sea's
<bundle>/include/limits.inc errors.inc rt.inc
<bundle>/runtime/x86_64_linux/*.s
<bundle>/tests/cross_run.sh
<bundle>/tests/include_check_x86_64.s tests/include_asserts.inc
<bundle>/tests/rt/run_rt_linux.sh     tests/rt/x86_64_linux/NAME.s + sidecars
<bundle>/baysick/Makefile.linux       Baysick's, with its include/*.inc and
<bundle>/baysick/include/*.inc        src/runtime_x86_64_linux/*.s (the x86_64
<bundle>/baysick/src/runtime_x86_64_linux/*.s   libbaysickrt.a is built from them)
<bundle>/cases/<kind>/NAME.s          the program as compiled on the Mac, kind programs,
                                      errors, passes, accept or ports
<bundle>/cases/<kind>/NAME.out .err .status .in .args .meta, NAME.files/, NAME.expect/
                                      copies of the sidecars present
<bundle>/cases/<kind>/NAME.packfail   instead of NAME.s when compiling failed: "status <n>",
                                      then the compiler's standard error (accept, ports: also
                                      when the Mac check failed, then its output)
```

**`tests/cross_pack.sh -o BUNDLE_DIR [PATTERN...]`** (Mac). `BUNDLE_DIR` must not exist or be
empty (else exit 2); PATTERN selects cases whose name contains it, as in `tests/run.sh`.
Environment: `SEA` (the driver, default `build/sea`), `BAYSICK` (the Baysick checkout, default
the parent of the Sea repository), `LIRCHK` (the `sea.lir` validator `tools/lirchk`, default
`build/tools/lirchk` beside the driver, 7e). Each case is compiled with the driver run in the test's own
directory with the bare file name, exactly as `tests/run.sh` does (so the site table names
`NAME.sea`): `sea build --target x86_64-linux -S -o <bundle>/cases/<kind>/NAME.s NAME.sea`
(`--no-prelude` for passes/); a pass-4 test runs `seagen_x64` on the retargeted LIR in a scratch
directory (the pass's file protocol, §2.2). Since 7e (Decision 116, L-hj) the driver runs with
`--keep-temps` (its line `sea: temporary files kept in DIR` is removed from the standard error
before the check below, and DIR is removed), and the x86_64 `sea.lir` of every case, the kept one of
a driver compilation or the input of a hand-written pass-4 test (after `seavec`, for a `.lirx64`
with a `.lir3`), is validated with `lirchk` (the vector classes and `LF` records included) before
it goes to `seagen_x64`: a rejection is a pack failure of the case (`NAME.packfail`, `lirchk
rejects sea.lir (status n)` and its first lines). The compile must exit 0 with empty standard output
and standard error, else `NAME.packfail` is written (the errors/ rule above decides first). It
prints `packed: <n> cases (<m> failed to compile)` and exits 0 when the bundle is complete, 2
on a setup error (driver, `seavec`, `seagen_x64` or `lirchk` missing, bad `-o`, copy failure). `make cross-pack`
writes `build/x86_64-linux-bundle` (removed first).

**`tests/cross_run.sh [-v] [BUNDLE_DIR]`** (Linux; default the directory above the script).
Environment: `SEA_TEST_TIMEOUT` (seconds per run, default 10), `AS` (default `as`), `CC`
(default `gcc`), `SEA_KERNELS` (when set, the one variant the programs run under, else both x86_64 variants, see
Phase 7 below). Setup (failure → message,
exit 2): the `BUNDLE` line; the host's `avx2` (Phase 7 below); `make -C BUNDLE_DIR/baysick -f Makefile.linux all AS="$AS"`; `make
-C BUNDLE_DIR -f Makefile.linux check-includes all BAYSICK=baysick AS="$AS"`. Per case, in a
`mktemp -d` directory: a `NAME.packfail` is a FAIL (`compile (on the Mac) failed`); otherwise
`$AS --64 -o prog.o NAME.s` and `$CC -no-pie -o prog prog.o <libsea.a> <libbaysickrt.a> -lm` (an
`rt/` case also links `obj/rt_main.o` first, §4.7.1), each of which must exit 0 with **empty
standard error** (a warning is a FAIL: `assemble failed` / `link failed`); then the program runs
exactly as `tests/run.sh` runs it on the Mac: in a fresh working directory holding the copied
`NAME.files/`, standard input `NAME.in` or `/dev/null`, the arguments of `NAME.args`, the
`NAME.meta` keys (`stdout=epipe`, `stdout=closed`, with the same mechanisms), the timeout.

**What "byte-identical" compares.** For each case, against the same expected files as on the
Mac: standard output with `NAME.out` (not compared under a `stdout=` key; empty when absent for
errors/), standard error with `NAME.err` (empty when absent), the exit status with
`NAME.status` (0 when absent), every file of `NAME.expect/` byte for byte, and that the working
directory holds nothing else but unchanged fixtures. The output format and exit status of the
script are those of `tests/run.sh` (`FAIL <name>: <reason>`, `----`, `passed: P  failed: F`,
`failed tests: …`; 0, 1, or 2 on a setup error).

**`tests/cross.sh [-v] [-H HOST] [PATTERN...]`** (Mac, the one command; `make cross`). Host:
`-H`, else `$SEA_CROSS_HOST`, else `desktop`, reached with `ssh -o BatchMode=yes --`. It packs
into a local `mktemp -d` directory, streams it as `tar -C <bundle> -cf - .` into one `ssh` call
whose remote `sh -c` script (no single quote in it) unpacks into a remote `mktemp -d` directory,
removed on exit and on HUP/INT/TERM/PIPE, and runs `SEA_TEST_TIMEOUT=<value> [SEA_KERNELS=<value>]
sh "$d/tests/cross_run.sh" [-v] "$d"`; `SEA_KERNELS`, when set, must be letters, digits and
underscores (else exit 2), and is then the one variant run; when unset the host runs both (Phase 7
below), and `cross.sh` passes its output through unchanged. Exit: the status of `cross_run.sh`; 2 if packing or `ssh` fails or
the remote status is anything else. Nothing is left on the host. All three scripts treat
HUP/INT/TERM/PIPE by removing their temporary directory and exiting 2, and match patterns
literally.

Phase 2 is done (§8) when `make cross` passes every case and `make cross-includes` passes, with
`make test` still passing on the Mac.

Phase 3 is done (§8) when, in addition, `make test-math` passes on the Mac (part of `make test`) and the
`math/math_check` case of `make cross` passes on the host (§4.10.6), with the `lib_math_*` programs
passing in `run.sh` and in the cross run.

Phase 4 (sub-phases 4c–4h, §8) adds to the cross run: the heap check of every program run
(`SEA_HEAP_CHECK=1`, the `heap: 0 live objects` line removed before comparing, §6.2), done by
`cross_run.sh` exactly as by `run.sh`; the `NAME.meta` keys `heap=off` and
`env=SEA_HEAP_CHECK=<value>` for program cases (the list above grows by these two); the
`accept/NAME` cases of §6.3 (kind `accept`, packed with the Mac's standard output as `NAME.out`
and no other sidecar; a Mac run that fails its check is a pack failure, `NAME.packfail`); and
the new runtime files `rt_mem.s`, `rt_arr.s`, `rt_str.s`, `rt_args.s`, `rt_sort.s` in the bundle's
`runtime/x86_64_linux/`. A program's arguments (`NAME.args`) reach `sea_args` on both targets
identically. Phase 4 is done (§8) when `make cross` passes every case, the accept cases among
them, with `make test` passing on the Mac.

Phase 7 (agreed with §2.12, 2026-10-29, revised after two reviews; Decision 104) adds
to the cross run: **both x86_64 kernel variants**. `tests/cross_run.sh` runs every program, error,
passes, fusion and ports case twice, first with `SEA_KERNELS` unset (the best usable variant: `avx2`
on the host) and then with `SEA_KERNELS=sse2`, against the same expected files (the variant changes
no class-E output, §4.4; the runtime selects its variant from `SEA_KERNELS` at start-up), naming a
failure `FAIL <name> [sse2]: …` in the second run; an `rt/` case keeps its own `env=` lines and runs
once. Its setup checks that the host offers `avx2` (`grep -qw avx2 /proc/cpuinfo`), else exit 2
(`host lacks avx2: the 4-lane code cannot be tested`), so a run never passes without having
executed the 4-lane copies; a `SEA_KERNELS` value given to `cross.sh` replaces the pair by that one
variant (as before). The `math/math_check` case runs its 4-lane part (§2.12.8). The bundle takes
`runtime/x86_64_linux/rt_vmath.s` by its existing wildcard. Phase 7 is done (§8) when `make cross`
passes every case under both variants, with `make test` passing on the Mac.

**As built in 7e** (L-hj, L-hl; `cross_run.sh`, `cross_pack.sh`, `cross.sh`). The program, error,
passes, accept and ports cases are assembled and linked once and run per variant: first with
`SEA_KERNELS` unset (the default variant, `avx2` on a host that passes the check), then with
`SEA_KERNELS=sse2`; a failure of the second run is `FAIL <name> [sse2]: …`. A `SEA_KERNELS` value
given to `cross.sh` (or to `cross_run.sh`) replaces the pair by that one variant, unlabelled. The
AVX2 check applies in that case too, because the 4-lane tests (`gen7_y*`) execute AVX2
instructions whatever the variant. The runs of `rt/` cases (which keep their own `env=` lines),
`math/math_check` and the build failures are counted once. After `----` the script prints one line
`variant <v>: passed: P  failed: F` per variant (the first labelled `default (SEA_KERNELS unset,
avx2)`), the line `once (build, rt, math): passed: P  failed: F`, then the totals `passed: P  failed:
F` and, with failures, `failed tests: …`; the exit status is as before. `cross_pack.sh` validates
every x86_64 `sea.lir` with `lirchk` and packs the `.lirx64` cases (the case list above). At
7e's close the host run packed 941 cases: default (`avx2`) 822 passed, 0 failed; `sse2` 822 and 0;
once-only 119 and 0; total 1 763 and 0.

**As built in 7f** (L-hx, L-hy; `cross_pack.sh`, `cross_run.sh`). The `fusion` cases (the case list
above) are built once and run per variant like the program cases, after them, and are counted in the
variant lines. At 7f's close the host run packed 954 cases: default (`avx2`) 826 passed, 0 failed;
`sse2` 826 and 0; once-only 128 and 0; total 1 780 and 0, both `fusion` cases passing under both
variants with the Mac's counts (`w1_bisect` 1 018 and 1 018, `w4_rb` 1 042 and 1 048).

**As built in 8d** (Decision 127 (a), §2.13.9 items 1–5, L-jw–L-jy; `cross_pack.sh`,
`cross_run.sh`, `cross.sh` and the new `cross_accept.sh`). `cross_pack.sh` reads a port's leading
`//` lines and writes the value of its `// cross: compare=accept [except=KEY,…]` line as a second
`NAME.meta` line (a malformed or repeated `// cross:` line is a setup error); W2 has
`compare=accept`, W3 `compare=accept except=f_nat,c_best`. **`tests/cross_run.sh [-v] [-k DIR]
[BUNDLE_DIR]`**: `check_meta` accepts both lines for the kind `ports` only (exit 2 elsewhere); such a
case is run under each variant with every port's checks (status 0, the heap line, empty standard
error, `NAME.json` written and no other file) but compared with nothing: its standard output as
written, the `Compute time` line included (L-jw), and its JSON are kept as
`DIR/ports/NAME.VARIANT.out` and `.json` (VARIANT the `VARIANTS` word, `default` or `sse2`, L-jy;
without `-k` in a new temporary directory, printed and left in place), the line `DEFER ports/NAME
(VARIANT)` is printed and the run counts as deferred, in no variant line; the totals line reads
`passed: P  failed: F, D deferred`. **`tests/cross.sh`** unpacks the bundle on the host into
`D/bundle` and passes `-k D/keep`; after a run ending with 0 or 1 the remote script writes the line
`#sea-cross-files N` and then the base64 text of `tar -C D/keep -cf - .` (N its byte count; N = 0
and nothing after the marker when no run was kept). An `awk` splitter copies every line before the
marker to the standard output and the text after it to `$TMP/kept.b64`, whose length must be N.
When D > 0 or N > 0 (L-jy), **`tests/cross_accept.sh [-v] BUNDLE_DIR KEPT_B64 REPORT`** (Mac, needs
`uv`) unpacks the kept files and judges each `DEFER` line's run: `compare.py --candidate` and
`compare_report.py` exactly as `accept.sh` calls them and, with `except=`, the byte comparison of
L-jx with the packed `NAME.expect/NAME.json` and `NAME.out` (the kept output without its `Compute
time` line); it prints `PASS`/`FAIL ports/NAME (VARIANT)` lines, `----` and `passed: P  failed: F`
(exit 0, 1, or 2 on a setup error: no `uv`, a base64 or tar failure, a `DEFER` line for an unmarked
port, a kept file no `DEFER` line names, a bad token map). `cross.sh` ends with the line `host: P
passed, F failed, D deferred; Mac: P2 passed, F2 failed`; D must equal P2 + F2, and the exit status
is 0 with no failure on either side, 1 with a failure on either, 2 on a setup error of either (a
missing marker, a length mismatch, disagreeing counts included). Tested at 8d on the deferred flow,
a truncated base64 stream (exit 2), a corrupted kept JSON (FAIL, exit 1), edits of the excepted keys
(pass) and of other keys (fail), missing kept files (fail) and a `compare=accept` line on another
kind (exit 2). At 8d's close the host run packed 1 089 cases (0 failed to compile): default
(`avx2`) 911 passed, 0 failed; `sse2` 911 and 0; once-only 176 and 0; 1 998 passed, 0 failed and 4
deferred, the 4 passing `cross_accept.sh` on the Mac; W1, W4, W5 and W7 stay byte-identical cases.

**As built in 9b** (§2.14.8 "Cross", L-la, L-lq; `cross_pack.sh`, `cross_run.sh`, `plots.sh`). The
`plots/` cases (the case list above) are packed after the `fusion` cases into

## 7. What Baysick must grow

### 7.1 Needs of the compiler, against Baysick 0.6.0

Every need of the compiler, checked against Baysick 0.6.0 (`docs/SEA_BOOTSTRAP.md` §2 rows and
LANGUAGE.md), with the calibration of §2.7:

| Compiler need | Baysick 0.6.0 | Sufficient? |
|---------------|---------------|-------------|
| read the source verbatim, detect end of input | `LINPUT #0` + `IF END #0` | yes, with the `#end` discipline (§2.2), because plain end of input exits with status 0 |
| options, file names | stdin header (§2.2) | yes, by the no-argv decision |
| input/output files per pass | `FILES` (≤ 8, fixed names), `PRINT #`, `LINPUT #` | yes: ≤ 2 per pass |
| diagnostics and failure status | `PRINT #-1`, `STOP e` | yes |
| strings: length, substring, search, concatenation, codes | `LEN SEG$ POS & ASC CHANGE STR$` | yes, avoiding the blank-padding traps (§2.7) |
| numbers to text | `STR$` (exact for integers < 10⁹) and digit arithmetic | yes |
| exact `f64` bit patterns, big integers | doubles exact below 2⁵³, arrays as limbs (§2.8) | yes |
| constants above 9 digits | built by arithmetic or read from `DATA` | yes, awkward |
| program size | 10 000 lines per program, 16 `SUB` parameters, no globals | **tight**: the passes measure 2 349–5 403 lines each in phase 1 and are re-estimated at about 42 000–53 000 lines in all for v1, with pass 2a reaching 10 000 around phase 6 and pass 3a near it from phase 7 (§2.7) |
| tables | arrays ≤ 10⁶ elements, 2-D string arrays, by-reference array parameters | yes, giving the capacity limits of §2.7 |
| message and template text | string constants ≤ 65 536 bytes outside `DATA` | yes, by keeping text in `DATA` |
| writing assembly text | `PRINT #` of strings writes bytes unchanged | yes |

**Conclusion.** No Baysick language change is needed to start, and none is proposed now. The
honest risk is size: the line limit and the absence of globals make the larger passes long and
repetitive, and the phase-1 recalibration of §2.7 puts pass 2a at the 10 000-line limit around
phase 6 and pass 3a near it from phase 7. §7.3 states the policy for that case (split the pass first);
Decision 2 in §9 agrees it in advance.

### 7.2 Changes to Baysick's runtime kernel contract

The GEMM reuse of §4.3 needs a **runtime contract change in Baysick** (no language change):

1. a new entry point `_bsk_kern_gemm_sub(C, A, B)`: `C ← C − A·B`, same view rules, statuses,
   blocking and class-R rules as `_bsk_kern_gemm`, implemented in all three variants
   (`baseline`/`neon` on arm64, `sse2`/`avx2` on x86_64);
2. the finite-input precondition of `_bsk_kern_gemm` and the new entry is replaced by IEEE
   propagation of non-finite inputs, with tests on every variant (Baysick's own MAT statements
   keep their `KS_NONFINITE` checks);
3. Baysick's `include/runtime.inc` and Baysick DESIGN.md §6.6 change together (Baysick's contract rule),
   and Sea's `rt.inc` names the Baysick version it was built against.

The link-isolation property Sea relies on (`rt_kinit.o` + `rt_k*.o` pulled alone from
`libbaysickrt.a`, §4.3) is already a Baysick rule; a Sea link test watches it. No new archive
or build target is needed. Decision 5 in §9 rejected the alternatives (Sea owns its GEMM, or a
shared kernel repository).

### 7.3 Growth policy for the language

If a measured need appears (a pass that cannot be written within a limit), the response is, in
this order:

1. **Restructure without Baysick changes**: split the pass into two programs with an
   intermediate file; move text to `DATA`; pack tables; build constants by arithmetic. (Applied
   first in phase 4a: pass 2a becomes `seaname` and `seacheck` with the file `sea.res`, Decision
   17, §2.7; the planned next seam is `sealoop` before `sealower`, §2.7.)
2. **Grow Baysick only on a measured need**, one change at a time, through Baysick's own
   process (spec first in LANGUAGE.md, `include/*.inc` with its doc section, tests on both
   targets), preferring a feature from a later Dartmouth edition where one exists, and
   otherwise a clearly labelled Baysick extension (Baysick LANGUAGE.md §15).

**Candidates**, with their status (none is proposed now):

| Limit | Candidate change | Dartmouth precedent | When |
|-------|------------------|---------------------|------|
| 10 000 lines per program | raise the 10 000-line limit (line numbers already go to 99 999) | none in the editions implemented (Second–Sixth); a **Baysick extension** | only if a pass cannot be split cleanly (its tables would have to be written and re-read) |
| no global variables; 16 `SUB` parameters | a `COMMON`-style shared block between the main program and its subprograms | Dartmouth's Fifth Edition `CHAIN`/`COMMON` concerns separate programs, not subprograms; this would be a **Baysick extension** | if table-passing overhead or parameter count becomes a measured problem |
| 16 parameters per `SUB` | more parameters | none; **Baysick extension** | only with the previous row rejected |
| 65 536 bytes of string constants | larger limit | none; **Baysick extension** | not expected: text lives in `DATA` |
| 1000 `FOR` statements per program | larger limit | none; **Baysick extension** | not expected (measured 55–127 per pass in phase 1; at most about 450 in v1, §2.7) |
| two-character variable names | longer names | the later Dartmouth editions' long names are not verified against a primary source here; treat as a **Baysick extension** unless such a source is found | readability only; not expected to be needed |

### 7.4 Watch list

| Limit | Expected use | If reached |
|-------|--------------|------------|
| 10 000 lines per program | 2 349–5 403 per pass measured in phase 1; pass 2a split in phase 4a before it reaches the limit (`seaname` 4 900–5 250 and `seacheck` 3 700–4 000 estimated after 4a, 5 900–6 600 and 7 000–9 250 at v1), pass 3a near it from phase 7 (§2.7) | §7.3: split the pass |
| 1000 `FOR` statements per program | 55–127 per pass measured in phase 1; at most about 450 in v1 (§2.7) | split the pass |
| 26 array letters per program unit | 6–8 tables per pass | pack tables into 2-D arrays |
| 10⁶ elements per array | the tables of §2.7 | lower a capacity limit or split the table |
| 1024 active `CALL`s | parser recursion ≤ nesting 64 × about 5 levels | iterative parsing of operator chains |

## 8. Milestones

Each phase ends with its "done when" checked by tests on **both targets** (the x86_64 side
through the cross scripts), spec text before code (the house workflow), and nothing left
half-built. Phases 0–2 build the skeleton end to end on the smallest real program.

| # | Phase | Done when |
|---|-------|-----------|
| 0 | **Agreement and contracts.** The decisions of §9 are taken; the document is split into LANGUAGE.md and DESIGN.md with the intermediate record formats (§0, §3); `sea/include/*.inc`, `passes.txt`; the Baysick kernel contract change of §7.2 (in Baysick, by its own process); `compare.py --candidate`, the token maps' format, and `run_all.m` report capture, with the MATLAB rerun (Decision 7) | the user has agreed the documents; include checks pass on both assemblers; Baysick's tests pass with the new GEMM entry |
| 1 | **Scalar core, arm64.** Driver with the `#end` discipline; passes 1–4 for: `i64`/`f64`/`bool`, `let`/`var`, arithmetic with the LANGUAGE.md §6.8 rules, `if`/`while`/`for` ranges, functions with scalar parameters, `ref`, multiple results, `const` items and `pi inf nan eps`, `printf` with `%d %i %f %F %e %E %g %G %s` (string literals only as `%s` arguments), `now()`, `f64()`, `i64()`, `idiv`; every other construct is `not supported yet` (§2.6.2, phase rule); no inlining (§3.6.6), pass 3b validates and copies (§3.6.5), the phase-1 allocator and the stack check (§4.9, §4.6), `std.sea` comments only (§2.5); runtime start-up, formatting, errors (`sea_printf`, `sea_now`, §4.8); float-literal conversion; the build of §2.6.3 and the layout of §2.10; **recalibration** of the size estimate of §2.7 from the real passes | a Sea program running W5's LCG for 11 M steps prints `lcg_final` = 2145635252 (the reference value) and the first uniforms bit-exact; spec tests for this subset pass; the estimate is updated in §2.7 |
| 2 | **x86_64 target.** `seagen_x64`, the x86_64 runtime for the same subset, `cross*.sh` | the phase-1 tests pass byte-identically on the Linux host |
| 3 | **Elementary functions.** Sea's own scalar `log exp sin cos pow hypot` on both targets (Decision 6) | `math/` tests pass on both targets: ≤ 1 ulp against the high-precision references, identical bits on both targets (§4.10.6: the runtimes reproduce the model's bits for every committed vector on both targets; the generator has checked each vector against mpmath; the `lib_math_*` programs pass in `run.sh` and the cross run) |

| 5 | **Scalar code quality.** Linear-scan allocation, invariant hoisting, strength reduction, bounds-check elimination, magic division; built in the sub-phases 5a–5d below (specified 2026-10-24, Decisions 58–73: `seaopt`'s T1–T10 of §5.8, the allocator and code selection of §4.9.2) | the W5 LCG and W4 SOR loops meet the §5.2 instruction shapes (checked on `-S` output: §5.2 "Targets for phase 5", `make test-shape` on both targets, §6.2); a micro-benchmark of each is recorded (§5.9). **Complete** (2026-10-25): 5a–5d done, the shapes met on both targets, the gate after phase 5 passed with Decision 78 (§2.7, "Measured after 5d") |
