**Decisions of phase 8** (written 2026-11-01 with the text of §2.13, revised after one
independent review, and decided by the user on 2026-11-01, each as option (a)). Each lists its
options with the recommendation as (a), its reasons, the decision, and what it affects; §2.13.11
holds the same text. Decision 130 was added in 8c (the user, 2026-11-01).

121. **The `eig_sym` algorithm** (§2.13.6; §4.3 names tridiagonal reduction and implicit QL).
     Options: (a) **EISPACK `tred1` (Householder reduction to a tridiagonal, eigenvalues only) then
     `tql1` (implicit QL with shifts), as published, under §2.13.6's notation, `pythag` =
     `sea_hypot`, the generalized form through `chol(M)` and the plain `dsygst` reduction**; (b) the
     same reduction then bisection with Sturm counts (LAPACK `dstebz`-like: every eigenvalue to a
     fixed tolerance; slower, more code, needs a tolerance rule); (c) cyclic Jacobi on the full
     matrix (simplest, very accurate for small n, O(n³) per sweep with 6–10 sweeps). Recommended:
     (a): §4.3's choice, O(n³) once plus O(n²) iterations, well known, about 400–700 runtime lines;
     W3's 2 × 2 and every test fit any of them. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-01). Affects
     §2.13.5, §2.13.6, §4.3, §6.2.
122. **Blocking of the factorizations and solves** (§2.13.6). Options: (a) **right-looking blocked
     LU, Cholesky and triangular solves with one panel width `SEA_LA_NB` = 32 on every target and
     variant, the panels in Sea's code (pinned, L-it) and every trailing update through
     `_bsk_kern_gemm_sub`; NB a contract value that phase 10 may retune by a contract change**; (b)
     the same with NB = 64 (fewer, larger Baysick calls; more of W2's 241 × 241 LU in the scalar
     panel: about 40 % against 20 % at NB = 32); (c) unblocked only, no `gemm_sub` (every result
     pinned, class E in practice, but W2's 301 member removals, about 4.2 GFLOP of LU and Cholesky,
     would run at panel speed, likely slower than MATLAB's 0.936 s); (d) a tuned NB per variant
     (results then differ between variants in more places). Recommended: (a): most of the work in
     GEMM's micro-kernel, one partition for both targets, and the smallest W2 panels; the bits it
     fixes are class R, so a later NB change needs only the contract change. **Decided: (a)** (the
     user, 2026-11-01). Affects §2.13.5–§2.13.6, §4.3, §4.8, `rt.inc`.
123. **The symmetric test of `solve(A, B)` and `eig_sym`** (LANGUAGE.md: "exactly symmetric";
     `eig_sym` of a non-symmetric matrix is an error; §10.8 also says NaN propagates). Options: (a)
     **A[i,j] and A[j,i] equal by `==` (so +0 and −0 are equal) or both NaN**; (b) plain `==` (a NaN
     pair is not symmetric: `eig_sym` then stops with `matrix is not symmetric` on a symmetric
     matrix holding a NaN, and `solve` takes LU); (c) equal bit patterns (−0 against +0 not
     symmetric, NaN pairs with equal payloads symmetric). Recommended: (a): the exact test MATLAB's
     choice needs, +0/−0 treated as the equal values they are, and a NaN in a symmetric matrix
     propagating (to n NaN eigenvalues, L-ip, or through LU after the Cholesky attempt fails on it)
     instead of raising a symmetry error. No tolerance in any option: "exactly" is LANGUAGE.md's
     word. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-01). Affects LANGUAGE.md §10.8, §2.13.6.
124. **Where matrix @ vector and vector @ matrix live** (§4.3 says Sea's GEMV kernel). Options: (a)
     **runtime entries `GEMV` and `VECMAT` with NEON, SSE2 and AVX2 forms, bit-identical (class E),
     materialized operands**; (b) inline loops written by `sealoop` (a j-outer, i-inner loop that
     `seavec` vectorizes, and L13's sum8 per column), which could later fuse an element-wise operand
     into the product (W3's `sin(argR) @ Ak` without the 7.7 MB `sin(argR)`), at 300–500 more
     `sealoop` lines (over its 7 000 at the upper end) and no cache blocking. Recommended: (a): fits
     every pass, the kernel's row panels keep y in registers, and operand fusion stays a phase-10
     candidate. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-01). Affects §2.13.4–§2.13.6, §4.3, §4.4.
125. **How `@` of fixed-size operands is built, and its result type** (LANGUAGE.md §6.8 makes class
     R only "the matrix @ matrix product on dynamic matrices", so a product of two fixed-size
     operands is class E at every extent; the sentence on extents ≤ 8 and `SEA_LIM_FIXED_MATMUL_E`
     restate part of it. §6.8 does not say what the result type is when it would exceed
     `SEA_LIM_FIXED_ELEMS` (256) elements, as `f64[256,1] @ f64[1,256]` would, nor whether a
     fixed-size operand beside a dynamic one makes the product "on dynamic matrices"). Options: (a)
     **two fixed-size operands: inline in the pinned order by `sealoop`'s L21 at every extent; the
     result fixed-size when it has at most 256 elements, else a dynamic matrix allocated by L21 (as
     a concatenation becomes dynamic, §6.9); one dynamic operand: the fixed one made dynamic
     (`dyn`), the runtime entry, a dynamic result, the matrix @ matrix case class R; §6.8 gains that
     sentence**; (b) as (a), but a class-E runtime entry (a pinned-chain `MATMUL_E`, a contract
     change) builds every fixed-size product whose result exceeds 256 elements, keeping L21 for the
     rest; (c) as (a), but a result over 256 elements is a compile error (a new error code, a
     contract change); (d) as (a), but a fixed-size operand beside a dynamic one keeps the product
     class E (through (b)'s `MATMUL_E`), reading §6.8's "dynamic matrices" as "both operands
     dynamic". Recommended: (a): no allocation below 256 elements ("fixed-size arrays never
     allocate", §4.2), one rewrite, the concatenation rule reused, no contract change, and the mixed
     case keeps GEMM's speed for a dynamic operand of any size. No workload multiplies fixed-size
     matrices (W2's `ke` and W3's state are element-wise). **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-01).
     Affects §2.13.2–§2.13.4, LANGUAGE.md §6.8 (one clarifying sentence).
126. **The sub-phase split** (§2.13.10). Options: (a) **8b contract and `@`; 8c factorizations,
     solves, `rcond`, `eig_sym` and handles; 8d the ports, the cross rule and the gate**; (b) one
     code sub-phase (8b everything) then the ports (8c); (c) four code sub-phases (`@`; LU,
     Cholesky, solves, `rcond`; `eig_sym`; ports). Recommended: (a): `@` is independent and
     exercises the new runtime files, the view mapping and `la_check` before the factorizations
     depend on them; the five calls share one `ck_lib` table and one mapping table, so splitting
     `eig_sym` off (c) adds a step without disjoint files. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-01).
     Affects §8.
127. **How the class-R ports are checked on the Linux host** (§6.6: W2 compared "with the acceptance
     rules, not byte for byte", W3 byte-identical except `f_nat` and `c_best`; §6.6.1's `ports` case
     compares bytes, which W2 under `avx2`'s FMA GEMM cannot meet; `cross.sh` is one `ssh` call that
     returns only text). Options: (a) **a `.meta` key `compare=accept [except=…]` makes the host
     defer the comparison and keep the port's output and JSON, which return after the report as a
     marked base64 tar stream on the same `ssh` output; the Mac's new `tests/cross_accept.sh` runs
     `compare.py --candidate` and `compare_report.py` on them for each variant, plus W3's byte
     identity outside the excepted keys and their report lines, and `cross.sh` combines both counts
     (§2.13.9, items 1–5)**; (b) the same comparison on the host (`uv` with NumPy there, which
     Decision 86 avoided; no return path); (c) byte comparison for every port (fails for W2 under
     `avx2`; it would test an accident of the build). Recommended: (a): the host stays free of
     Python, the checks are §6.6's exactly, and the results are judged by the rules that judge the
     Mac's. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-01). Affects §6.6, §6.6.1, `tests/cross*.sh`.
128. **W2's condition test and solve in the member removal** (MATLAB: `rcond(Kr(freeDof, freeDof))`,
     an LU and the estimator, then `\`, a Cholesky). Options: (a) **as MATLAB: `rcond(lu(Kff))`,
     then `solve(Kff, Fr)` (its Cholesky path)**; (b) one factorization: `let F = lu(Kff)`,
     `rcond(F)`, then `solve(F, Fr)` (about a third less work per removal, a different class-R path
     from MATLAB's). Recommended: (a): the ports keep MATLAB's operations (§6.3), the work is the
     reference's, and phase 10 compares like with like. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-01).
     Affects `ports/w2_truss_fem.sea`, §2.13.9.

129. **NaN in LU pivoting, and the precedence of `rcond`'s special values** (§10.8: "Inf and NaN
     propagate"; but partial pivoting compares magnitudes, so for A = [0, 1; NaN, 1] a search that
     never lets a NaN win records a zero pivot and `solve` reports `matrix is singular`, and `rcond`
     returns 0 if the zero-pivot test comes before the NaN-norm test). Options: (a) **LAPACK's rule
     (`idamax`, `dgetf2`): a NaN never wins the pivot search unless it is the first candidate, a
     column of zeros and NaNs gives a zero pivot, and `solve` then reports `matrix is singular`;
     `rcond`'s values in the order order 0 → +∞, ‖A‖₁ NaN → NaN, zero pivot → 0, ‖A‖₁ = 0 or +∞ → 0,
     non-finite estimate → 0 (so a matrix holding a NaN always has `rcond` NaN); the proposed
     LANGUAGE.md text states both**; (b) a NaN wins the pivot search (a candidate replaces the
     current one when it is NaN or strictly larger), so a NaN column never gives a zero pivot and
     the NaN propagates through `solve`; `rcond` as in (a); (c) `lu` records whether A holds a NaN;
     `solve(F, B)`, `solve(A, B)` and `rcond` then return all-NaN results (NaN) before any singular
     test, and pivoting is (a)'s. Recommended: (a): it is what LAPACK and so MATLAB's factorization
     do (MATLAB's `\` then warns and returns what the factorization gives, Sea stops), a NaN-free
     matrix is unaffected under every option, and `rcond` never hides a NaN; (b) changes the pivot
     rule for every matrix holding a NaN and departs from the reference factorization; (c) adds a
     scan and a flag for a case no workload has. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-01). Affects
     LANGUAGE.md §10.8, §2.13.2, §2.13.6, L-in, L-io.

130. **`rcond` when the estimator's solves overflow** (2026-11-01, found by 8c's implementation and
     two independent transcriptions; §2.13.6's RCOND, L-io). §2.13.6 said "an overflow makes est
     non-finite, giving 0", which is false: for diag(1, 2⁻¹⁰⁷⁰) a solve overflows, 0·∞ = NaN
     arises mid-solve, the later steps discard it, and the literal steps give rcond = 1. Options:
     (a) **after every solve of steps 1–3 (each "x ← U⁻¹L⁻¹x" and each "x ← L⁻ᵀU⁻ᵀx"), s = Σ|x| in
     index order; if s is +∞ or NaN, rcond = 0 at once (the scratch freed); step 4 gives 0 when est
     is +∞, NaN or 0, else (1 / est) / ‖A‖₁**; (b) keep the steps as written and document the wrong
     estimate. Recommended: (a): an estimate built from an overflowed solve means nothing, and 0 is
     what LAPACK ≥ 3.10's `dgecon` returns for a non-finite estimate; a matrix whose solves stay
     finite is unaffected. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-01). Affects §2.13.6, L-io,
     LANGUAGE.md §10.8, `rt_lu.s` (both runtimes), `la8_cases.py`, `la_check.c`.

**Decisions of phase 9** (written 2026-11-02 with the text of §2.14, revised after one independent
review, and decided by the user on 2026-11-02, each as the recommended option (133 (b), the others (a))). Each
lists its options with the recommendation in bold, its reasons, the decision, and what it affects;
§2.14.11 holds the same text.

131. **MATLAB figure features that §12 lacks** (§2.14.3: of the six figures sections only W7's
     `'MarkerSize', 3` has no §12 form; the other differences are appearance, accepted by Decision
     13). Options: (a) **keep §12's API: W7 draws 6 px markers, the port's header notes it**; (b)
     add an option `marker_size: f64 (6.0)` to `plot` (marker offsets scale with it; a LANGUAGE.md
     change, one `f` argument more in `PLOT`, the marker templates written with the size); (c) a
     figure-wide `marker_size:` option of `figure`. Recommended: (a): the smallest API that draws
     all six figures (Decision 13 judges structure, not appearance), no contract or entry change;
     (b) is a later, additive library change if wanted. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-02).
     Affects §2.14.3, `ports/w7_drivetrain.sea`,
     (b) LANGUAGE.md §12.3, §2.14.5, §2.14.6.
132. **The colour of a contour without `color`** (§12.3's bullet reads "use the style letter, else
     the axes' next cycle colour", but `contour` has no style, and MATLAB colours each level by the
     colour map). Options: (a) **each level in the colour map's entry ⌊256·k / (n + 1)⌋, the cycle
     not advanced (LANGUAGE.md §12.3 and §12.6 gain the sentence of §2.14.2 items 2 and 8)**; (b) the
     next cycle colour for every level (§12.3's general rule read literally; no amendment); (c)
     black. Recommended: (a): it is what MATLAB draws (W1's 15 levels are told apart by colour), the
     map exists already for images, and the cost is one integer division per level.
     **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-02). Affects
     LANGUAGE.md §12.3, §12.6, §2.14.6.
133. **`panel` on a cell an earlier panel holds** (§12.2 is silent; MATLAB's `subplot` deletes the
     old axes, which a handle model cannot do). Options: (a) allowed: both panels are drawn, in
     creation order, on top of each other; (b) **the run-time error `grid cell %d,%d already holds a
     panel` (`PANEL_TAKEN`, new code 25), the first occupied cell in row-major order**; (c) the new
     panel replaces the old one, whose handles then draw nowhere. Recommended: (b): an overlap is a
     program mistake in every workload layout (W2's and W4's spans are disjoint), the check is a
     bitmap test, and (c) would make existing handles silently useless. Under (a) code 25 is not
     added and the later codes move down by one. **Decided: (b)** (the user, 2026-11-02).
     Affects LANGUAGE.md §9.2, §12.2, `errors.inc`.
134. **`twin_y` called again, or on a twin** (§12.2 is silent). Options: (a) **`twin_y` of an axes
     that has a twin returns that twin (a new handle to the same axes record), and `twin_y` of a
     twin returns the twin itself; never an error**; (b) both are a run-time error (a new code);
     (c) each call makes another right axis (several twins per panel, which §12.5's single right
     margin cannot lay out). Recommended: (a): MATLAB's `yyaxis right` behaves so (it selects the
     one right axis), no new error, and the layout keeps one twin per panel.
     **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-02). Affects LANGUAGE.md
     §12.2, §2.14.5, §2.14.6.
135. **The colours of a `twin_y` axes** (§12.3: a colour cycle "per axes", so a twin's first
     series is `#0072bd` like the base's; MATLAB's `yyaxis` colours the left side `#0072bd` and the
     right side `#d95319`). Options: (a) **the twin's cycle starts at its second colour, `#d95319`;
     the base's is unchanged**; (b) §12.3 as written (W3's two curves both blue); (c) MATLAB's rule
     exactly: every series of a twinned base in colour 1 and every twin series in colour 2.
     Recommended: (a): one stored start index, and W3's figure then matches MATLAB's colours
     (one series per side); (c) needs a rule for a base that gains its twin after its series.
     **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-02).
     Affects LANGUAGE.md §12.3, §2.14.6.
136. **The new run-time errors and limits** (§12 names only `invalid line style` and `invalid
     color`; the other failures need messages). Options: (a) **eight new codes 22–29 with the texts
     of §2.14.2 (`invalid figure grid %dx%d`, `invalid figure size %dx%d`, `panel at %d,%d spanning
     %dx%d is outside the %dx%d grid`, `grid cell %d,%d already holds a panel`, `invalid axis limits
     %g, %g`, `invalid legend location "%s"`, `invalid number of contour levels %d`, `invalid width
     %g`) and the limits `SEA_LIM_PLOT_GRID` 64 and `SEA_LIM_PLOT_PX` 100 000**; (b) reuse existing
     codes where one fits (`index %d out of bounds for dimension %d of extent %d` for a panel cell,
     `invalid array size %d` for the grid, sizes and levels) and add only `invalid axis limits` and
     `invalid legend location`, with no limits (the grid bitmap then grows with nrows · ncols); (c)
     no checks: clamp silently (a zero-row figure draws nothing, reversed limits are swapped).
     Recommended: (a): each message names the plot argument that failed, as LANGUAGE.md's other
     messages do; reusing `index … out of bounds` for a panel misleads; the limits bound the
     occupancy map and every coordinate, and no figure comes near them (W1–W7 use 2 × 2 at 960 ×
     720). **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-02).
     Affects LANGUAGE.md §9.2, §12.2, `errors.inc`, `limits.inc`, §2.6.1, §2.6.2.
137. **The structural test runner** (§6.2 promises well-formedness and structure; the compiler and
     runtimes contain no C and Python is used only through `uv`). Options: (a) **`tests/plot_struct.py`,
     Python standard library only (`xml.etree.ElementTree`, `re`), run with `uv run --no-project`
     on the Mac; the Linux host only compares bytes**; (b) POSIX sh and awk over §2.14.6's
     one-element-per-line grammar, with `xmllint --noout` (in macOS) for well-formedness; (c) both
     on both machines (needs `xmllint` on the host). Recommended: (a): an XML parser independent of
     the writer's line format is a real oracle (an awk reader of the writer's own layout would accept
     a layout bug that a viewer rejects), `test-accept` already needs `uv`, and no parser is needed on
     the host. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-02).
     Affects §2.14.8, §6.2, `Makefile`.
138. **W2's figure across targets and variants** (W2's data are class R, Decision 127; its SVG may
     differ in the last `%.2f` digit or in a tick that sits on a boundary). Options: (a) **kept on
     the host with the JSON and judged on the Mac: its structure (`ports/w2_truss_fem.struct`) and
     the skeleton comparison of §2.14.8 (every number in an attribute replaced by `#` equal, the
     numbers within one hundredth, compared as integers, element texts equal); the port's header gains `svg=approx`**; (b) its
     structure only; (c) no SVG check for W2 on the host. Recommended: (a): it checks on the host
     what the Mac checks and every byte that class R cannot change, as Decision 127 does for the
     JSON; (b) would not see a host-only layout defect. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-02).
     Affects §2.14.8, §2.14.9, §6.6, §6.6.1,
     `tests/cross*.sh`.
139. **The sub-phase split** (§2.14.10). Options: (a) **9b the contract, the front end (all 21
     calls) and the runtime core (objects, line series, decorations, legend, ticks, the SVG writer);
     9c bars, contours, images, the colour map and PNG; 9d the ports, their structural files,
     acceptance, the cross handling and the gate**; (b) one code sub-phase (9b everything) then the
     ports (9c); (c) four (front end; runtime core; bars, contours and images; ports).
     Recommended: (a): the front end is one table for all 21 names and is finished once; the core
     runtime and the test runner are exercised by line plots before the harder kinds depend on them;
     9c's files are new and disjoint from 9b's but for `rt_plot.s`'s dispatch; (c) splits the front
     end from the runtime that tests it. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-02).
     Affects §8.
140. **Whether the SVG grammar becomes normative** (Decision 13 (a) judges plots by structure, not
     bytes; §2.14.6 fixes every byte so that the targets agree, and §2.14.2's item 10 would say so
     in LANGUAGE.md §12.8, moving Decision 13 toward its option (b)). Options: (a) **keep the
     grammar a DESIGN-only runtime contract: item 10 is not added; tests compare bytes across
     targets and variants, never against hand-derived bytes**; (b) adopt item 10: §12.8 declares the
     bytes fixed, so a hand-derived expected SVG becomes a legitimate test and every later layout
     change is a language change; (c) make only the structure normative: §12.8 gains the element
     classes and their order (what a `.struct` checks), not the attribute bytes. Recommended: (a):
     it is Decision 13's agreed reading, it keeps layout fixes inside the runtime, and the byte
     equality across targets that phase 9 needs comes from the DESIGN contract alone; (c) is the
     smaller step if programs that post-process SVGs should be promised the classes.
     **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-02). Affects
     LANGUAGE.md §12.8 (b, c), §2.14.2 item 10, §2.14.8.
141. **`sealower`'s budget for phase 9** (§2.14.7: the increment 91–171 exceeds Decision 52's
     phase-9 estimate of 80–120, 31 of its lines being the generated contract lines, the 21
     `entries` `DATA` lines and ten error and constant records, which that estimate did not count;
     Decision 50's gates end with "after phase 8", whose condition reserved 120 lines for phase 9;
     Decision 71 gives the form of a gate after a phase). Options: (a) **accept the increment and
     record it against Decision 52's estimate; keep 60 of the 120 lines for fixes ("Remaining after
     phase 9"); add `sealower`'s condition "after phase 9: built + 60 ≤ 9 000 and built + 90 ≤ 9
     000" to §2.7 and to the gate after phase 9 (amending Decisions 50, 52 and 71)**; (b) hold
     Decision 52's figure: 9b keeps `sealower`'s increment at most 120 (the mapping rows packed
     denser, two entry ids per `DATA` line), measured after 9b, an excess being a relief before 9c's
     code; (c) no reserve after phase 9: the gate after phase 9 checks only built ≤ 9 000 for
     `sealower`, and later fixes draw on what is left. Fallback under every option: if the
     measurement after 9b fails its condition, the next unused reserve of §2.7's list for `sealower`
     is specified and agreed with the user before 9c's code. Recommended: (a): even the upper end
     leaves 1 898 lines under 9 000 at the stress line, the excess is generated lines rather than
     growth of the lowering, and (b) would spend effort on density with no limit at risk.
     **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-02). Affects
     §2.7, §2.14.7, L-kv, Decisions 50, 52, 71 (their text amended, 141 (a)).
142. **Tick labels that repeat on narrow ranges** (§12.5 writes ticks `%g` when the step is below
     1e-4 or at least 1e6; six significant digits make adjacent ticks equal on a range such as 1 …
     1.00001, step 2e-6, where 1 and 1.000002 are both `1`, or 1e12 … 1e12 + 5e6). Options: (a)
     **amend §12.5: when two adjacent tick texts of an axis would be equal, every numeric tick of
     that axis is written `%.{q}g` with q the smallest of 7 … 17 that makes the adjacent texts
     differ (17 always does, since equal tick values are not drawn)**; (b) keep §12.5 as written and
     choose test ranges that avoid repeats (the six ports' data do); (c) a fixed `%.{p}g` with p
     derived from the step and the magnitude (the digits of max(|lo|, |hi|) / s). Recommended: (a):
     labels are then always distinct, the rule is a loop over at most eight texts at `save_svg`, and
     (b) leaves a known defect in the language; (c) needs a magnitude rule with edge cases of its
     own. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-02).
     Affects LANGUAGE.md §12.5 (§2.14.2 item 6), §2.14.6, L-kk, `plot_ticks_*`.

**Decisions of phase L** (written 2026-11-02/03 with the text of §2.15, revised after one
independent review, and decided by the user on 2026-11-03: 143–149 each as the recommended option
(a); 150 the user's four rulings of the same day, one of them (d) changing the draft). Each lists
its options with the recommendation in bold, its reasons, the decision, and what it affects;
§2.15.10 holds the same text.

143. **What a malformed number text does** (`parse_i64`, `parse_f64`; LANGUAGE.md has no
     exceptions, so the choice is how a program learns of the failure). Options: (a) **a run-time
     error naming the text (`cannot parse "%s" as i64 in base %d`, `cannot parse "%s" as f64`);
     the program validates beforehand if it wants to skip a line**; (b) a result plus a flag,
     `let (v, ok) = parse_i64(s)` (a multiple-result library call as `ind2sub` is; the value 0 or
     NaN when `ok` is false; no parse error code); (c) both: the raising forms of (a) and
     `try_parse_i64`/`try_parse_f64` returning `(v, ok)`; a sentinel alone (NaN for `parse_f64`)
     is not offered, since `i64` has no free value. Recommended: (a): W8's log is written by the
     project's own simulated sketch, so a malformed field is a defect that should stop the run with
     the file line of the failing call; the decode of §2.15.3 reads naturally; and (c)'s `try_`
     forms can be added later without changing (a). Under (b) or (c) items 3 and 5 of §2.15.2's
     LANGUAGE.md text change, `PARSE_I64`/`PARSE_F64` return a second result (Args/Results `pi`/`ii`,
     `p`/`fi`: a two-result entry, which §4.8's convention has not had so far) and §2.15.3 checks
     `ok`. Affects LANGUAGE.md §9.2, §10.9, §2.15.2, §2.15.5, §2.15.6, `errors.inc`. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-03).
144. **The spelling of the i64 bitwise operations** (`&` and `|` are already the `bool`
     element-wise operators at precedence 7 and 8, below the comparisons; `^` is the power; `~`,
     `<<`, `>>` are not tokens). Options: (a) **elemental functions `bitand bitor bitxor bitnot
     shl shr sar` (§2.15.2), no syntax change; `&`, `|`, `^` keep their meanings**; (b) operators
     on `i64`: `&` and `|` overloaded for `i64` operands at their present precedence (so `a & 0xFF
     == 0` parses as `a & (0xFF == 0)` and is a type error), a new prefix `~` and new `<<` `>>`
     (logical? arithmetic? one of them a function), xor a function since `^` is power: a lexer,
     parser and Appendix B change, `seaparse` (3 953 lines) growing by an estimated 60–120
     lines; (c) operators with C's precedence (bitwise above comparison: changes the
     meaning of existing `bool` expressions such as `gc >= LSL & gc <= USL`, so it would need new
     tokens for the bitwise forms, e.g. `.&`). Recommended: (a): no grammar change and no pass-1
     growth, no precedence trap, the names say what they do (MATLAB uses `bitand bitor bitxor`),
     the functions are elemental like `idiv`, and the LIR already has the instructions; the cost
     is that a mask is not a constant expression (L-ml). Affects LANGUAGE.md §10.14 (a), or
     §3.6, §3.7, §6.1, §6.4, Appendix B (b, c); §2.15.4. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-03).
145. **The form of file input** (§10.13 names `read_lines`; W8 reads one log of a few MB).
     Options: (a) **`read_lines(path) -> str[]`: the whole file read at once and split into lines
     by LANGUAGE.md §3.1's rule (LF; one CR before an LF or at the end removed; a final line
     without LF counts; a final LF adds no empty line; an empty file gives no line)**; (b)
     `read_text(path) -> str` (the whole file as one string) and lines as `split(text, "\n")`
     with the program removing CRs (one primitive fewer, but every reader repeats the CRLF and
     final-newline handling, and a file over 2³¹ − 1 bytes cannot be one `str`); (c) a streaming
     reader: a new handle type `File` with `open_read`, `read_line`, `at_end`, `close` (no whole
     file in memory; a new handle type, more entries and errors, effects on every call).
     Recommended: (a): the decode needs exactly a list of lines, the rule is the one Sea already
     applies to source files, a file of a few MB is a few MB of strings, and (c) can come later if
     a workload needs files larger than memory. Affects LANGUAGE.md §10.10, §11.3, §2.15.2,
     §2.15.5, §2.15.6. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-03).
146. **Substring access** (§10.13 lists `s[a..b]`, `byte`, `starts_with`, `find_str`; the decode of
     §2.15.3 needs only taking bytes lo … hi − 1). Options: (a) **one function `substr(s, lo, hi)`
     with exactly the meaning and the checks of the index range `lo..hi` (§5.1, §5.4)**; (b) the
     slice syntax `s[a..b]`, `s[a..=b]` with `$` = `len(s)`, written by `seacheck` as the same
     entry (a `str` base of an `idx` with one range; `$` bound to a hidden local of the base; a
     scalar index on a `str` stays 250): no parser change, but `seacheck` grows by an estimated
     150–250 lines instead of the few rows of (a), and `seaname`'s `$` binding learns a `str` base;
     (c) (a) now and (b) later as sugar over the same entry, plus `byte(s, i) -> i64`. Recommended:
     (a): the smallest change that the decode needs, its semantics are §5.4's so (b) remains a
     pure syntax addition later, and W8 needs neither `byte` nor a search. Affects LANGUAGE.md §4.4,
     §10.9, §10.13, §2.15.2, §2.15.4. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-03).
147. **`%x` and `%X` in `printf`/`format`** (§10.13 lists them; a CAN report naturally writes
     identifiers in hex, as `candump` does, but W8's report is not specified yet). Options: (a)
     **add `x` and `X` for `i64` with C99's width, precision and `- 0 #` flags (§2.15.2): a
     `passes.txt` enum line, `seacheck`'s format check, `rt_fmt.s`'s digit loop in base 16**; (b)
     leave them out; W8 prints decimal identifiers, or builds hex text in Sea (a prelude-free loop
     over `shr`/`bitand` with a 16-letter `str[]`); (c) a library function `hex(x, digits) -> str`
     instead of conversions. Recommended: (a): about 60–110 lines in all, the familiar spelling
     (C, MATLAB `sprintf('%X')`), usable in `format` and `error` messages, and decided now so that
     W8's report format can rely on it. Affects LANGUAGE.md §11.1, §10.13, `passes.txt`, §3.5.5,
     §3.6, §4.8 (`SEA_FP_CONV`), §2.15.4, §2.15.6. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-03). The flags `+` and space with
     `x`/`X` are Decision 150 (d).
148. **The new run-time errors** (§2.15.2's table). Options: (a) **six new codes 30–35:
     `cannot read '%s': %s`, `cannot parse "%s" as i64 in base %d`, `cannot parse "%s" as f64`,
     `invalid base %d`, `empty separator`, `invalid shift count %d`; the existing `cannot open`,
     `index … out of bounds`, `invalid array size` and `out of memory` reused**; (b) fewer codes: one
     `invalid argument to %s: %s` for the base, the separator and the shift count, and one parse
     error for both types; (c) no checks for the base, the separator and the count: the base
     clamped to 2 … 36, an empty separator splitting into single bytes, the count taken mod 64
     (C's undefined behaviour made defined). Recommended: (a): each message names what failed, as
     LANGUAGE.md's other messages do; (c) silently turns mistakes into plausible values, which Sea
     avoids everywhere else (bounds checks, `integer overflow`). Affects LANGUAGE.md §9.2,
     `errors.inc`, §2.6.2, §2.15.2. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-03).
149. **The sub-phase split** (§2.15.9). Options: (a) **Lb the contract, the front end of all
     twelve functions and `%x`, the bitwise functions and `%x` finished with their tests, the rt
     runners' fixtures; Lc the text runtime entries on both targets, their tests and the gate**;
     (b) one code sub-phase Lb with everything; (c) three: bitwise and `%x`; `read_lines`, `split`
     and `substr`; the parse functions. Recommended: (a): the front end is one change across the
     passes made once (as 9b did), the bitwise functions and `%x` need no new runtime file and are
     tested end to end in Lb, and Lc is pure runtime work against fixed front-end output (as 9c
     was); (b) puts every package in one integration; (c) touches every pass twice. Affects §8,
     §2.15.9. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-03).
150. **The user's rulings on four readings of the draft** (2026-11-03, asked with Decisions
     143–149; each a ruling, not a choice among options): (a) `parse_i64` and `parse_f64` reject
     leading and trailing blanks (`" 5"`, `"1.0 "` are parse errors), as drafted; (b) `parse_i64`
     in base 16 rejects a `0x`/`0X` prefix (`"0x1F"` is a parse error), as drafted; (c) `shl`
     discards the bits shifted out and never reports `integer overflow`, as drafted; (d) the flags
     `+` and space with `%x`/`%X` are accepted and have no effect, as C defines them for signed
     conversions only, **changed** from the draft, which made them the compile error 234. Affects
     LANGUAGE.md §10.9, §10.14, §11.1 (items 5, 9, 10 of §2.15.2), §2.15.4, §2.15.6, §2.15.8, L-mm.
     **Decided** (the user, 2026-11-03).

**Decisions of W8** (written 2026-11-04 with the text of §2.16, sub-phase W8a, agreed by the user
the same day: 151–157 asked with the workload's outline and decided by the user that day, each as
option (a); 158–160 decided by the user with the agreement, each as option (a); 161 found in W8c and
decided by the user on 2026-11-04 as option (a)). Each lists its options with the
recommendation in bold, its reasons, the decision, and what it affects; §2.16.13 holds the same
text.

151. **Who writes the controller sketch.** Options: (a) **an agent writes an original sketch to
     §2.16.4; the user reviews it and flashes it to the board if they wish**; (b) the user writes
     the sketch and the agents build the mock and the model around it (the control law and the
     message set then follow the user's code, and the analysis is written after it); (c) an
     existing example sketch is adapted (excluded by the workloads' originality rule). Recommended:
     (a). Affects §2.16.4, §2.16.12 (W8b). **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).
152. **The reference oracle.** Options: (a) **a MATLAB script `sea/workloads/w8_ev_can.m`, written
     like W1–W7; the user runs it once to produce `reference/w8_ev_can.json`, the `.txt` report and
     the figure; no agent runs MATLAB**; (b) a NumPy script only, run by the agents (W8 would be the
     one workload without a MATLAB reference and without a MATLAB timing, so "faster than MATLAB"
     could not be judged); (c) the simulator writes the expected analysis itself (the oracle would
     share the simulator's code and defects). Recommended: (a). Affects §1.2, §2.16.8, §2.16.12
     (W8c). **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).
153. **How the log reaches the tests.** Options: (a) **a fixed committed log of a few MB; a
     separate target (`make w8-log`) rebuilds it with the simulator and checks it is
     byte-identical; ordinary `make test` and `make cross` need no C++ compiler**; (b) the log is
     generated by `make test` before acceptance (every test run, and the Mac half of `make cross`,
     then needs `xcrun c++`, and a compiler change could silently change the reference input); (c)
     a short log generated at test time plus the committed one. Recommended: (a). Affects §2.16.7,
     §2.16.11, §2.16.12. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).
154. **The real ESP32.** Options: (a) **optional: the same `.ino` compiles and flashes; in TWAI
     self-test mode (no other node needed) it prints a real log over Serial in the same format,
     which Sea can read too; acceptance uses only the simulated log**; (b) required: a hardware log
     is part of acceptance (acceptance would depend on a board and a bench); (c) no hardware path
     (the sketch would not be checked against the real core). Recommended: (a). Affects §2.16.4,
     §2.16.7, §2.16.9, Decision 160. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).
155. **Where the sketch, the mock and the model live.** Options: (a) **`sea/workloads/w8_ev_can/`
     (the sketch folder, the mock, the motor and vehicle model and their build), outside the
     compiler and the runtimes, so the rule "no C in the compiler or runtimes" still holds**; (b) a
     repository of its own as a submodule; (c) `sea/tools/w8/`, beside the compiler's tools.
     Recommended: (a) (the user had no preference). Affects §2.16.2, §2.16.12. **Decided: (a)** (the
     user, 2026-11-04).
156. **What the analysis and the figure show.** Options: (a) **per motor, commanded against
     measured torque and the response delay; for the pair, the torque split against the yaw demand;
     the bus load, the frame counts and every dropped or late frame; a four-panel figure**; (b) frame
     counts and bus load only, one panel; (c) (a) plus spectra of the signals (an FFT, which Sea does
     not have). Recommended: (a). Affects §2.16.8. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).
157. **W8 in the acceptance set.** Options: (a) **W8 joins the acceptance set as W7 did (Decision
     114), with its own MATLAB timing file `reference/baseline_timings_matlab_w8_ev_can.json`; the
     committed W1–W5 baseline stays untouched**; (b) W8 stays a reference workload outside the set,
     as W6 is; (c) W8 joins and all seven workloads are rerun into the main baseline file.
     Recommended: (a). Affects §1.2 (the set, the versions paragraph, W8's baseline), §6.3, §6.5,
     §8 (rows W8 and 10), LANGUAGE.md §1.2 and §10 (with the agreement, §2.16.15). **Decided: (a)**
     (the user, 2026-11-04).
158. **How the acceptance run gets the log** (§6.3's run directory may hold only the
     executable and what the port writes). Options: (a) **a header line `// fixture: PATH` in the
     port (PATH relative to `sea/`); `tests/accept.sh` copies each fixture into the run directory,
     which may then also hold the fixtures, unchanged; `cross_pack.sh` packs them as the case's
     `NAME.files/`, which the host already copies and checks; a port may hold several such lines,
     and the same line twice or two fixtures with the same base name are a setup error**; (b) a
     committed copy
     `ports/w8_ev_can.files/w8_ev_can.log` copied as the tests' `NAME.files/` are (the same rule
     change, but a second 3.6 MB copy of the log to keep identical); (c) `accept.sh` passes the port
     `--log <absolute path>` into the workloads directory (per-port arguments in `accept.sh`, a run
     that reads outside its directory, and a host bundle that must rebuild the same path).
     Recommended: (a): one committed copy, a header line in the style of Decision 127's `// cross:`
     line, and `cross_run.sh` unchanged. Affects §6.3, §6.6.1, §2.16.9, §2.16.10, `tests/accept.sh`,
     `tests/cross_pack.sh` (W8d), `bench/workloads.sh` (phase 10). **Decided: (a)** (the user,
     2026-11-04).
159. **A NumPy cross-check of the MATLAB script** (W1–W7 each have one in
     `reference_py/`, written before MATLAB could be run). Options: (a) **yes: `reference_py/
     w8_ev_can.py`, written in W8c from §2.16.8 by an agent that did not write `w8_ev_can.m`, run
     before the script goes to the user; `reference/w8_ev_can.py.json` committed and compared in
     `compare.py`'s NumPy mode**; (b) no: MATLAB is the only reference, and a defect of the script
     shows only when the port disagrees after the user's run, which then needs a second run.
     Recommended: (a): two independent readings of §2.16.8 agree before the user spends a MATLAB
     run, as for W1–W7. Affects §2.16.12 (W8c), `workloads/README.md`. **Decided: (a)** (the user,
     2026-11-04).
160. **How the bench lets the ESP32 hear itself** (Decision 154's hardware log needs the
     controller to receive its own frames). The core 3.3.7 offers, in the polled driver
     `driver/twai.h`, `TWAI_MODE_NO_ACK` with the per-frame self-reception flag `self`, and in the
     newer `esp_twai_onchip.h` a node configuration with `flags.enable_self_test` and
     `flags.enable_loopback`. Options: (a) **the polled driver with `TWAI_MODE_NO_ACK` and `self = 1`
     (§2.16.4), and one jumper wire from GPIO 21 (TX) to GPIO 22 (RX), no transceiver: the
     controller then reads its own bits**; (b) the same code with a CAN transceiver board on the
     bench (terminated), as in the car; (c) the newer driver with `enable_loopback`, which this text
     has not established to work without any wire on the original ESP32, and which changes the API
     the sketch uses and the mock must copy (event callbacks and receive in interrupt context instead
     of a polled queue). Recommended: (a): no extra hardware beyond a wire, the same code as (b), and
     the small polled mock of §2.16.5; whether (a) works on the user's board is checked when the user
     first flashes it (not part of acceptance). Affects §2.16.4, §2.16.5, §2.16.7. **Decided: (a)**
     (the user, 2026-11-04).
161. **The driving traces** (W8c; found by a physics review of the W8b log). The pedal is a torque
     request with no speed loop, and §2.16.6's first traces held 35–100 % pedal for 8–25 s: the car
     sat on the motor speed-fade limiter (30.6 m/s, 8 780 rev/min) in 74 % of the cycles and took
     every curve there, at up to 2.3 g of lateral acceleration (the model has no tyre saturation,
     L-ny); derate frames were over 60 %, `track_err` (24 N·m) measured only the speed governor,
     `split_gain` was −8.63 with the yaw limiter engaged in 88 % of A9's cycles, and switching the
     torque vectoring off changed nothing. The code and the definitions were correct; only the
     traces were at fault. Options: (a) **retune the pedal and steering traces (a light cruise
     pedal, smaller steering angles), keeping the narrative and the faults, and regenerate the
     committed log**; (b) keep W8 as specified; (c) keep the traces and restrict A9 to the cycles
     with `YawLimit` = 0. Recommended: (a): the workload's engineering content then holds with no
     change to the sketch, the mock, the analysis or any key, at the cost of a new log before the
     MATLAB run; (b) keeps a case whose numbers mean nothing; (c) hides the symptom in one key and
     leaves the rest. With §2.16.6's retuned traces the committed log gives `split_gain` 34.01 N·m
     per rad/s (the realised split of the `TorqueAct` values 33.86), a peak lateral acceleration
     v·r_meas of 5.49 m/s², `YawLimit` in 250 of A9's 4 200 cycles, `DERATE` only in the
     full-throttle run (893 and 890 frames, 33.92–42.85 s), `v_max` 30.36 m/s, and in an independent
     re-simulation with the `S_ADC`, `S_MOT` and `S_IMU` noise set to 0 (A9's `yaw_err_rms` over
     the same cycles) 0.0441 rad/s with the split and 0.0582 without it; the line and byte
     counts, the fault counts and the order of the five state changes are unchanged. Affects
     §2.16.6, §2.16.12 (W8b's built facts), `host/model.cpp`'s two trace tables and the committed
     `w8_ev_can.log`, `serial.txt` and `bench_serial.txt`. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).

**Decisions of phase 10** (written 2026-11-04 with the text of §2.17, sub-phase 10a, agreed by the
user the same day after one independent review: 162–167 asked with the phase's outline and decided
by the user that day, each as option (a); 168–172 left to the user with the text, 170–172 added
after the review, and decided by the user with the agreement, each as option (a)). Each lists its
options with the
recommendation in bold, its reasons, the decision, and what it affects; §2.17.12 holds the same
text.

162. **Which benchmarks phase 10 runs.** Options: (a) **the seven workloads against MATLAB (§6.5),
     the existing micro-benchmarks (§5.9), and a small set of Sea-level matrix benchmarks written in
     Sea: GEMM (`@`), `solve` and one fused element-wise loop, compared with Apple Accelerate on the
     Mac and OpenBLAS on Linux by C harnesses in `bench/` only, never linked into Sea, with stated
     sizes and methodology; their results are reported, and the only pass rule is §6.5's workload
     rule**; (b) the workloads and the micro-benchmarks only; (c) a full kernel suite like Baysick's
     (every kernel, every size, peak loops). Recommended: (a). Affects §2.17.6, §2.17.7, §5.7 (its
     list of measured kernels, with the agreement). **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).
163. **Who takes the final measurement.** Options: (a) **an agent, in one go, unniced, on the idle
     M2 Pro, when the user says "go"; it records the load average before and after, the machine,
     the OS and the commit**; (b) the user runs the `make` target and pastes the output.
     Recommended: (a). Affects §2.17.3, §2.17.10, row 10c. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).
164. **What follows a miss.** Options: (a) **if any workload misses on either measure, a targeted
     optimisation sub-phase, agreed with the user, follows, and then everything is re-measured**;
     (b) the miss is recorded and v1 waits. Recommended: (a). Affects §2.17.11 (row 10o), §2.17.9
     (the kept attempts), Decision 168. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).
165. **Linux numbers.** Options: (a) **Linux x86_64 numbers are measured on the ssh host `desktop`
     (Intel Core i7-4790) and reported, compared with nothing**; (b) no Linux numbers. Recommended:
     (a). Affects §2.17.4, §2.17.6, §2.17.7, `make bench-cross`, `BENCH.md` §8. **Decided: (a)**
     (the user, 2026-11-04).
166. **The version after the pass.** Options: (a) **when §6.5 passes, Sea's version becomes 1.0.0
     (Decision 79) wherever it is recorded: the driver's `--version` text (`driver/sea`, the only
     place in code), §1.2 and §2.2, `sea/CLAUDE.md`'s status and version line, and `README.md`**;
     (b) the version stays 0.y. Recommended: (a). Affects row 10d. **Decided: (a)** (the user,
     2026-11-04).
167. **NumPy timings.** Options: (a) **the NumPy reference timings are an extra reported column,
     never judged**; (b) MATLAB only. Recommended: (a). Affects §2.17.5, `BENCH.md` §4.
     **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).
168. **What an optimisation sub-phase may change** (Decision 164's 10o). Options: (a) **the
     compiler passes, the runtimes and the prelude only; a port changes only where it departs from
     its MATLAB script's algorithm (a defect of the port), never to restructure an accepted port for
     speed**; (b) also port rewrites that keep the MATLAB script's algorithm and outputs but change
     how the Sea code is written (for example a hand-vectorized loop or a preallocated buffer), each
     still accepted by `tests/accept.sh`; (c) anything that keeps acceptance, a different algorithm
     included. Recommended: (a): a gain in the compiler or runtime holds for every Sea program, the
     ports stay the programs that were accepted, and the comparison stays "the same program written
     plainly in each language"; (b) measures how well the port was tuned as much as Sea; (c) would
     no longer compare like with like. Affects row 10o. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).
169. **The README after 1.0.0.** Options: (a) **10d adds to `README.md` a short "Performance"
     table (per workload, Sea's best of 5 and MATLAB's best on both measures, and the machine),
     generated by `report.py` from the committed results, with a link to `docs/BENCH.md`**; (b) the
     README only states the version and links `docs/BENCH.md`. Recommended: (a): the speed goal is
     Sea's first goal (§1.1), and a generated table cannot drift from the measurement. With (a),
     `report.py` has a `--readme` option printing that table (written in 10b), and row 10d's
     WP-VERSION pastes it. Affects row 10d, §2.17.9. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).
170. **The start condition of each measurement.** An independent review saw this Mac at a 1-minute
     load average of 1.68–2.28 while idle with an agent session open, so the draft's limit of 1.0
     could not be reached. Options: (a) **a separate build step before any timed run, then before
     each tool's measurement a cool-down of at least 120 s, then a wait (15-minute timeout) until the
     1-minute load average is at most 2.0; the wait and the load are recorded; on timeout the driver
     stops and the agent reports instead of measuring**; (b) the same with the limit 1.0; (c) no load
     condition: the load is only recorded. Recommended: (a): the build's heat and the agent's own
     background load are allowed for, a measurement on a busy machine is still refused, and every
     wait is in the record; (b) would in practice never start; (c) could publish numbers taken on a
     loaded machine. Affects §2.17.3, §2.17.10, L-po, L-pl. **Decided: (a)** (the user,
     2026-11-04).
171. **What `axpby` measures, and how hoisting is excluded.** In a loop, `w = 0.75 * x - 1.25 * y`
     reuses `w`'s buffer and allocates nothing per call (§5.4, §2.12's F2 (6)), so an allocation
     count cannot show that each call ran. Options: (a) **the natural Sea form, reusing `w`'s
     buffer, guarded for every implementation by an input that changes with the call number (r mod
     2, so the checked result is that of the last call) and by the rule that a batched call may not
     be more than twice as fast as a single one**; (b) a form that allocates a fresh result on every
     call (for example a function returning the expression), so the heap count of the first draft
     works. Recommended: (a): it measures what a Sea user's loop costs, the input change makes
     hoisting impossible rather than merely detectable, and the guard is the same for Sea and C; (b)
     measures an allocation the language avoids in practice. Affects §2.17.6, L-pg. **Decided: (a)**
     (the user, 2026-11-04).
172. **NumPy's threads.** Options: (a) **NumPy's default threads, as MATLAB's pass baseline ran
     with its default threads: no thread variable is set, and the BLAS and thread settings NumPy
     reports are recorded**; (b) single-threaded (`VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS=1`,
     `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1`), like Sea. Recommended: (a): the column sits beside MATLAB's default
     baseline and is not judged; (b) would make it comparable with the single-threaded MATLAB file
     instead. Affects §2.17.3, §2.17.5. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-11-04).

**Lead decisions of phase 5** (2026-10-24, within Decisions 58–73, each taken because one answer is
clearly right, reported to the user and agreed with the phase-5 text; each is written into its
normative section): L-ac,
`seagen_a64` and `seagen_x64` use all 26 numeric array letters, so the allocator adds none: its
per-register state widens the code generator's `D` and the module keeps small SUB-local arrays
(§2.7, §4.9.2); L-ad, `seaopt` keeps its facts in the six phase-5 columns of `R`, widened to
`R(99999,9)`, and takes one new letter, `W`, leaving `S` and `V` (§2.7); L-ae, §3.6.4 states the
four properties of `sea.lir1` that phase 5 relies on (headers never stored to, definite assignment,
`ref` memory reached only through the parameter, slots only through their `sa` registers); L-af,
`ref` parameters and private slots are unaliased within a function, which follows from LANGUAGE.md
§7.2 (no global variables) and §8.3 (no shared roots) with rule 31's copy on write (§5.8); L-ag, a
value kept in a register need not be stored back on a path that ends in a run-time error, because
the process ends and releases nothing (LANGUAGE.md §9.2, §4.2; §5.8); L-ah, the x86_64 forms of
§4.9.2 (two-address rules, `leaq` for an add of an immediate, `imulq $v`, `xorpd` before `cvtsi2sdq`,
`andpd`/`xorpd` for `fabs`/`fneg`); L-ai, the loop-closing sequences of §4.9.2; L-aj, only loads
without an index are hoisted, since an indexed load is valid only after its check (§5.8 T8);
L-ak, the `.lir` goldens a transformation changes (not `gen_arith`, a hand-written pass-4 test, L-bj) are re-derived from §5.8,
as L-i did for 4g-1 (§3.6.5); L-al, `f64` division by a normal power of two only (−1022 ≤ e ≤ 1023;
for e = 1023 the reciprocal is the exact subnormal 2⁻¹⁰²³), never `%` on `f64` (§5.8 T2); L-am,
`seaopt` computes the magic numbers with its own 128-by-64-bit division on 16-bit limbs instead of
loading `limb` (801 lines, of which it needs none) (§2.7, §5.8).

**Lead decisions of phase 5 after the review of its text** (2026-10-24; an independent review of
the agreed text found defects that the text could not leave open; none changes a user decision, and
each is written into its normative section): L-an, pass 4's templates (§4.9.2): every LIR
instruction is *direct* (allocated registers in place, with the multi-instruction forms written so
that a destination may share an operand's register: arm64 `imulc` computes the high half first, the
x86_64 `isel`/`psel`/`fsel` forms depend on whether d is a or b, `imulh` and variable shifts go
through `%rax`/`%rdx` and `%rcx`, addresses are formed in `x16` or `%r11`, `retain`/`release`
count in `x16` or `%rcx`) or *staged* (`idivf imodf rcount ftoi fmin fmax ffloor fceil ftrunc fround
mcopy`: §4.9's and §4.9.1's sequences on the scratch registers, renamed, with operands moved in and
results out; arm64 `mcopy`'s data through `d29`; x86_64 `ffloor`/`fceil`/`fround` adjusting t as an
integer instead of using `%xmm10`), and every parallel move is emitted in three steps (memory
destinations, then register moves with cycles broken through `x17`/`d31`, `%r11`/`%xmm15`, then
memory and immediate sources straight into their destinations); L-ao (split by L-be: T1–T4 and T10 in `seaopt`, the rest in `sealopt`), `seaopt` runs T8 before T7
and again after it (T1–T6, T8, T7, T8, T9, T10), because T7 needs invariant bases and index terms
that only T8 moves out of the loop (§5.8); L-ap, T1's facts are a state that the walk carries and
joins: the symbol bounds L, U and every narrowing hold only in the part or loop that made them (a
guard's facts end at its `endif`, a loop's at its closing record, which restores the loop's entry
state with what the loop writes unknown), a symbol other than a constant has the interval [s, s]
with what its definition computes in L(s), U(s), the bounds rows ≥ 0 hold from the `rcall` that
creates the array, a dominating comparison of a symbol with a constant narrows its L(s) or U(s) in
that part, and a narrowing between incomparable bounds keeps the old bound (§5.8); L-aq, a
loop whose hidden count register would be numbered above `SEA_LIM_LIR_REGS` keeps its count in a
spill slot, so pass 4 never fails on the register limit (§4.9.2, as Decision 72 does for `seaopt`);
L-ar, a shape test identifies its loop by its properties: the line passes when one of the named
function's innermost loops, found from `--emit lir`, meets all of them, so no block number is
derived by hand (§6.2); L-as, the condition codes of fused comparisons, whose inverses hold for
unordered operands on both targets, and x86_64 `fcmp eq`/`ne` as two branches (`jp` with `jne` or
`je`) and never fused into a selection (§4.9.2); L-at, an anticipated load is hoisted only through
an object pointer (a parameter, a `call`/`rcall` result, an `ldp`, an `sa`, or a `mov` of one), which
is non-null and points to a live object wherever it is read, so running it before a failing
instruction of the loop reads valid memory (§5.8 T8).

**Lead decisions of phase 5 during its build** (2026-10-24; questions the 5b and 5c-1 work
packages raised that implementers and golden writers must answer alike; none changes a user
decision, and each is written into its normative section): L-au, T1 compares two different symbols
through their bounds, s + k ≤ t + m when U(s) + k ≤ L(t) + m, and F2 gives a symbol extent its L, U
from rows(A) or cols(A), so `chkb k E` with symbols is proven when L(k) ≥ 0 and U(k) < L(E) (§5.8);
L-av, the readings of T1–T3 made normative because `seaopt`'s output is canonical (Decision 69): F4

and two notes: `opt5_promote_exit` covers only the exits Sea can write (an `exit` or `next` of an
enclosing loop from a nested one arises only through inlining), and Decision 72's skips are
covered by review, not by a golden (§6.2); during WP-LOPT's build: L-bu, the label rules "numbered
by first reference" and "every defined label is referenced" hold for `sea.lir1` only, since T10 may
delete `la` instructions while pass 3b keeps every label and data record; `sea.lir2` and `sea.lir`

§2.10); after independent reviews of the 5c-2 working tree: L-bv, (1) T5's destination rewriting
of `mov X V` also requires that no instruction strictly between the `mov` and the last read of V in
record order writes X (the last read may itself write X), since otherwise a read of V rewritten to
X sees a later store into the promoted location (`s = a + b; let t = s; s = 0; w += t` printed 0
for `w`); a region holds no block record, so a read of V in a nested part or loop is outside it and
blocks the rewriting; (2) T7's accesses share one Q and Δ only with equal D, k, c, σ, t and scale z,
since both depend on z; (3) a pass's own scratch tables (`seaopt`'s, `sealopt`'s `S()`, `V()` and
its columns of `R`) are bounded by their regions, and a transformation whose table would overflow
is not applied to that loop or function, extending Decision 72 from LIR limits to the pass's tables
so that no input can crash a pass or make tables overlap; (4) T8's object pointer excludes a data
pointer (an `ldp` of `SEA_ARR_DATA`): its buffer may hold no element, so no field offset is known to
lie inside it; no `.lir2` golden holds an index-free load through a data pointer, so no
optimization a golden shows is lost; (5) the array registers are the greatest fixpoint of their
recursive definition, so a loop-carried `mov` cycle of candidates stays in the set, as the code
computes; (6) `SEA_LIM_LIR_LABELS` is the user error `TOO_LARGE` only on `sea.lir1` input: in
`sea.lir2` or `sea.lir` a label number above it, defined or referenced, is a malformed record
(`BAD_RECORD`), and L-bd's "`sea.lir2` holds exactly what `sea.lir1` may hold" reads "except the
two `sea.lir1`-only label rules"; (7) `lirrw`'s API states that entry 69440 overwrites `I(n,0)`
and `R(r,2)` and that the reader's data-record scalars (`Z8` among them) are never written by the
pass, and the reserved scalars are 173 (149 numeric, 24 string) with `H5` and `V8`; (8) `ra_else`
requires B to be the innermost open block, of kind `if`/`ifz`, with its first part current, and
reports any other call through `dg_bug` before changing anything (so `ralloc` needs `diag`, which
both code generators load, and names itself `ralloc` in the message); (9) T5's destination rewriting
also requires that every read of V lies after V's definition in record order (the read at the
definition itself, which reads the old value, counts as before it), since a read before it sees a
value the definition does not produce and would be rewritten to read X before the new definition
writes it; and the bounds of the pass's tables are tested for the rows of `C` and `G` (the capacity
test of a transformation also requires that the rows it may add fit) and for the nesting stack of
`ANC` (a `loop` record counts against it too) (§3.6.2, §3.6.5, §5.8 Terms, T5, T7, T8, §2.6.3;
`passes/lib/API.md`).

**Readings fixed by the 5c-2 build** (where the specification was silent; recorded by the implementers
and kept by the lead, after L-bv; normative for the goldens).

*WP-LOPT* (`sealopt`):

* L-br counts one level of `mov` only: a start or step that is an `li` register, or a `mov` from one;
  a `mov` of a `mov` is not constant.
* T7's folded start term must lie within ±2⁵². T7 does not reduce when Q = D.
* A missing `ldi` means no copy-on-write (no cow is recognized without it).
* T5 skips dead records. Offsets outside ±2⁵² are unknown.
* L-bm renames with the final duplicate map (the one complete after the copier has finished).
* Decision 72 is applied with upper bounds and the pass's internal buffer limits: a transformation
  whose bound or buffer could be exceeded is not applied.
* L-bv fix (3), the T9 `PLACE` scratch table: when it overflows, the split is kept and only the
  placement is dropped; the output equals that of a `PLACE` that placed nothing, and is still correct.
* `V8` is a contract scalar (`passes/lib/API.md`), reserved by `lirrw`.

*WP-PIPE*: "the loop" of the `ra5_live` frame-access check is read as every innermost loop.

*WP-RA2*: a register read before any write counts as written at record 0.

**Lead decisions of phase 6** (written 2026-10-25 with the text of §2.11 and agreed by the user
together with Decisions 80–93 on 2026-10-26; each is a reading where
LANGUAGE.md or the earlier rules leave a choice, written into its normative section):

* **L-bw** A `ref` parameter with a default is 227 at the default expression (§2.6.2's `at` table
  says so for the `ref` position); a named argument for a `ref` parameter is 254 at its value
  (`name: ref x` does not parse, so a `ref` parameter is given positionally only, Decision 93).
  LANGUAGE.md §8.1 gains the sentence (§2.11.2).
* **L-bx** Per Decision 91: `seaname` makes a default's structural checks (236, 227, its names) in
  the signature step; `seacheck` checks its value with the `const` items, as the value of a `const`
  item annotated with the parameter's type (237, 201, 260, 261 at the nodes the `const` rules name,
  a named constant's outcome per Decision 25), in source order with every other error; a correct
  default is copied into each call that omits it with its own positions (§2.11.2).
* **L-by** A library function other than a prelude function accepts only its option names as named
  arguments; any other name is 224 at the `narg` (the promise of "Readings fixed by 4f") (§2.11.2).
* **L-bz** JSON layout: two-space indentation per depth, `"key": value`, `,` after every member or
  element but the last, `{}` and `[]` for empty containers, a matrix as an array of rows, a matrix
  with no element `[]`, one LF after the top value; escapes `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\t`, and every other
  byte below 0x20 as `\u00` with two lowercase hex digits; 0x7F and bytes 0x80–0xFF verbatim;
  `-0` written as `-0` (`%.17g`). LANGUAGE.md §11.4 gains the sentence (§2.11.6).
* **L-ca** A run-time error while a JSON file is open: `_sea_err` flushes and closes it, ignoring a
  failure of that flush, then reports the original error; an emitter's own failed flush or close is
  `CANNOT_WRITE` with the path and the errno. `JSON_OPEN` allocates the emitter's state (descriptor
  −1) before it opens the file, and `_sea_err` acts only when the descriptor is set (§2.11.6).
* **L-cb** `make_dir`'s details are Decision 89's: the path copied into a NUL-terminated buffer
  (freed on every exit; a NUL byte in the path is `EINVAL`), `mkdir(buf, 0777)` under the umask, on
  any failure the errno saved and the directory test by `open(buf, O_RDONLY | O_DIRECTORY)`, no
  `stat` (§2.11.6).
* **L-cc** A `format` result longer than `SEA_LIM_STR_BYTES`, like a failed allocation, is
  `out of memory` (no new error code); LANGUAGE.md §9.2's out-of-memory row names `format` (§2.11.6).
* **L-cd** `print` has its own entry `PRINT` writing into the standard-output buffer that `printf`
  uses, so the two interleave in program order and fail alike (§2.11.6).
* **L-ce** Pass 2b's step 4 writes `jvec (dyn e)` / `jmat (dyn e)` for a fixed-size value, so the
  emitter's entries take heap arrays only (§2.11.3).
* **L-cf** Inlined code of the program's own functions keeps its own positions (§3.6.4 "Sites");
  the `xblk`, its `tmp`s, the `iblk` and the `loc` records of the `.i` locals take the call's P
  (§2.11.4).
* **L-cg** After L19 and L20, `sealoop` drops the prelude, `elem` and `inl` functions and renumbers
  the rest densely (L-v extended); `sea.hirl` holds no `inst`, `emap` or kind `elem`/`inl`
  (§2.11.4).
* **L-ch** §8.6 (b) counts `call` nodes on the source over every function of the program's file,
  reachable from `.main` or not, including the function's own body; each call written counts once,
  however often it runs (inside a loop, or in an elemental function's body applied to an array);
  LANGUAGE.md §8.6 states it, since the guarantee is the programmer's to check (§2.11.3).
* **L-ci** §8.6 (c)'s statement count is one per Appendix A `statement`: an `if … else if … else`
  chain counts 1, a bare block statement counts 1, every other statement 1, and the statements
  inside every block (bodies, branches, arms, bare blocks) count; LANGUAGE.md §8.6 states it
  (§2.11.3).
* **L-cj** "Recursive" is membership in a cycle of the call graph of every `call` node of the
  stream (direct or mutual) (§2.11.3).
* **L-ck** An elemental application evaluates every argument once, in full, before any element;
  elements run in increasing linear (column-major) order, so an error in the body is raised at the
  first failing element with the callee's line (§2.11.4).
* **L-cl** `ind2sub` with an array `r` is a two-result elemental application of rule 36's scalar
  sequence by L19, every check at the call's site; L11 keeps the scalar case (§2.11.4).
* **L-cm** `FMOD`: b = ±0 returns a's bits; an infinite a or a NaN operand returns
  `#7FF8000000000000`; otherwise r = the C library's `fmod(a, b)` (exact by IEEE 754, the same bits
  on both C libraries), adjusted once by + b when r ≠ 0 and r and b differ in sign; not folded by any
  pass. The test vectors are computed with `math.fmod` and the adjustment, never Python's `%`, and
  committed as `tests/vectors/fmod6.vec` for the runtime tests (§2.11.6, §6.2).
* **L-cn** On the Linux host a port's standard output is compared with the Mac's byte for byte
  after removing, on both sides, the lines matching `^Compute time: .* s$`; its JSON byte for byte;
  the filter is a new case attribute `filter=compute-time` of `cross_pack.sh` and `cross_run.sh`,
  WP-ACCEPT's (§6.3).
* **L-co** The JSON emitter's container stack lives on the heap, grows as needed (no depth limit,
  `out of memory` if it cannot) and is freed by `JSON_CLOSE` (§2.11.6).
* **L-cp** Named arguments are evaluated in source order: when that differs from parameter order,
  pass 2a writes the `seq` of `.t` temporaries of "Evaluation order" (§3.5.5), which makes R11's
  `seq` case reachable (§2.11.2).
* **L-cq** 228 and 232 are reported by `seaname`'s call pre-pass through `rerr`, the first check at
  a `call` node, keeping "Order across the two programs" (§2.11.2).
* **L-cr** Rule 39 lowers only the nodes of its table; rules 8, 9, 14, 24, 34 and 35 stay as written,
  so no earlier golden changes (§2.11.5).
* **L-cs** The `entries` capacity of `sealower` (now 22) and of `seagen_a64` and `seagen_x64` (now
  29) becomes 64 (room for phases 8 and 9), two edited lines per pass; `seaopt` and `sealopt` keep
  399 (§2.11.1).
* **L-ct** A golden that §8.6 inlining changes is re-derived from the rules by T2, never copied
  from output, as Decision 90 says (the 21 lowering dump tests of §6.2 and the `.res`, `.hir1` and
  `.hir` goldens of `el` 2 and kind `inl`); `stack_gap` of `tests/accept/w5_stats.sea` becomes
  inlined, which changes no output (§3.6.6, §6.2).
* **L-cu** For `write_json`, `str` is a JSON scalar: a `str` value is a `jval`, a `str[]` or `str[,]`
  a `jvec` or `jmat` (fixed-size ones through `dyn`), although §4.5's classes count `str` as a
  reference type (§3.5.7 step 4 as amended).
* **L-cv** A matrix of structs or records with no element (r × 0 or 0 × c) is written `[]` by a
  guard in pass 2b's expansion, matching LANGUAGE.md §11.4 (§3.5.7 step 4 as amended).
* **L-cw** `seaname`'s call pre-pass is iterative (a worklist for the effects fixpoint, an explicit
  stack for the cycle search), so Baysick's limit of 1 024 active `CALL`s does not bound the call
  graph (§2.11.2).
* **L-cx** `tests/accept.sh` writes a port's standard output and standard error outside its run
  directory, which must then hold only `NAME.json` and the executable; a path that is a directory is
  tested with `write_json(".", …)`, since git keeps no empty directory (§6.2, §6.3).
* **L-cy** (6b, agreed 2026-10-28) In a call that reports `unknown parameter` (224), `missing
  argument` (226) is not reported, because the unknown name may be the missing parameter. Amends
  §2.11.2 ("Named arguments"); code: `passes/seacheck/sc9call.bas`.
* **L-cz** (6b, 2026-10-28) Inside an `iblk`, the "one statement" of §3.6.6 rule 12 is each statement
  of the inlined body (the callee's statements, L-w), and an `iret` is a statement just as a `ret`
  is; the rule's "statements inside an `xblk` belong to the statement that holds the `xblk`" applies
  to the `xblk`s of the body, not to the body itself. Amends R26 and §3.6.6 rule 12.
* **L-da** (6b, 2026-10-28) R32's home H is always a new home, allocated before `do B` after the
  `tmp`s of the inline `xblk`. Under a `bind` H is copied (moved) into the local; under a `tbind`,
  `tasg`, `tret` or `eval` H is copied into the home the parent provides, in R27's place of the
  `mov`. The order before `do B` is the R32 homes first, then the deferred rule-31 stores. A struct
  literal value goes into its own home V, then `li N size; mcopy H V N`, as rule 27 (d) stores a
  value into a home. Amends R32 (§2.11.5).
* **L-db** (6b, 2026-10-28) In a reordered call (L-cp), an index expression of a `rarg` target that
  holds its own `$` (a `dol`) is written in place, not bound, since a `dol` may appear only inside
  its `idx`; if such an index also has effects, they run at the argument's position in parameter
  order, not in source order. Amends §3.5.5 "Evaluation order" and the `dol` rule of the validation
  of the same section.
* **L-dc** (6b, 2026-10-28) A reordered call whose bound values are all constants writes `seq … 0`,
  as struct literals already do. "Constant" for binding is the existing `cst` rule (`ci`, `cf`, `cb`,
  `cs` leaves, `pi`, `inf`, `nan`, `eps`), so `-5` and a named constant are bound. Amends §3.5.5
  "Evaluation order".
* **L-dd** (6b, 2026-10-28) `seaname` evaluates a constant `f64` `%` (`const M = 5.5 % 2.0`) and writes
  `rcnf`; `seacheck` then sees `rcnf`, not a `bin` (§3.4.1 step 3, LANGUAGE.md §7.2).
* **L-de** (6b, 2026-10-28) `make_dir("")` reports `No such file or directory` (`ENOENT` on both
  targets) (§4.8, `MAKE_DIR`).
* **L-df** (6b, 2026-10-28) Decision 90 with several inlinable functions in one test: each gets the
  `while false {}` loop. Where every such function already has two or more call sites, no second
  call site is added and the `.out` is unchanged (§6.2, "Goldens that inlining changes").
* **L-dg** (6b, 2026-10-28) `res_err_param_shadow`'s function has 0 call sites and 1 statement, so it
  is class (c) and its `.res` is re-derived with `el` 2, not "checked and unchanged" (§6.2).
* **L-dh** (6b, 2026-10-28) `make_dir` on an existing directory without read permission: Decision
  89's `open(O_RDONLY | O_DIRECTORY)` test fails with `EACCES`, and `make_dir` then reports the saved
  `mkdir` errno (`File exists`). This is accepted; no code change (§4.8, `MAKE_DIR`).
* **L-di** (6c, agreed 2026-10-28) `elemental function cannot be recursive` (232) stands at the
  first `call`, in source order, that is an edge between two functions of the elemental function
  E's strongly connected component of the call graph (E reaches the caller, E itself included, and
  the callee reaches E). It agrees with "on a cycle through E" about whether 232 is reported but may
  name another call: with `b` calling `a` (line 3, first), `a` calling `b` and `e`, and the elemental
  `e` calling `a`, it reports `b`'s call, which lies on no simple cycle through `e`; the exact
  simple-cycle rule is the directed two-disjoint-paths problem. Amends §2.11.2 and LANGUAGE.md §8.5;
  code: `passes/seaname/sn9cls.bas` (`cpre`).
* **L-dj** (6c, agreed 2026-10-28) For 228, the plotting calls of LANGUAGE.md §8.1 are every function
  of §12's tables (`figure`, `panel`, `plot`, `bar`, `barh`, `contour`, `image`, `xline`, `title`,
  `xlabel`, `ylabel`, `legend`, `grid`, `xlim`, `ylim`, `axis_equal`, `x_ticks`, `y_ticks`,
  `y_reverse`, `twin_y`) and `save_svg`, those that only build a figure included (§2.11.2).
* **L-dk** (6c, agreed 2026-10-28) At one `call` 228 is checked before 232, so a call that is both
  reports 228. 253 is reported at the `fn` item after its parameters' errors and result types, and
  not when a result type is the error type (an error already reported in it) (§2.11.2; code:
  `passes/seaname/sn3item.bas`, `sn9cls.bas`).
* **L-dl** (6c, agreed 2026-10-28) Pass 2b's step 3 as built (§2.11.3, §3.5.3, §3.5.7): it runs at
  `#end` over every function in file order, before reachability, and turns a `call` into an `emap`
  when an argument of an elemental (`f64`, `i64`, `bool`) parameter is an array; instances are
  numbered in order of first reference by an `emap` across all functions, and step 5 renumbers the
  kept ones (those an `emap` of a kept function names) densely in that order, their types numbered
  before the functions' (§3.5.1); beyond G12's argument checks it checks the call's type against
  the results (`void` for none, else each result as an array of the array arguments' rank; one type
  per instance), else `BAD_RECORD`; its capacity is `SEA_LIM_SYMBOLS` instances (`program too
  large: symbols` at the call). Code: `passes/seaexpand/seaexpand.bas`.
* **L-dm** (6c, agreed 2026-10-28) In `seacheck`'s elemental calls, an array argument of an
  elemental parameter whose element type does not convert is 201 at the argument with the
  parameter's type expected (`type mismatch: expected f64, found bool[2]`); the broadcast checks
  (202, 217) run in parameter order, the order of L19's run-time checks, while the arguments are
  still evaluated and checked in source order; an argument of the error type at an elemental
  parameter makes the call's type the error type (§2.11.2; code: `passes/seacheck/sc9call.bas`,
  `ecv`, `ebc`).
* **L-dn** (6c, agreed 2026-10-28) L19's *array argument* is an array-typed argument of a scalar
  (`bool`, `i64`, `f64`) elemental parameter; an array argument of a uniform parameter gets `lv Ai`
  like a scalar. Corrects §2.11.4, which said pass 2a allows an array only at an elemental
  parameter.
* **L-do** (6c, agreed 2026-10-28) L19's forms as built (§2.11.4; code:
  `passes/sealoop/lpbelm.bas`): the homes of all kept results are allocated first, then a
  fixed-size broadcast's extents are read from the first kept home; with no kept result and a
  fixed-size broadcast, the extents are `tmp`s of `ci` of the static extents; the `emap` of an `eval`
  (any k) becomes a new `block P n` statement, with no `xblk` of type 1; a `seq` whose value is the
  `emap` in a statement form has its `bind`s become statements, and the `seq` is dropped.
* **L-dp** (6c, agreed 2026-10-28) `ind2sub` with an array `r` (L-cl): the element body is a
  `block` of `tmp d` (r's element), `tmp g` (k's element), `tmp f = bin mod g d`, `tmp h = lib idiv
  g d`, both always computed (a discarded result's errors are raised), every node at the `lib`'s
  position, then one `est` per kept result; as a call statement (`eval`) every result is discarded
  and both are still computed (§2.11.4).
* **L-dq** (6c, agreed 2026-10-28) `sealower`'s R25 validation: an `est` of `lv Li`, Li a `.l` local
  whose type holds no counts and that the `tbind` beginning the `est`'s own block lists (L19's body
  for k ≥ 2), takes the plain `est` path; any other `est` of a marked L12 local that is not R25's
  move stays `BAD_RECORD` (§3.5.9 R25; code: `passes/sealower/sl4fix.bas` 42060–42086).
* **L-dr** (6d, agreed 2026-10-28) An empty struct or record is written `{}` (`jobj`, `jend`), and
  an array of them one `{}` per element, as LANGUAGE.md §11.4's "an empty object is `{}`" says
  (§3.5.7 step 4; test: `json_struct_empty`).
* **L-ds** (6d, agreed 2026-10-28) A fixed-size vector or matrix of structs or records is written
  like a dynamic one, by the `fore` form and the guarded `forr` form; step 4's `dyn` applies only to
  arrays of JSON scalars (L-ce). Amends §3.5.7 step 4; test: `json_fixed_structs`.
* **L-dt** (6d, agreed 2026-10-28) `write_json("", v)` reports `cannot open '': No such file or
  directory`: `JSON_OPEN`'s `open` gives `ENOENT` on both C libraries, as `make_dir("")` (L-de).
  Amends §4.8 (`JSON_OPEN`); test: `r_json_empty_path`.
* **L-du** (6d, agreed 2026-10-28) A path error is reported before a value error, and no file is
  created when either fails: `bind J1` and then `bind J2` precede `jopen` (§3.5.7 step 4, now said
  there; tests: `r_json_path_error_first`, `r_json_value_error`, `r_json_call_error`).
* **L-dv** (6d, agreed 2026-10-28) Each `jkey` node gets its own new `str` data record (rule 7's
  `la`); repeated keys share none, and a key inside a loop has one record, made per node, not per
  run (§3.6.2). Amends §2.11.5 rule 39's `jkey` row; code: `passes/sealower/sl3hirl.bas` 34830–34839.
* **L-dw** (6d, agreed 2026-10-28) `sealoop`'s validation of the `j*` records as built: a `j*` record
  only as a child of a `block`, between a `jopen` and its `jclose` in file order, no `jopen` nested
  in that span; balance per block (every `jobj`/`jarr` closed by a `jend` of the same block, a
  `jkey`'s object opened in the same block, `jclose` the block's last statement after its `jopen`);
  between `jopen` and `jclose` the statements `bind`, `tbind`, `eval`, `asg`, `tasg`, `while`,
  `break`, `cont`, `ret`, `tret`, `match` and `arm` are `BAD_RECORD`; `jopen`'s child a `str`; the
  value grammar (the order of keys and values) is not checked. Amends §2.11.4 ("write_json (6d)");
  code: `passes/sealoop/lp0main.bas` 826–987.
* **L-dx** (6d, agreed 2026-10-28) The `.j` loop locals are numbered in the file order (post-order)
  of their declaring records, so a matrix's inner `forr C` precedes its outer `forr R` (C `.j3`, R
  `.j4` in `json6_matstruct`), as the `.i` locals of §2.11 are. Amends §3.5.7 step 4 (§3.5.4).
* **L-dy** (6d, agreed 2026-10-28) `write_json(…, ref x)` is 255 naming the function, `'write_json'
  is not a ref parameter`, following 6b's `print` and `make_dir` (§2.11.2, "Library calls of phase
  6"; code: `passes/seacheck/sc9call.bas`, `lout`).
* **L-dz** (6d, agreed 2026-10-28) `seacheck`'s handle-type test (`hct`) walks each type at most once
  (a seen mark per type row), so its work list and time are linear in the number of types however
  the structs nest (the independent review's defect, an unbounded work list, fixed before commit). A
  tuple value would be 243 too, but is unreachable: `multiple-result call used as a value`
  (LANGUAGE.md §8.4) is reported first (§2.11.2; code: `passes/seacheck/sc9call.bas` 25555–25780).
* **L-ea** (6d, agreed 2026-10-28) `sealower` and the `j*` records: placement is `sealoop`'s
  validation (L-dw); `sealower` checks a `j*` record's child type (§2.11.5's validation bullet) and
  its operand count and classes against the entry's Args; no JSON entry has a result; a borrowed
  operand (an `lv`, a field loaded by `ldp`, `ldf`, `ldi` or `ldb`) is neither retained nor
  released, an owned one (L10's `xblk` under a `jvec`, a `str` temporary) is released right after
  the `rcall`. Amends §2.11.5; code: `passes/sealower/sl3hirl.bas` 34798–34932.
* **L-eb** (6d, agreed 2026-10-28) Step 4's capacity as built: its new records against
  `SEA_LIM_NODES`, its `.j` locals counted program-wide against `SEA_LIM_SYMBOLS` (a guard for
  `seaexpand`'s table of them, not a count of all the symbols, so §3.5.9's "no running count" stands
  for the total), its added types against `SEA_LIM_TYPES`. Amends §2.11.3 and §3.5.9 ("Capacity").
* **L-ec** (6d, agreed 2026-10-28) The other readings behind the `json6_*` goldens: the matrix guard
  is `if P 1` of `bin or` of two `bin eq` (`lib rows`/`cols` of a fresh `lv J2`, `ci 0`), its
  branches `block`s, each range `rng P i64[] 0 0` from `ci 0` to `lib rows`/`cols`, the element `idx
  P S 2` of `lv J2`, `lv R`, `lv C`; a type step 4 adds (`i64[]`, the dynamic type of a `dyn`) is
